en: The Abhidharma-saṃgīti-paryāya-pāda-śāstra, Fascicle One.
Spoken by the Venerable Śāriputra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
Chapter One: On Dependent Origination. At one time, the Blessed One was traveling among the Mallas and arrived at the town of Pāvā, where he stayed in the Cāpāla Grove.

At that time, the multitude of Mallas from that town had constructed a pavilion at the site of the ancient shrine of Uvavanaka, located between the villages of East and West where they regularly gathered for recreation; it was newly completed and adorned, yet had not yet been occupied by any śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or Mallas.

When the multitude of Mallas heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, together with the community of bhikṣus, was staying in a nearby forest, they congratulated one another and deliberated together, saying:

"Our magnificent palaces and pavilions should first be offered as a dwelling for the Buddha and the bhikṣu-saṃgha, the unsurpassed field of merit; thereafter, we shall enjoy within them the wealth and resources obtained through our superior wholesome karma."
"By this, we have obtained benefit and happiness throughout the long night; how excellent this is!
Having deliberated thus, the multitude of Mallas each gathered their followers and kinsmen, departed from the village of Pāvā, and proceeded to where the Tathāgata was.
Having arrived, they prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit at one side.

Then the Bhagavān, with a voice of loving gentleness, greeted the Mallas and their retinue; he further instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them by means of various subtle and wondrous Dharma-gates. Having spoken these words, he remained silent.

When the Mallas heard what the Buddha had said, they were filled with joy and leaped for gladness; immediately rising from their seats, they joined their palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha together, saying:

“The multitude of Mallas in this our town have, at the ancient shrine of Uvavanaka between the villages of Hastigāma and Pūtigāma—a place where people often gather to play—jointly constructed a pavilion. It has been newly completed and beautifully adorned, yet no śramaṇas, brahmins, or other Mallas have ever yet made use of it.”
"We only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and dwell among us with his disciples, so that we may enjoy benefit and peace for a long night.

At that time, out of compassion for them, the Tathāgata took his disciples and went to reside there; furthermore, with a wondrous voice, he proclaimed to the Mallas the various distinctions regarding the fruits of giving.

The exchange of questions and answers continued until the first watch of the night had passed; having heard the Dharma, the Mallas and their retinues departed with joy after paying homage to the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
"I now have a backache; I shall rest for a while."
“You should act on my behalf and proclaim the essential points of the Dharma to the community of bhikṣus; do not let the time pass in vain.
At that time, Śāriputra silently accepted the instruction.

The Buddha then folded his *uttarāsaṅga* robe four times to spread it out as a bed, used his great outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) as a pillow, and lay down on his right side with his body straight and feet叠叠 (one upon the other). With proper mental attention, he dwelt in the perception of light and the thought of rising, possessing mindfulness and clear comprehension, as motionless and serene as a great mountain of jewels.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the assembly of bhikṣus, saying:

"This son of the Nirgranthas from the village of Pāvā, while amidst a crowd of the shameless, styled himself a teacher. Not more than ten days have passed since his death, yet his disciples have formed pairs of factions, engaging in constant disputes and mutual disparagement. Each claims, 'I understand the doctrine and discipline, not others; as I know it, this is the Dharma and this is the Vinaya;
what I speak is logical and conforms to proper conduct; you all are entirely excluded from this.'"

Regarding the teachings of their masters, each followed their own attachments, rearranging the sequence, omitting or adding elements, and fragmenting them through analysis until they became numerous schools.

Desiring to determine superiority or inferiority, they engaged in heated debates; seeking to escape the difficulty of refutation, they mutually slandered one another. Though they possessed words of debate, they lacked the path of debate; with mouths spewing swords and spears, they sought to harm one another.
“Those laypeople who have faith in his doctrine, seeing his disciples quarreling in such a manner, all together become resentful and disdainful, reviling him and abandoning him.
Then Śāriputra again addressed the assembly, saying:

“The doctrine and discipline of the son of the Nigaṇṭhas in this village of Pāvā are poorly expounded and poorly received; they do not lead to liberation, nor do they tend toward perfect awakening. They are a destructible dharma, devoid of a goal and lacking a refuge.”

The Dharma and Vinaya of our Teacher, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, are well-expounded and well-received; they lead to eternal transcendence and to perfect enlightenment, being indestructible dharmas that possess a destination and a support.

We should now hear the Buddha while he remains in the world so that we may harmoniously compile the Dharma and Vinaya, lest there be any discord among the World-Honored One’s disciples after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa. We shall ensure that the discipline and law of the holy life endure for a long time, bringing benefit, peace, and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, out of compassion for the multitudes of devas and humans in the world, so that they may attain supreme benefit, welfare, and bliss.
2. Chapter on the Single Dharma. *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* (Saṃgītiparyāya), Chapter Two: The Chapter on the Single Dharma. At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the assembly, saying:
"Venerable sirs, you should know that there is one dharma which the Buddha, having himself thoroughly mastered and realized through perfect awakening, has proclaimed and revealed to his disciples."

"We should now assemble in harmony to hold a council; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, let there be no discord or dispute. We must ensure that the Dharma and Vinaya, which accord with the holy life, endure for a long time, bringing benefit and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, and out of compassion for the world of gods and humans, enabling them to attain supreme benefit, welfare, and peace."
"What is the one dharma?
The summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
The one dharma refers to sentient beings; they abide dependent upon nutriment and dependent upon conduct."
Among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is supreme.
All sentient beings subsist upon food; all sentient beings subsist upon volitional formations. Among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is preeminent—this is called the one dharma.
Regarding the statement that "all sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment," what is this nutriment such that it is said all sentient beings subsist by means of it?
As the Blessed One said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that there are four kinds of nutriment which enable corporeal sentient beings to remain stable, and which provide sustenance for those seeking birth."
What are the four nutriments?
First is edible food, whether coarse or subtle; second is the nutriment of contact; [third is the nutriment of mental volition;
fourth is the nutriment of consciousness].
Third is the nutriment of mental volition;
fourth is the nutriment of consciousness.
By means of these four nutriments, it is said that all sentient beings subsist by depending on food.
For what reason is it known that all classes of sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment?

It is because, within their respective aggregates, due to the cause of these nutriments not yet being exhausted, there arise the various distinctions of perception, designation, convention, speech, vitality, abiding, preservation, and sustenance.

If, among various groups of sentient beings, due to these various foods having been exhausted as the cause, there arise the designations, conceptualizations, and verbal expressions of "death," "passing away," "perishing," and "departing" in their various forms.
From this, it is known that all classes of sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment.
Question:
Regarding these four nutriments, should they be said to be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
Answer: It should be said that they are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Question:
Regarding these four kinds of nutriment, should they be said to be permanent or impermanent?
Answer: They should be said to be impermanent.
Question:
Regarding these four kinds of nutriment, should they be said to be constant or should they be said to be non-constant?
Answer:
One should say they are not constant.
Question:
Regarding these four kinds of nutriment, should they be said to be subject to transformation or not subject to transformation?
Answer:
One should say it is "transformation.
Question:
Regarding these four nutriments, should they be said to be dependently arisen or not dependently arisen?
Answer: They should be said to be dependently arisen.
Question:
Regarding these four nutriments, should they be said to be comprised within the category of name (*nāma*) or the category of form (*rūpa*)?
Answer:
Edible food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra) should be said to be comprised within form (rūpa); the other three foods should be said to be comprised within name (nāma).
Question:
Regarding these four foods, should they be said to be visible (sanidarśana) or invisible (anidarśana)?
Answer: It should be said that there is no seeing.
Question:
Regarding these four kinds of nutriment, should they be said to be with resistance (*sapratigha*) or without resistance (*apratigha*)?
Answer: It should be said that edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) is with resistance; the other three nutriments should be said to be without resistance.
Question:
Regarding these four nutriments, should they be said to be mind, or should they be said not to be mind?
Should they be said to be mental factors, or should they be said not to be mental factors?
Should it be said that it is associated with the mind, or should it be said that it is dissociated from the mind?
Answer:
It should be said that edible food is neither mind, nor mental factors, nor dissociated from the mind.
The nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*) and the nutriment of mental volition (*manosaṃcetanāhāra*) should be said to be mental factors (*caitasika*) associated with the mind;
the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) should be said to be the mind alone.
Question:
Regarding these four kinds of nutriment, should they be described as wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?
Answer:
Edible food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra) should be described as indeterminate; the remaining three nutriments should be described as either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is the nutriment of wholesome contact?
Answer:

If wholesome, out-flowing contact serves as a condition, it can cause the sense faculties to grow and the primary elements to increase; furthermore, it moistens and thoroughly moistens, satisfies and thoroughly satisfies, protects and thoroughly protects, transforms and thoroughly transforms, and sustains and thoroughly sustains. This is called the nutriment of wholesome contact.
What is the nutriment of unwholesome contact?
Answer:

If unwholesome contact serves as a condition, it can cause the sense faculties to grow and the primary elements to increase; furthermore, it can moisten, further moisten, and even sustain and further sustain them. This is called the nutriment of unwholesome contact.
What is the nutriment of contact that is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?

Answer: If indeterminate contact serves as a condition, it can cause the sense faculties to grow and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) to increase; furthermore, it can moisten, continue to moisten, and so forth, up to sustaining and continuing to sustain. This is called the nutriment of contact that is indeterminate.
What is the mental nutriment of volition (*manosaṃcetanāhāra*) that is wholesome?
Answer:

It refers to those volitions (*cetanā*) associated with wholesome, out-flowing contact (*sāsrava-sparśa*), including various types of volition—volition as it manifests, volition as already performed—which constitute the mental and volitional karma of the mind. This is called the wholesome mental nutriment of volition.
What is the nutriment of mental volition that is unwholesome?
Answer:
Whatever volitions, such as equal volitions, up to mental karma, are associated with unwholesome contact—this is called the unwholesome nutriment of mental volition.
What is the indeterminate mental nutriment of volition?
Answer:
It refers to all volitions, equal volitions, and even mental actions associated with indeterminate contact; this is called the indeterminate mental nutriment of volition.
What is the nutriment of wholesome consciousness?
Answer:
Those minds, mentations, and consciousnesses that are associated with wholesome, out-flowing volition (cetanā)—this is called the nutriment of wholesome consciousness.
What is the nutriment of unwholesome consciousness?
Answer:
Those minds, mentations, and consciousnesses that are associated with unwholesome volition; these are called the nutriment of unwholesome consciousness.
What is the indeterminate nutriment of consciousness?
Answer:
Those minds, mentals, and consciousnesses associated with indeterminate volition are called the indeterminate nutriment of consciousness.
Question:
Regarding these four nutriments, should they be said to be with-outflows (sāsrava) or without-outflows (anāsrava)?
Answer:
One should say they are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Question:

Regarding these four nutriments (*āhāra*), should they be said to belong to those in training (*śaikṣa*), to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), or to those who are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*)?
Answer: It should be said that it is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Question:
Regarding these four nutriments, should they be said to belong to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm?
Answer:
Edible food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra) should be said to belong to the desire realm; the other three nutriments should be said to belong either to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.
Question:
Are all forms of nutriment *kavaḍīkāra-āhāra* (edible food)?
Answer:
All types of edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) are indeed food; however, there is that which is food but not edible food, namely the other three types of nutriment and the mundane [nutriment].
Question:
Are all types of nutriment contact-nutriment (*sparśa-āhāra*)?
Answer:
All *āhāra* (nutriments) are indeed food; however, there are those that are food but not *sparśa-āhāra* (contact-nutriments), namely the other three nutriments and the mundane (*laukika*).
Question:
Are all nutriments mental volition-nutriment?
Answer:
All mental volition-nutriments are indeed nutriments; however, there are nutriments that are not mental volition-nutriment, namely the other three nutriments and the mundane [nutriment].
Question:
Are all nutriments (āhāra) nutriment as consciousness (vijñānāhāra)?
Answer:
All consciousness-foods (*vijñānāhāra*) are indeed food; however, there are things that are food but are not consciousness-food, namely the other three foods and the mundane (*laukika*).
Question:
Are all edible morsels (*kavaḍīkāra*) food?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

There is that which is a morsel (*kavaḍīkāra*) but not nutriment: namely, when a morsel serves as a condition for the deterioration of the sense faculties and the transformation of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
There are those which are nutriment but not edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*); namely, the other three nutriments and worldly [existence].

There are those which are both edible food and nutriment; namely, when edible food serves as a condition for the nourishment of the sense faculties, the increase of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and furthermore, for their moistening, subsequent moistening, up to their sustaining and subsequent sustaining.
There is that which is neither *kavaḍīkāra* nor nutriment, namely, excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Question:
Are all contacts (*sparśa*) nutriments?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

There is that which is contact but not nutriment; namely, when untainted contact (*anāsrava-sparśa*) or tainted contact (*sāsrava-sparśa*) serves as a condition for the impairment of the sense faculties and the deterioration of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
There is that which is nutriment but not contact; this refers to the other three nutriments as well as mundane [contact].

There is that which is both contact and nutriment; this refers to tainted contact acting as a condition for the nourishment of the sense faculties and the increase of the primary elements, as well as for moistening, further moistening, up to supporting and further supporting.
There is that which is neither contact nor nutriment; this refers to everything except the aforementioned characteristics.
Just as there are four propositions regarding the nutriment of contact, it should be understood that the same applies to the nutriments of mental volition and consciousness.
Is there any case where nutriment serves as a condition to produce nutriment, to produce non-nutriment, or to produce both nutriment and non-nutriment?
Answer:
It arises.
How does nutriment arise with nutriment as its condition?
Answer:
With edible food as a condition, the other three types of nutriment arise.
How is it that nutriment serves as a condition for the arising of non-nutriment?
Answer:
With edible food as a condition, feeling, perception, attention, and so forth arise.
How is it that with food as a condition, both food and non-food arise?
Answer:
With edible food as a condition, the other three types of nutriment, as well as feeling, perception, and attention, arise.

Is it possible for that which is not nutriment to arise with that which is not nutriment as a condition, or for that which is not nutriment to arise with nutriment as a condition, or for that which is both nutriment and non-nutriment to arise [with nutriment as a condition]?
Answer:
It arises.
How does that which is not nutriment arise with that which is not nutriment as its condition?
Answer:
Just as the eye and visible forms serve as conditions for the arising of feeling, perception, attention, and so forth,
how can that which is not nutriment serve as a condition for the arising of nutriment?
Answer:
For example, with the eye and visible forms as conditions, there arise the nutriment of contact, the nutriment of mental volition, and the nutriment of consciousness.
How is it that non-nutriment arises as a condition for both nutriment and non-nutriment?
Answer:
Just as with the eye and visible forms acting as conditions to produce the nutriments of contact, mental volition, and consciousness, as well as feeling, perception, and attention—
could there be cases where that which is both nutriment and non-nutriment acts as a condition to produce both nutriment and non-nutriment, or produces nutriment, or produces non-nutriment?
Answer:
It arises.
How do nutriment and non-nutriment arise with nutriment and non-nutriment as conditions?
Answer:

Just as, with the eye and visible forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises, giving rise to contact, mental volition, the nutriment of consciousness, as well as feeling, perception, attention, and so forth.
How do nutriment and non-nutriment serve as conditions for the arising of nutriment?
Answer:
Just as the eye and visible forms, with eye-consciousness as a condition, give rise to the nutriments of contact, mental volition, and consciousness.
How do nutriment and non-nutriment serve as conditions for the arising of non-nutriment?
Answer:
Just as the eye, visible forms, and eye-consciousness serve as conditions for the arising of feeling, perception, and attention.
Question:
If edible food has already been abandoned and fully understood, is the same true for contact-food?
Answer:
If the nutriment of contact has been abandoned and fully understood, the nutriment of physical food is likewise so.

However, there are cases where the nutriment of physical food has been abandoned and fully understood, but the nutriment of contact has not; this refers to one who is already free from the defilement of desire but not yet free from the defilements of the higher realms.

Just as it is with edible food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra) in relation to contact-food (sparśa-āhāra), so it is in relation to mental volition-food (manosañcetanā-āhāra) and consciousness-food (vijñāna-āhāra).
Question:
If contact-food has been abandoned and fully understood, is mental volition-food also [abandoned and fully understood] in the same way?
Answer: It is so.
Just as with the nutriment of contact in relation to the nutriment of mental volition, it is likewise in relation to the nutriment of consciousness.
Question:
If the food of mental volition has been abandoned and fully understood, is the same true for the food of consciousness?
Answer:
Thus it is.
Question:
If one has already abandoned and fully understood nutriment, has one already become detached from the realms of desire, form, and formlessness?
Answer:

If one has abandoned and fully understood edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), one has become free from passion regarding the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), but not regarding the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*).
If one has abandoned and fully understood the remaining three types of nutriment, one has become free from passion regarding the desire, form, and formless realms alike.
At that time, because one has already become free from defilement regarding all things, in every respect, in every mode, in every stage, in every location, and in regard to all fetters.
Regarding the statement that "all sentient beings abide dependent upon formations (*saṃskāra*)," what are these formations, such that it is said that all sentient beings abide dependent upon them?
As the Blessed One said:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that if sentient beings, in this or that assembly, do not die, do not perish, are not destroyed, do not vanish, do not lose [their state], and do not fall back, it is entirely due to their abiding by means of life-span (*āyus*) and the continuity of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)."
This life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is called "conditioned formations" (*saṃskāra*); by means of these formations, all sentient beings are sustained, preserved, and kept alive.
These formations protect and guard them, and they turn and follow along with them; for this reason, it is said that all sentient beings abide in dependence upon formations.
For what reason is it known that all classes of sentient beings subsist by depending on formations (*saṃskāra*)?

It is because, within their respective aggregates, sentient beings—due to the cause of these life-formations (*jīvitasaṃskāra*) not yet having been exhausted—proceed with the distinctions of perception, designation, conventional expression, vitality, subsistence, and survival.

If, among various classes of sentient beings, there occurs a distinction—such as perception, designation, conventional expression, death, passing away, or demise—due to the exhaustion of the life-force (*āyus-saṃskāra*) therein.
From this, it is known that all classes of sentient beings subsist and abide by means of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
Question:
Should such life-formations (*āyusaṃskāra*) be described as conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
Answer: It should be said that they are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Question:
Regarding such life-force (āyus-saṃskāra), should it be said to be permanent or impermanent?
Answer: It should be said to be impermanent.
Question:
Regarding such life-force formations (*āyus-saṃskāra*), should they be said to be constant or should they be said to be non-constant?
Answer:
One should say it is not constant.
Question:
Regarding such life-formations (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*), should they be said to be subject to transformation or not subject to transformation?
Answer: It should be said that it undergoes transformation.
Question:
Regarding such formations of life-force (*āyus-saṃskāra*), should they be said to be dependently arisen (*pratītyasamutpanna*) or not dependently arisen?
Answer: They should be said to be dependently arisen.
Question:
Regarding such life-force formations (āyuḥ-saṃskāra), should they be said to be comprised within the mental (nāma) or within the material (rūpa)?
Answer:
It should be said that they are subsumed under "name" (nāma).
Question:
Regarding such life-force formations (jīvitasaṃskāra), should they be said to be visible (sanidarśana) or invisible (anidarśana)?
Answer: It should be said that there is no seeing.
Question:
Regarding such life-constituents (*āyus-saṃskāra*), should they be said to be resistant (*sapratigha*) or non-resistant (*apratigha*)?
Answer: They should be said to be non-resistant.
Question:
Regarding such life-force formations (*āyus-saṃskāra*), should they be said to be mind (*citta*) or not mind?
Should they be said to be mental factors (*caitasika*) or not mental factors?
Should it be said that it is associated with the mind, or should it be said that it is dissociated from the mind?
Answer:
It should be said that it is neither mind, nor mental factors, nor dissociated from the mind.
Question:
Regarding such life-force formations (*āyus-saṃskāra*), should they be described as wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral?
Answer:
It should be said that they are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Question:
Regarding these life-formations (*āyusaṃskāra*), should they be said to be with-outflows (*sāsrava*) or without-outflows (*anāsrava*)?
Answer: It should be said that they are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Question:
Regarding such life-force formations (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*), should they be called "in training" (*śaikṣa*), "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*), or "neither in training nor beyond training"?
Answer: They should be called neither in training nor beyond training.
Question:

Regarding these life-formations (*āyus-saṃskāra*), should they be said to belong to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
Answer:
One should say that it is either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm.
What is bound to the desire realm?
Answer:
Regarding the lifespan of the desire realm:
how is it bound to the form realm?
Answer:
Regarding the lifespan of the form realm:
how is it bound to the formless realm?
Answer:
The lifespan of the formless realm.
Question:
If the lifespan of the desire realm has been severed and fully understood, is the lifespan of the form realm likewise?
Answer:
If the life-span of the form realm has been severed and fully understood, the life-span of the desire realm is likewise so.

There are cases where the life-span of the desire realm has been severed and fully understood, but that of the form realm has not; this refers to one who has already abandoned the defilements of desire but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm.
Question:
If the life-span of the desire realm has been severed and fully understood, is the same true for the life-span of the formless realm?
Answer:
If the life-span of the formless realm has been severed and fully understood, the life-span of the desire realm is likewise so.

There are cases where the life-span of the desire realm has been severed and fully understood, but not that of the formless realm; this refers to one who has already abandoned the defilements of desire but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the formless realm.
Question:
If the life-span of the form realm has been abandoned and fully understood, is the same true for the life-span of the formless realm?
Answer:
If the life-span of the formless realm has been severed and fully understood, the life-span of the form realm is likewise so.

Or, the life-span of the form realm has been severed and fully understood, but not that of the formless realm; this refers to one who has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm but has not yet become detached from the defilements of the formless realm.
Question:
If one has already abandoned and fully understood the formations of vitality (*āyusaṃskāra*), has that person already become free from passion regarding the desire, form, and formless realms?
Answer:
If one has already severed and fully understood the formations of life within the desire realm, one is already detached from the desire realm, but not from the form or formless realms.
If one has already severed and fully understood the formations of life within the form realm, one is already detached from both the desire and form realms, but not from the formless realm.

If one has already severed and fully understood the life-force formations (*āyus-saṃskāra*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), that person has become detached from the realms of desire, form, and the formless.
At that time, because they have become detached from all things, in every respect, in every way, in every stage, in every location, and regarding all fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Regarding the preeminence of heedfulness (*apramāda*) toward all wholesome phenomena (*kuśaladharma*), what is meant by heedfulness?
Answer:

To sever unwholesome phenomena and to bring wholesome phenomena to fulfillment, one constantly practices and cultivates them, acting with firmness and constancy, repeatedly cultivating them without ceasing; this is called heedfulness.
3. Chapter on the Two Dharmas, Part One. From the *Saṃgītiparyāya-pāda-śāstra*, Chapter Three, Part One, on the Two Dharmas. At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the assembly, saying:
"Venerable ones, you should know."
The Buddha has personally and thoroughly mastered these two dharmas; having manifested full awakening, he has proclaimed and revealed them to his disciples.

We should now assemble in harmony to compile them, so that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa there may be no discord or dispute. We must ensure that the holy life and the Dharma-Vinaya endure for a long time, bringing benefit and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings and showing compassion for all the devas and humans in the world.
"May they obtain supreme benefit, welfare, and happiness.
What are these two dharmas?
The summary verse (uddāna) says:
The two dharmas refer to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), continuing thus until the exhaustion of suffering and non-arising;
in total there are twenty-seven sections, which should be explained individually in their proper order.
There are two dharmas: namely, name and form.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas, namely ignorance and craving for existence.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas, namely the view of existence and the view of non-existence.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas, namely lack of shame and lack of remorse.
Furthermore, there are two qualities: namely, shame and dread of blame.
Furthermore, there are two qualities: namely, harsh speech and evil friends.
Furthermore, there are two qualities: namely, gentle speech and virtuous friends.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas: namely, skillfulness in entering into offenses and skillfulness in emerging from offenses.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas: namely, skillfulness in entering meditative concentration and skillfulness in emerging from meditative concentration.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas: namely, skillfulness regarding the elements (*dhātu-kauśalya*) and skillfulness regarding mental attention (*manasikāra-kauśalya*).
Again, there are two dharmas: namely, straightforwardness and gentleness.
Again, there are two dharmas: namely, forbearance and being pleasant to dwell with.
Furthermore, there are two qualities: namely, harmony and compliance, and making offerings.
Furthermore, there are two qualities: namely, mindfulness and clear comprehension.
Furthermore, there are two qualities: namely, the power of discernment and the power of cultivation.
Furthermore, there are two things: namely, not guarding the doors of the sense faculties and not knowing moderation in eating.
Furthermore, there are two things: namely, being able to guard the doors of the sense faculties and knowing moderation in eating.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas: namely, deficiency in ethical discipline and deficiency in view.
Again, there are two dharmas: namely, violation of ethical discipline and violation of view.
Again, there are two dharmas: namely, perfection of ethical discipline and perfection of view.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas: namely, pure ethical discipline and pure view.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas: namely, vision and excellence in accordance with reality.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas: namely, disenchantment and excellence in accordance with reality.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas: namely, being insatiable regarding the wholesome and not obstructing the abandonment [of afflictions].
Furthermore, there are two dharmas: namely, śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas, namely: illumination and liberation.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas, namely: the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
Within this context, regarding the two dharmas called name and form, what is "name"?
Answer:

The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, the aggregate of consciousness, as well as space, cessation through deliberation, and cessation not through deliberation—these are called "name.
What is "form"?
Answer:
The four great elements and the matter derived from them are called "form.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas, namely ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*). What is ignorance?
Answer:
As stated in the *Dharmaskandha-śāstra*:
"What is craving for existence (*bhavarāga*)?"
Answer:

The various forms of craving and pervasive craving for the realms of form and formlessness—the grasping, hoarding, guarding, and relishing of attachment—this is called "craving for existence" (*bhavarāga*).
Furthermore, there are two views: the view of existence (*bhavadiṣṭi*) and the view of non-existence (*vibhavadiṣṭi*). What is the view of existence?
Answer:
If one asserts that the self and the world are eternal, and based on this gives rise to acceptance, delight, and speculative views, this is called the view of existence (*astidṛṣṭi*).
What is the view of non-existence (*nāstidṛṣṭi*)?
Answer:

If one asserts that the self and the world are annihilated, and based on this gives rise to a view characterized by patient acceptance and contemplation, this is called the view of non-existence (*vibhava-dṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, there are two other dharmas, namely lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*). What is meant by lack of shame?
Answer:
As the Blessed One has said, there are those who lack a sense of shame (*ahrīka*), who do not feel shame regarding things that ought to evoke shame.

"Things that ought to evoke shame" refers to all evil and unwholesome states (*akuśala-dharma*) that conduce to defilement (*saṃkleśa*), conduce to future existence (*punarbhava*), result in the maturation of burning suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death.

When such evil and unwholesome states arise within him, he is without shame (*ahrī*), without a sense of shame (*anapatrāpya*), and without distinct shame; without modesty (*avatrāpya*), without a sense of modesty (*anavatrāpya*), and without distinct modesty; without reverence (*gaurava*), without a sense of reverence, without submissiveness (*vaśavartitā*), and without a sense of submissiveness; and he acts without fear toward those who are powerful. This is called "shamelessness" (*ahrī*).
What is lack of shame (*āhrīkya*)?
Answer:
As the Blessed One has said, one who lacks shame does not feel shame regarding those things for which one ought to feel shame.
That which is shameful by nature refers to all evil and unwholesome phenomena, up to and including those that lead to future birth, aging, and death.

When such evil and unwholesome phenomena arise, one feels no shame, has nothing for which to feel shame, and no distinct sense of shame; one feels no modesty, has nothing for which to feel modesty, and no distinct sense of modesty; one does not dread or fear these transgressions, nor does one perceive them as fearful—this is called a lack of shame (*ahrīkya*).
Furthermore, there are two qualities, namely, shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*). What is shame?
The answer is:
as the Blessed One has said, those who possess shame feel shame regarding things that should inspire shame.
The phenomena that inspire shame (*hrī*) refer to all evil and unwholesome phenomena, up to and including those conducive to future birth, aging, and death.

When such evil and unwholesome phenomena arise, there is shame, there is that which is shameful, and there is distinct shame; there is modesty, there is that which is modest, and there is distinct modesty; there is reverence, there is that which is revered, and there is distinct reverence; there is subordination, there is that to which one is subordinate, and there is the arising of fear toward the Sovereign One. This is called shame.
What is shame (*hrī*)?
Answer:
As the Blessed One has said, those who possess shame feel shame regarding things that are shameful.
The dharma that is shameful refers to all evil and unwholesome dharmas, up to those that lead to future birth, old age, and death.

When such evil and unwholesome dharmas arise, one feels shame, has a sense of shame, and possesses distinct shame; one feels modesty, has a sense of modesty, and possesses distinct modesty; one feels dread and fear toward various transgressions, and is able to perceive that dread and fear—this is called shame (*hrī*).
Furthermore, there are two factors: namely, harsh speech and evil companions. What is meant by harsh speech?
Answer:
As explained in the *Dharmaskandha-śāstra*.
What is a bad friend?
Answer:
It is also as explained in the *Dharmaskandha-śāstra*.
Furthermore, there are two things: namely, well-spoken words and virtuous friends. What are well-spoken words?
Answer:

Suppose there is a certain person who is addressed by someone in accordance with the Dharma—whether it be their preceptor (*upādhyāya*), one who shares a preceptor, their instructor (*ācārya*), one who shares an instructor, or any other respected and trustworthy friend with whom they associate. [That person] says to them:

“From this day forward, do not corrupt your physical actions, do not corrupt your verbal actions, and do not corrupt your mental actions; do not engage in improper conduct, do not associate with evil friends, and do not perform deeds that lead to the three evil realms.”

Thus, this instruction is in accordance with the Dharma and timely; it accords with the path to be cultivated, polishing and refining it, increasing its adornment, and being suitable, constant, and deliberate.

Regarding this instruction, the companions and provisions respond with joy, affection, and delight, accepting and following it. They do not take it to the left but take it to the right; they do not reject, oppose, disparage, or deny it. This is called "well-spoken words."
What is a virtuous friend?
Answer:
As it is stated in the *Dharmaskandha-śāstra*.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas: namely, skillfulness regarding the entry into offenses and skillfulness regarding the emergence from offenses.
What is meant by skillfulness regarding the entry into offenses?
Answer:
"Offenses" refers to the offenses of the five classes consisting of the five aggregates. What are these five?
First, the defeat (pārājika);...
Second, the remainder of the assembly;
third, the offense involving boiling;
fourth, the confession before another individual.
Fifth is *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).

Skillfulness regarding the entry into offenses means knowing and seeing things as they truly are: namely, that such a bhikṣu has committed a *pārājika* offense; such a bhikṣu has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; such a bhikṣu has committed a *pāyattika* offense; such a bhikṣu has committed a *pratideśanīya* offense; and such a bhikṣu has committed a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Furthermore, knowing and seeing things as they truly are: such a bhikṣu commits an offense leading to defeat (pārājika); such a bhikṣu commits an offense leading to communal confession (saṃghāvaśeṣa); such a bhikṣu commits an offense leading to falling into [the hot hells] (sthūlātyaya/pāyattika); such a bhikṣu commits an offense requiring confession before another (prādeśika/pratideśanīya); and such a bhikṣu commits an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).

Furthermore, one knows and sees things as they truly are: "This bhikṣu has committed such-and-such a pārājika offense; this bhikṣu has committed such-and-such a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense; this bhikṣu has committed such-and-such a pāyattika offense; this bhikṣu has committed such-and-such a pratideśanīya offense; this bhikṣu has committed such-and-such a duṣkṛta offense."

Furthermore, one knows and sees things as they truly are: "This bhikṣu has committed an offense leading to defeat (pārājika) such as this; this bhikṣu has committed an offense leading to formal meeting with the community (saṃghāvaśeṣa) such as this; this bhikṣu has committed an offense leading to falling into the cauldron (sthūlātyaya/pātayantika) such as this; this bhikṣu has committed an offense requiring confession before another (pratideśanīya) such as this; this bhikṣu has committed an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta) such as this."

Furthermore, knowing and seeing things as they truly are: regarding the offenses committed by bhikṣus—whether grave or light, deep or shallow, with remainder or without remainder, concealed or unconcealed, manifest or unmanifest, confessed or unconfessed, eliminated or not eliminated, expressible or inexpressible, permissible or impermissible—they understand, comprehend, closely examine, and fully investigate these various types of offenses. Possessing keen intelligence, penetration, discernment, and sagacity; with awakened clarity and the practice of wisdom (*vipaśyanā*), this is called skillfulness regarding the entry into offenses.
What is skillfulness regarding the expiation of offenses?
Answer:
"Offenses" refers to the offenses of the five classes within the five aggregates, as previously explained.

Skillfulness regarding offenses refers to knowing and seeing, as they truly are, the four types of offenses: those involving a formal assembly (saṃghāvaśeṣa), those involving falling into boiling [hell] (pārājika), those requiring confession before another person (pratideśanīya), and those involving remorse (duṣkṛta).
How is it that these matters may be remedied?
As it is said: "I have spoken thus and manifested thus; regarding such an offense, I have neither spoken nor manifested it.
I have spoken thus and manifested thus; regarding such an offense, I have indeed spoken and manifested it."
"Although I have thus manifested, thus confessed, and thus performed the ritual act, this offense has not been confessed nor has it been eliminated.
Yet, through such manifestation, such confession, and such performance of the ritual act, this offense is indeed confessed and indeed eliminated."
To understand these various ways of emerging from transgressions, up to and including *vipaśyanā*, is called skillfulness regarding the emergence from transgressions.
*Abhidharma-sangīti-paryāya-pāda-śāstra*, Volume One.
*Abhidharma-sangīti-paryāya-pāda-śāstra*, Volume Two.
Spoken by the Venerable Śāriputra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Three, Part Two: The Two Dharmas. Furthermore, there are two dharmas, namely: skillfulness in entering meditative absorption and skillfulness in emerging from meditative absorption. What is meant by skillfulness in entering meditative absorption?
Answer:
Concentration refers to the concentration of eight classes and eight aggregates, namely the four dhyānas and the four formless absorptions.

Skillfulness in entering concentration means knowing and seeing, as they truly are, that such a person enters the first dhyāna, and that such a person enters the concentrations up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Furthermore, one knows and sees such a person as being skilled in the mental application (*manasikāra*) regarding the first dhyāna concentration, and likewise skilled in the mental application regarding the concentrations up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Furthermore, one knows and sees as it truly is that such a person enters the path of the first dhyāna, and likewise that such a person enters the paths up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Furthermore, one knows and sees such a person as follows: they possess skillful attention regarding the path for entering the first dhyāna, and likewise possess skillful attention regarding the paths for entering all stages up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
What is that matter? It is as some say:

"I direct my attention in this way, I direct my attention in that way; regarding the entry into the first dhyāna concentration up to the entry into the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, I have well-evaluated it, well-investigated it, well-discriminated it, well-pondered it, and well-penetrated it."

With such a thought, such an observation, such a resolute conviction, such a sustained application, and such a discrimination, I have well equanimously balanced and even thoroughly realized the entry into the first dhyāna concentration up to the entry into the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

In this way, by collecting the mind, exerting the mind, subduing the mind, maintaining the mind, uplifting the mind, relinquishing the mind, restraining the mind, and releasing the mind, I have well equanimously discerned and even well thoroughly penetrated the entry into the first dhyāna concentration up to the entry into the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Regarding these qualities of mine concerning meditative absorption and skill in absorption, they are without function, without benefit, and of little utility, serving only as obstacles; I have thoroughly equanimously evaluated them, up to and including their thorough penetration.

Regarding these dharmas of mine, which pertain to entering meditative absorption and skillfulness in absorption, they are functional, beneficial, and productive of much; they do not constitute an obstacle, for I have thoroughly equanimously evaluated them, up to and including having thoroughly mastered them.

Within such entry into various meditative absorptions, one understands, comprehends, closely examines, and pervasively discerns; with mental agility, penetration, investigation, and sagacity, one practices vipaśyanā through the clear realization of awakening and wisdom—this is called skillfulness in entering meditative absorption.
What is skillfulness regarding emergence from meditative absorption?
Answer:
Absorption refers to the eightfold collection of aggregates of absorption, namely the four dhyānas and the four formless absorptions.

Skillfulness in emerging from meditative absorption refers to knowing and seeing, as they truly are, that such a person emerges from the first dhyāna absorption, and that such a person likewise emerges from all absorptions up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Furthermore, one knows and sees as it truly is that such a person possesses skillful attention upon emerging from the first dhyāna, and likewise that such a person possesses skillful attention up until emerging from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Furthermore, one knows and sees according to reality that such a person emerges from the path of the first dhyāna, and likewise that such a person emerges from the paths up to and including the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Furthermore, one knows and sees as it truly is that such a person possesses skillful attention regarding the path of emerging from the first dhyāna, and likewise possesses skillful attention regarding the paths of emerging from all stages up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
What is this matter? It is as some say:

"I have directed my attention in this way, I have directed my attention in that way; in emerging from the first dhyāna up to emerging from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, I have well-equanimated, well-attended to, well-discriminated, well-reflected upon, and well-penetrated."

With such a conception, such an observation, such a resolute conviction, such a sustained application, and such a discrimination, I have well equanimously discerned and even well penetrated the emergence from the first dhyāna up to the emergence from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

In this way, by concentrating the mind, exerting the mind, subduing the mind, maintaining the mind, uplifting the mind, relinquishing the mind, restraining the mind, and releasing the mind, I have become well-equanimous and even well-penetrated regarding the emergence from the first dhyāna up to the emergence from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Regarding these dharmas of mine, from the time of emerging from meditative absorption until the skillfulness of emerging from it, they are without function, without benefit, and do not accomplish much, but are merely obstacles; I have correctly equanimated these dharmas and even thoroughly mastered them.

Regarding these dharmas of mine, from the act of emerging from meditative absorption up to skillfulness in emerging from it, they possess function, benefit, and much that is accomplished without obstruction; I have correctly equanimously understood these dharmas and even fully mastered them.
Within such emergence from various meditative absorptions, the thorough understanding up to and including *vipaśyanā* is called skill in emerging from concentration.
Furthermore, there are two other factors: skill in the elements (*dhātu*) and skill in mental attention (*manasikāra*). What is meant by skill in the elements?
Answer:

It is as when a bhikṣu knows and sees the eighteen elements as they truly are—namely, the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element; the nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element; the body element, the tangible-object element, and the body-consciousness element; and the mind element, the mental-phenomena element, and the mind-consciousness element.
Furthermore, one knows and sees the six elements as they truly are: namely, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.

Furthermore, one knows and sees the six elements as they truly are: namely, the element of sensual desire, the element of ill will, the element of harmfulness, the element of renunciation, the element of non-ill will, and the element of non-harmfulness.

Furthermore, one knows and sees the six elements as they truly are: namely, the element of pleasure, the element of pain, the element of joy, the element of grief, the element of equanimity, and the element of ignorance.
Furthermore, one knows and sees the four elements as they truly are: namely, the element of feeling, the element of perception, the element of mental formations, and the element of consciousness.
Furthermore, one knows and sees the three realms as they truly are: namely, the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.
Furthermore, one knows and sees the three realms as they truly are: namely, the realm of form, the formless realm, and the realm of cessation.
Furthermore, one knows and sees the three realms as they truly are: namely, the past realm, the future realm, and the present realm.
Furthermore, one knows and sees the three realms as they truly are: namely, the inferior realm, the middling realm, and the sublime realm.
Furthermore, one knows and sees the three realms as they truly are: namely, the wholesome realm, the unwholesome realm, and the indeterminate realm.

Furthermore, one knows and sees the three realms as they truly are: namely, the realm of those in training (*śaikṣa*), the realm of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and the realm of neither those in training nor those beyond training.
Furthermore, one knows and sees two realms as they truly are: namely, the realm of outflows (*sāsrava-dhātu*) and the realm without outflows (*anāsrava-dhātu*).
Furthermore, one knows and sees two realms as they truly are: namely, the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛta-dhātu*) and the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*).

Regarding these various elements (*dhātu*), to understand them, comprehend them, closely examine them, and thoroughly investigate them—with keen intelligence, penetrating insight, careful scrutiny, sagacity, and the practice of clear awakening and wisdom through *vipaśyanā*—this is called skillfulness regarding the elements (*dhātukuśala*).
What is skillfulness in mental attention (*manasikāra*)?
Answer:

Suppose there is a bhikṣu who either upholds the Sūtras, or upholds the Vinaya, or upholds the Abhidharma; or hears it taught by his preceptor (*upādhyāya*), or hears it taught by his instructor (*ācārya*), or hears it transmitted through successive lineage, or hears it taught by someone who is in accordance with reason. Relying upon such wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) induced by what is reasonable, he applies skillful mental attention toward the eye-element up to the mind-consciousness-element, contemplating them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
One possesses skillful attention regarding the element of earth up to the element of consciousness, contemplating them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
One possesses skillful attention regarding the element of desire, the element of ill will, and the element of cruelty, contemplating them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
One applies skillful attention to the elements of renunciation, non-ill will, and non-harming, contemplating them as impermanent, empty, and non-self.
One applies skillful attention to the elements of pleasure, pain, joy, grief, equanimity, and ignorance, contemplating them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
One possesses skillful attention regarding the elements of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, contemplating them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
One possesses skillful attention regarding the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, contemplating them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
One possesses skillful attention regarding the realms of form and formlessness, contemplating them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self;
one possesses skillful attention regarding the realm of cessation, contemplating it as empty and non-self.
One possesses skillful attention regarding the realms of the past, future, and present, contemplating them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
One possesses skillful attention regarding the inferior and middling realms, contemplating them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self;
one possesses skillful attention regarding the sublime realm, contemplating it as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
One possesses skillful attention regarding the realms of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate, contemplating them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
One possesses skillful attention regarding the realms of those in training and those beyond training, contemplating them as impermanent, empty, and non-self.
One possesses skillful attention regarding the realm of neither those in training nor those beyond training, contemplating it as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
One applies skillful attention to the realm of outflows, contemplating it as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self;
one applies skillful attention to the realm without outflows, contemplating it as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
One applies skillful attention to the conditioned realm, contemplating it as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self;
one applies skillful attention to the unconditioned realm, contemplating it as empty and non-self.

Furthermore, suppose there is a bhikṣu who, in accordance with reality, knows and sees mental orientations (manasikāra) of the past, future, and present; wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral mental orientations; mental orientations bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; mental orientations of those in training (śaikṣa), those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and those who are neither in training nor beyond training; and mental orientations to be abandoned by seeing, abandoned by cultivation, and not to be abandoned. Regarding such various mental orientations, he understands them up to the point of insight (vipaśyanā); this is called skillfulness regarding mental orientation (manasikāra-kauśalya).
Furthermore, there are two qualities: integrity and gentleness. What is integrity?
Answer:

A mind that is not rigid, a mind that is not forceful, a mind that is not hard, a mind that is pure and simple, a mind that is upright, a mind that is smooth, a mind that is flexible, and a mind that is well-disciplined—this is called integrity.
What is suppleness?
Answer:

The body’s lack of rigidity, the body’s lack of strength, the body’s lack of hardness, the body’s quality of purity, the body’s quality of rectitude, the body’s quality of lubricity, the body’s quality of softness, and the body’s quality of tractability—this is called suppleness.
Furthermore, there are two qualities: namely, endurance (*kṣānti*) and being delightful (*priya*). What is meant by endurance? The answer is:

it refers to being able to endure the touch of cold, heat, hunger, thirst, wind, sun, mosquitoes, gadflies, snakes, scorpions, and the like; furthermore, it refers to being able to endure harsh and evil speech from others, and being able to endure the intense, piercing, heart-rending, life-threatening painful sensations that arise within the body. This is called endurance.
What is "pleasant"?
Answer:

Even when circumstances arise that cannot be accommodated, cannot be maintained, cannot be diverted, and cannot be endured, one remains toward them neither violent nor malicious, neither coarse nor unruly; being patient and pleasant, easy to dwell with, and ceasing all evils.

If, when circumstances arise, one is able to accommodate, maintain composure, turn away from them, and endure; and if one can remain toward them neither violent nor malicious, neither coarse nor fierce, but rather patient, pleasant, and easy to dwell with—stopping all evils—this is called being "pleasant."
Furthermore, there are two qualities, namely: being harmonious and making offerings. What is meant by "being harmonious"? Answer:

If one delights in acting with words that are pleasing, delightful, and sweet; if one’s countenance is serene and free from frowning; and if one is the first to speak words of greeting and consolation:
“Venerable one, welcome!
Are you able to endure your circumstances?
Are you able to sustain yourself?”
"Are you dwelling in peace?
Is food easy to obtain?
To engage in such pleasant speech and other matters that bring joy and delight is called "concord."
What is worship?
Answer:
There are two kinds of worship:
First, material offering;
second, Dharma offering.
What is material offering?
Answer:

To be able to bestow, to give, and to follow through with giving; to be able to relinquish, to abandon, and to completely renounce agreeable forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, as well as clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other requisites for the sake of other sentient beings—this is called material offering (*āmiṣa-pūjā*).
What is the offering of Dharma?
Answer:

By means of the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or the Abhidharma; or by the words of one’s own teacher, the words of a preceptor, or the transmitted Piṭakas; or by the words of any other trustworthy person—whatever one is able to bestow, give, or further bestow upon other sentient beings, whatever one is able to relinquish, abandon, or completely renounce—this is called the offering of Dharma.
These two types are collectively termed "offering.
Furthermore, there are two further factors, namely: being endowed with mindfulness and being endowed with clear comprehension. What is meant by "being endowed with mindfulness"?
Answer:

If, based on renunciation, seclusion, and wholesome qualities, one possesses mindfulness, recollection, focused attention, and memory—being without forgetfulness or loss, without omission or leakage, possessing the nature of non-forgetfulness and the mental faculty of clear recollection—this is called being endowed with mindfulness.
What is right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*)?
Answer:

It is that which, based on renunciation, distance, and wholesome phenomena, consists of the discernment, thorough discernment, and supreme discernment of phenomena; it is understanding, equal understanding, proximate understanding, and comprehensive understanding; it is mental acuity, penetration, investigation, sagacity, awakening, clarity, wisdom, and the practice of *vipaśyanā*. This is called right knowledge.
Furthermore, there are two factors, namely the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna-bala*) and the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bala*). What is the power of discernment?
Answer:
As the Blessed One has said:

"Monks, you should know that the learned noble disciple should train himself thus: 'All bodily misconduct brings about a bad ripening of results, both in the present life and in the future. That is to say, if I were to engage in bodily misconduct, I would reproach and despise myself in the present; furthermore, I would be censured by other deities and Buddhas, and I would be criticized according to the Dharma by wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life. My ill repute would spread throughout all worlds, and at the dissolution of the body after death, I would fall into a miserable destination and be reborn in hell.'"

By correctly understanding that bodily misconduct brings about unpleasant karmic results in both the present life and the future, one is able to diligently abandon all bodily misconduct and diligently cultivate all excellent bodily conduct.
The detailed explanation for verbal misconduct and mental misconduct is likewise the same, up to the point of diligently cultivating excellent verbal and mental conduct.

If one can thus, by means of investigation, rely upon investigation, and abide in investigation, abandon unwholesome dharmas and cultivate all wholesome dharmas—this is called the power of investigation (*pratisaṃkhyā-bala*), and it is also termed the power of analytical discernment. This is what is meant by the power of investigation.
What is the power of cultivation?
Answer:
As the Blessed One said:

"Monks, you should know that the learned noble disciple cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness, which is based on disenchantment, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and directed toward relinquishment;
he likewise cultivates the awakening factors of discrimination of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity."
Relying on revulsion, relying on detachment, and relying on cessation, one turns toward relinquishment.

If one can thus cultivate through causes, rely upon cultivation, and abide in cultivation—thereby abandoning unwholesome phenomena and cultivating all wholesome phenomena—it is called "cultivation" and is also termed "power"; this is known as the power of cultivation.
Question:
For what reason is it called "power" (bala)?
Answer:

Because one is able to sever, shatter, and destroy all fetters, latent tendencies, secondary afflictions, and entanglements by means of this power, relying on this power, and abiding in this power, it is therefore called "power."
Furthermore, there are two dharmas: namely, not guarding the doors of the sense faculties and not knowing moderation in eating. What is meant by "not guarding the doors of the sense faculties"?
Answer:
As the Blessed One said:

“Bhikṣus, you should know that when an unlearned worldling sees a form with the eye, he grasps at its general appearance and its secondary details because of the eye-faculty. Failing to guard the eye-faculty in that regard, he dwells in non-guarding, whereby worldly greed and sorrow arise; thus, evil and unwholesome states grow within his mind.”
Because he neither guards nor protects the faculty of the eye, it is said that he does not protect the faculty of the eye.
Through this failure to protect the faculty of the eye, greed, hatred, and delusion grow; the same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

Furthermore, regarding the faculty of mind (*manendriya*): once the mind has cognized mental objects, it apprehends their primary marks and secondary characteristics by means of the faculty of mind. If one does not guard the faculty of mind in this regard, through that lack of restraint, worldly greed and sorrow arise, and evil, unwholesome states grow within the mind.

He neither guards nor protects the faculty of mind; for this reason, it is said that he does not protect the faculty of mind. Because he does not protect the faculty of mind, greed, hatred, and delusion grow and increase, as he gives rise to improper mental deliberation.

When one sees various forms with the eye, hears various sounds with the ear, smells various odors with the nose, tastes various flavors with the tongue, feels various tangibles with the body, and cognizes various phenomena with the mind, yet fails to guard the doors of the six sense faculties, fails to guard them equally, fails to guard them completely, and does not conceal, cover, shield, pacify, subdue, or protect them—this is called "not guarding the doors of the sense faculties."
What is meant by "eating without moderation"?
It is as the Blessed One said:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that unlearned worldlings eat without reflection or discernment; they eat for the sake of strength, for the sake of pride and indulgence, for the sake of complexion, and for the sake of physical beauty."
"Eating without reflection" refers to eating what is consumed while dwelling in a state induced by improper reflection.
"Eating what is consumed for the sake of vigor and strength" refers to when a certain class of person, at the time of eating, gives rise to this thought:

"I shall eat this food so as to ensure fullness, making my body vigorous and strong, enabling me to perform heavy labor and carry heavy burdens; it shall sustain my lifespan so that I may dwell long in this world; it shall enable me to crush enemies, to excel in chariot racing, to leap great distances, and to engage in various worldly sports."
Regarding eating for the sake of pride and indulgence: this refers to a certain class of people who, when eating food, give rise to such a thought:

"By eating this food, I shall certainly become satiated; let it cause pride, indulgence, arrogance, and intoxication to arise, to arise repeatedly, to be produced, and to be produced repeatedly; let it continue to incite me to look down upon all others and, according to my whims, engage in acts of dissipation."
Regarding eating food for the sake of one's appearance: this refers to when a certain class of people, while consuming food, gives rise to such a thought:
"By eating this food, I shall certainly become satiated; it shall cause my countenance to be radiant and my skin and body to be smooth and supple."
Regarding eating food for the sake of physical beauty: this refers to when a certain class of people, while consuming food, gives rise to such a thought:
"By eating this food, I shall certainly become fully satiated; it shall cause my body to achieve a supreme and exquisite form and complexion, which will be loved and respected by all."

Those who thus cherish and value food and drink, yet regarding that food and drink fail to understand its unevenness, fail to know moderation, and lack wisdom; failing to comprehend these characteristics, they do not exercise self-restraint by thinking, "I should now eat only this much food"—this is called "not knowing moderation in eating."
Furthermore, there are two dharmas: namely, guarding the doors of the sense faculties and knowing moderation in food. What is meant by "guarding the doors of the sense faculties"?
Answer:
As the Blessed One has said:

"O bhikṣus, you should know that when a learned noble disciple sees forms with the eye, by means of the faculty of the eye, he does not grasp at their signs nor grasp at their secondary characteristics. He is thus able to guard the faculty of the eye; by so guarding it, he gives rise to neither worldly greed nor sorrow, and evil, unwholesome states do not arise and grow within his mind."

He is able to guard and protect the faculty of the eye; for this reason, it is said that he is able to protect the faculty of the eye. Because he protects the faculty of the eye, greed, hatred, and delusion do not arise; the same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

Furthermore, regarding the faculty of mind (*manendriya*): it means that once the mind has cognized a phenomenon, by means of the faculty of mind, one does not grasp at its signs (*nimitta*) nor its secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*). Thus, one is able to guard the faculty of mind in that very state; by abiding in this guarding, worldly greed and sorrow do not arise, and evil, unwholesome states do not grow within the mind.

He is able to guard and protect the faculty of mind; for this reason, it is said that he is able to protect the faculty of mind. Because he protects the faculty of mind, greed, hatred, and delusion do not arise, as he initiates appropriate reflection and discernment.

When seeing various forms with the eye, hearing various sounds with the ear, smelling various odors with the nose, tasting various flavors with the tongue, feeling various tangibles with the body, and cognizing various phenomena with the mind, one is able to guard, equally guard, thoroughly guard, conceal, cover, shield, pacify, subdue, and protect the doors of the six sense faculties; this is called "guarding the doors of the sense faculties."
What is moderation in eating?
Answer:
As the Blessed One said:

"Monks, you should know that the learned noble disciple eats with discernment; he does not eat for the sake of strength, nor for the sake of pride or indulgence, nor for the sake of beauty, nor for the sake of physical splendor. He eats his food only for the sake of maintaining this body for a time, for its preservation, for the cessation of hunger and thirst, and for the support of the holy life (*brahmacarya*). He eats his food so as to terminate old feelings and prevent new feelings from arising, and so as to dwell in comfort, free from fault, sustained by strength and at ease."
One who eats with discernment means one who dwells in discernment induced by correct reasoning when eating what is consumed.
One does not eat for the sake of physical vigor; that is, unlike a certain class of people who, at the time of eating, give rise to such a thought:

"I shall eat this food so as to ensure fullness, making my body vigorous, able to perform heavy labor and carry heavy burdens, sustaining my lifespan so as to dwell long in the world, and enabling me to defeat enemies, to excel in chariot-racing, to leap great distances, and to engage in various worldly frolics."
Regarding "not eating for the sake of pride and indulgence": this is not like those who, at the time of eating, give rise to such a thought:

"By eating this food, I shall certainly make myself full; it shall cause pride, indulgence, and a mind of haughty intoxication to arise, to co-arise, to be born, and to co-become; it shall continue to incite me to look down upon all others and act with reckless abandon according to my whims."

One who does not consume food for the sake of physical appearance does not, like some people, give rise to such thoughts while eating: "I shall eat this food so as to ensure I am fully satiated, and it shall make my countenance radiant and my skin supple."
Regarding "not eating for the sake of physical beauty": this is not like a certain class of people who, when eating, give rise to such a thought:
"By eating this food, I shall certainly become satiated; it shall cause my body to achieve a supreme, exquisite form and complexion that is beloved and respected by all."

However, that which is consumed for the sake of this body’s temporary maintenance and survival is called "body" (*kāya*). This refers to what is termed the body, the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), the five material faculties, and the aggregate produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Within this context, it is the aggregate produced by the four great elements that is designated as the "body."
When the noble disciples eat their food, they give rise to this thought alone:
"By eating this food, I cause this body, which is a composite of the four great elements, to abide, abide equally, abide closely, and abide securely; therefore, it is called 'abiding for a time.'"
When the noble disciples eat their food, they give rise to this thought alone:

"By eating this food, I shall cause this body, which is a collection produced by the four great elements, to endure and continue to endure, to be sustained and continue to be sustained, to be protected and continue to be protected, and to function and continue to function; therefore, it is called 'sustenance'."
When one eats food merely for the purpose of ceasing hunger and thirst, the painful sensation arising from hunger and thirst is here termed "hunger and thirst.
When the noble disciples eat food, they give rise to this thought alone:
"By eating this food, I shall cause the painful sensation arising from hunger and thirst to cease temporarily and not be afflicted by it."

Regarding "eating what is eaten for the sake of sustaining the holy life" (*brahmacarya*): sexual abstinence is called the holy life, and the Noble Eightfold Path is also called the holy life; in this context, it is the Noble Eightfold Path that is designated as the holy life.
When the noble disciples eat their food, they give rise to this thought alone:
"I eat this food with the desire to sustain, conform to, and increase the eightfold noble path."

Regarding "eating what is eaten for the sake of severing old feelings and not giving rise to new feelings": the painful feeling arising with the condition of not eating is called an "old feeling," while the painful feeling arising with the condition of overeating is called a "new feeling."
When the noble disciples eat their food, they give rise only to this thought:
"I eat this food in order to terminate old feelings and prevent new feelings from arising, not for the sake of gratification."
Regarding "eating what one eats for the sake of blameless sustenance," there are two kinds of sustenance:
first, blameworthy sustenance;
second, blameless sustenance.
What is survival through sinful means?
Answer:

It is when a certain class of people, being deceitful, fraudulent, and hypocritical, manifest false appearances and engage in contentious displays, seeking food and drink by using profit to seek further profit.

Having obtained food and drink through such means, one enjoys them with delight, becoming infatuated by craving and attachment, clinging to them without relinquishing; failing to perceive their faults and not knowing the way of escape—this is called a culpable mode of subsistence.
What is meant by "subsistence free from fault"?
Answer:

It is not like a certain class of people who, through hypocrisy, deception, and guile, manifest artificial signs and engage in contentious friction, seeking food and drink by using profit to seek further profit.

Having obtained food and drink through appropriate means, one uses them in accordance with the Dharma—without greed, without craving, without delusion, without infatuation, without attachment, and without clinging; being able to perceive their faults and knowing well the way of escape, this is called blameless sustenance.
The noble disciples eat their food solely for the sake of blameless sustenance.
Regarding those who eat their food for the sake of strength and happiness, this means that when the noble disciples eat, they give rise only to this thought:
"I eat this food desiring that the strength of my body shall not decline, so that my mind may experience joy and happiness and be able to accomplish wholesome deeds."
Regarding "eating what is eaten for the sake of abiding": this means that when a noble disciple eats food, they give rise to only this thought:
"I eat this food desiring that my body and mind be peaceful and secure while walking, standing, sitting, lying down, reciting, and practicing meditative concentration."

All those who do not value food and drink in this way, who possess equanimity toward all food and drink, who possess the quality of knowing moderation, and who possess the quality of wisdom, are able to understand their characteristics; having understood these characteristics, they are able to exercise self-restraint, thinking, "I should now eat only this much. This is called knowing moderation in food.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas, namely, deficiency in ethical discipline (*śīla*) and deficiency in view (*dṛṣṭi*). What is deficiency in ethical discipline?
Answer:
taking life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter.
Furthermore, if one takes life, takes what is not given, or engages in unchaste conduct;

furthermore, whatever unwholesome precepts there are, whatever precepts induced by improper means there are, and whatever precepts that obstruct meditative concentration there are—these are called the deficiency of ethical discipline.
Question:
Why is it called "deficiency in ethical discipline"?
Answer:

The intrinsic nature of this phenomenon is unlovely, unpleasant, disagreeable, and contrary to the mind; it is not peaceful, not upright, not delightful, not pleasing, and contrary to right principle.
