Furthermore, this dharma can result in an undesirable fruit, an unpleasant fruit, an unjoyful fruit, an unwelcome fruit, a fruit of insecurity, a fruit that is not upright, a fruit that is not delightful, a fruit that is disagreeable, and a fruit that contradicts right principle.

Furthermore, because this dharma can induce undesirable maturation (*vipāka*), unpleasant maturation, disagreeable maturation, unwholesome maturation, unstable maturation, dishonest maturation, unsatisfactory maturation, displeasing maturation, and maturation contrary to right principle, it is therefore called "deficiency in ethical discipline" (*śīla-vipatti*).
What is the deficiency of views? Answer:

It consists of all those views which maintain that there is no giving, no affection, and no sacrifice; no wholesome conduct and no unwholesome conduct; no ripening of the results of wholesome and unwholesome actions; no this world and no other world; no mother, no father, and no spontaneously born beings; and no arhats in the world who have attained and practiced rightly, having personally realized and witnessed for themselves in this world and the next: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."
Furthermore, all unwholesome views, all views induced by irrationality, and all views that obstruct meditative concentration—these are called "views of deprivation."
Question:
Why is it called "deprivation of views"?
Answer:
The intrinsic nature of this phenomenon is unattractive and even contrary to right principle;
furthermore, this phenomenon can produce unattractive results and even results contrary to right principle.
Furthermore, because this dharma can induce undesirable maturation (*vipāka*) up to maturation that contradicts correct principle, it is called "impoverishment of view" (*dṛṣṭivighāta*).
Just as with the impoverishment of morality and the impoverishment of view, one should know that the breaking of morality and the breaking of view are likewise.
Furthermore, there are two qualities: namely, being endowed with ethical discipline and being endowed with right view.
What is meant by "being endowed with ethical discipline"? Answer:

He abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, abstains from divisive speech, abstains from harsh speech, and abstains from idle chatter.
Furthermore, it is abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, and abstaining from unchaste conduct.

Furthermore, all the precepts of those in training (śaikṣa), all the precepts of those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and all the wholesome precepts of those who are neither in training nor beyond training—this is called being endowed with ethical discipline (śīla).
Question:
For what reason is one called "possessed of ethical discipline" (śīlavat)?
Answer:
This dharma is by its very nature lovely, delightful, pleasing, agreeable, peaceful, upright, joyful, gratifying to the mind, and in accordance with right principle.

Furthermore, this Dharma can obtain desirable fruits, pleasant fruits, joyful fruits, agreeable fruits, fruits of peace and security, upright fruits, fruits of delight, pleasing fruits, and fruits that accord with correct principle.

Furthermore, because this dharma can induce desirable maturation, delightful maturation, joyful maturation, agreeable maturation, secure maturation, upright maturation, gratifying maturation, pleasing maturation, and maturation that accords with right principle, it is called "possessing ethical discipline."
What is meant by "possessing vision"?
Answer:

All views that there is giving, there is loving-kindness, there is sacrifice, there is wholesome conduct, there is unwholesome conduct, there is the ripening of the fruit of the results of wholesome and unwholesome actions, there is this world and another world, there is mother and father, there are spontaneously born beings, and there are in the world Arhats who have attained and practiced rightly—having personally realized, witnessed, and fully dwelt in this very life and the next, knowing according to reality: "Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence. This is what is meant by possessing vision.

Furthermore, all views that are of those in training (śaikṣa), all views that are of those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and all wholesome views that are neither of those in training nor beyond training—these are called "possessing view" (dṛṣṭisampanna).
Question:
Why is it called "endowed with vision"?
Answer: Because the intrinsic nature of this dharma is lovely, and so forth, up to being in accordance with correct reasoning.
Furthermore, this dharma can attain desirable fruits up to fruits that accord with correct principle.
Furthermore, this dharma can bring about desirable maturation up to maturations that accord with correct principle; therefore, it is called "possessing vision."
Just as it is with being endowed with ethical discipline and being endowed with right view, one should know that the same applies to pure ethical discipline and pure right view.
Furthermore, there are two factors, namely: view and that which is superior through accordance with reality. What is "view"?
Answer:

It refers to the discernment, thorough discernment, and supreme discernment of phenomena based on renunciation, seclusion, and wholesome qualities; the understanding, equal understanding, proximate understanding, and pervasive understanding; the mental acuity, penetration, investigation, sagacity, awakening, clarity, wisdom, and practice of *vipaśyanā*—this is called "view."
What is the excellence of accordance with reality?
Answer:

It refers to a bhikṣu who, according to what he has seen, if through such characteristics and signs of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) the right view of the world has not yet arisen, it arises; he then reflects upon those characteristics and signs of conditioned phenomena in accordance with reality.

By means of such reasoned reflection on the characteristics of these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), he causes the Noble Path to arise, to arise fully, to be born, to be born fully, to turn, to manifest, to proceed, to be cultivated, to be accumulated, and to appear; this is called the excellence of the path through reasoned reflection.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu, according to his vision, perceives that through any one of these characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), renunciation, seclusion, or wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*) that have not yet arisen do arise, he then correctly contemplates those characteristics of conditioned phenomena.

By means of such reasoned reflection upon the characteristics of these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), he causes the Noble Path to arise, to arise fully, to be born, to be born fully, to proceed, to manifest, to proceed further, to be cultivated, accumulated, and brought forth; this is called the "superiority of the path through reasoned reflection."
These two types are collectively termed "excellence through accordance with reality.
Furthermore, there are two further dharmas, namely: revulsion and excellence through accordance with reality.
What is revulsion?
Answer:
It refers to the arising of revulsion based on four kinds of phenomena that accord with revulsion.
What is the excellence of such accordance with reality?
Answer:
It refers to right reflection that induces the Noble Path.
What are the four factors conducive to revulsion?
First, phenomena associated with aversion regarding one's own decline;
second, phenomena associated with aversion regarding the decline of others;
third, phenomena associated with aversion regarding one's own prosperity.
Regarding the fourth [category], the phenomena conducive to disenchantment through the prosperity of others:

when one generates disenchantment based on the phenomena conducive to disenchantment through one’s own decline, as is the case for a superior practitioner who reflects upon how their own misconduct of body, speech, and mind has reached its ultimate fulfillment, excellence, and full maturity, they then think:
"Because of negligence, relying on negligence, dwelling in negligence, and due to negligence, I have committed these evil deeds."
"I shall now ensure that unwholesome and unvirtuous states that have not yet arisen do not arise, and those that have already arisen are permanently severed.
The disenchantment produced by such courageous exertion for renunciation is called "disenchantment" (nibbidā).

Having already given rise to revulsion, one reflects according to reality, causing the Noble Path to arise, co-arise, be born, co-become, proceed, manifest, and fully develop; this is called the excellence of reflection according to reality regarding the Path. This is termed the excellence of reflection according to reality based on revulsion toward one's own decline.

Regarding the arising of revulsion toward phenomena that accord with aversion due to the decline and loss of others, for one who is superior and acts according to reason: suppose there is a certain person who, through equal and successive contemplation, perceives the culmination, perfection, increase, and full maturation of the misconduct of body, speech, and mind in both themselves and others, and then forms this thought:
"These individuals have committed such evil deeds because of negligence, relying on negligence, dwelling in negligence, and due to negligence."
"I shall now ensure that unwholesome and unvirtuous states which have not yet arisen do not arise, and those which have already arisen are forever abandoned.
The revulsion produced by such courageous exertion for renunciation is called "revulsion" (nibbidā).

Having already produced revulsion, one reflects according to reality, causing the Noble Path to arise, to arise thoroughly, to be born, to be born thoroughly, to turn, to manifest, to turn fully, to be cultivated, accumulated, and brought forth; this is called the excellence of reflection according to reality regarding the Path. This is termed the excellence of reflection according to reality regarding revulsion based on the decline of others.

Regarding the superior practitioner who generates disenchantment toward phenomena that are conducive to disenchantment based on their own prosperity: it is as when a certain person correctly contemplates the ultimate perfection, excellence, and full maturity of their own excellence of bodily conduct, excellence of verbal conduct, and excellence of mental conduct, and then reflects:
"It is because of heedfulness, by relying on heedfulness, by abiding in heedfulness, and through heedfulness that I have performed these wholesome deeds."
"I shall now cause those excellent and wholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen to arise, and those already arisen to increase and expand further.
Through such renunciation and vigor, the state of weariness that is induced is called "weariness" (nirveda).

Having already produced revulsion, one reflects according to reality, further causing the Noble Path to arise, to arise fully, to be born, to be born fully, to turn, to manifest, to turn fully, to be cultivated, accumulated, and brought forth; this is called the excellence of reflection according to reality regarding the Path. This is termed the excellence of reflection according to reality based on the revulsion arising from one's own prosperity.

Regarding the arising of disenchantment toward phenomena that are conducive to disenchantment through the flourishing of others, for one who is superior in accordance with reality: it is as when a certain person observes another’s excellence in physical conduct, verbal conduct, and mental conduct, seeing them as ultimately perfected, predominant, and fully matured, and then forms this thought:
“That person has performed these wholesome deeds because of heedfulness; they rely upon heedfulness, abide in heedfulness, and act out of heedfulness.”
"I shall now cause all excellent and wholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen to arise, and those already arisen to increase and expand further.
The weariness produced by such courageous exertion for renunciation is called "weariness" (nirveda).

Having already produced revulsion, one reflects according to reality, causing the Noble Path to arise, to arise fully, to be born, to be born fully, to turn, to manifest, and to become fully manifest; this is called the excellence of reflection according to reality regarding the Path. This is what is meant by the excellence of reflection according to reality based on the flourishing of revulsion toward others.

Furthermore, there are two dharmas: namely, lack of contentment with regard to the wholesome and non-restraint regarding abandonment. What is meant by "lack of contentment with regard to the wholesome"?
Answer:
Regarding contentment with the wholesome, it is as when a certain class of persons, having obtained only a small amount of ethical discipline, gives rise to contentment; only...
One becomes content merely with having attained a minor restraint; one becomes content merely with having attained freedom from desire;
one becomes content merely with having attained the contemplation of impurity; one becomes content merely with having attained mindfulness of breathing and so forth;
or one becomes content merely with having attained the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna; or one becomes content merely with having attained loving-kindness...

They become satisfied upon attaining only limited [attainments], such as the immeasurables; or they become satisfied upon merely attaining the concentration of the base of infinite space up to the concentration of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
or they become satisfied upon merely attaining the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning;
or they become satisfied upon merely attaining the supernormal power of the knowledge and realization of the movement of the psychic faculties.

The supernormal power of the realization of the divine ear, the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of others' minds, the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of recollecting past lives,
and the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of death and rebirth— arising in contentment with these is called "contentment regarding the wholesome."

Regarding "not being content with what is wholesome": it is as when a certain class of persons does not become satisfied merely by obtaining a small amount of ethical discipline, and so on, up to and including not becoming satisfied merely by obtaining the realization of the knowledge of death and rebirth.
He forms this thought:
"I shall cultivate all wholesome qualities; until I have attained the fruit of arhatship, I will never be content in the interim.
This is called non-contentment with regard to the wholesome.
How is it that there is no obstruction regarding abandonment?
Answer:

Regarding obstruction to abandonment, it is as follows: suppose there is a certain class of person who, for the sake of abandoning unwholesome dharmas and for the sake of fulfilling wholesome dharmas, exerts themselves with vigor and diligence, burning with zeal and delight, practicing assiduously without ceasing, and thinks to themselves:
"How might I swiftly realize the wholesome dharmas that accord with reality?
While he is thus practicing with fierce diligence, burning with zeal, and applying himself with effort, yet fails to realize those wholesome dharmas that accord with reality, he then thinks:
"The abandonment I have cultivated is empty and fruitless; it is without benefit, without purpose, without flavor, and without profit."
Because they perceive no benefit in abandoning [unwholesome states], they give rise to weariness, revilement, and disparagement; this is called the obstruction to abandonment.

Furthermore, there is another class who, for the sake of abandoning unwholesome dharmas and perfecting wholesome dharmas, exert themselves with vigor, ardor, and joyful enthusiasm, practicing without ceasing, and think to themselves:
"How may I swiftly realize the wholesome dharmas that accord with reality?"

While he is thus practicing with such fierce diligence, burning with zeal, and applying himself with effort, he has not yet realized the wholesome dharmas in accordance with reality; or, though he has realized them, he does not clearly understand them. He then thinks:
"The abandonment I have cultivated is empty and fruitless; it is without benefit, without purpose, without flavor, and without profit."
Because they perceive no benefit in abandonment, they give rise to weariness, repudiation, and disparagement; this is also called the obstruction of abandonment.
*Abhidharma-samgītiparyāya-pāda-śāstra*, Fascicle 2.
*Abhidharma-samgītiparyāya-pāda-śāstra*, Fascicle 3.
Spoken by the Venerable Śāriputra;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Part Three of the Second Chapter on the Two Dharmas: Regarding non-restraint in abandonment. Suppose there is a certain class of person who, for the sake of abandoning unwholesome dharmas and for the sake of perfecting wholesome dharmas, practices with courageous diligence, fervent zeal, and joyful application without ceasing, thinking to themselves:
"How might I swiftly realize the wholesome dharmas that accord with reality?
While he is thus practicing with fierce diligence, burning with zeal, and applying himself with effort, he does not yet realize the wholesome dharmas that accord with reality. He then thinks:

"As the Blessed One has said, there is no possibility and no occasion for a son of good family who practices the correct conduct with diligence not to realize the wholesome dharmas that accord with reality."
Because my cultivation of right practice has not yet reached fulfillment, I have not yet realized the wholesome dharmas that accord with reality.
My cultivation of the meditative absorptions for abandonment should not be empty or vain; it should possess fruit and benefit, meaning, flavor, and advantage.
Because they perceive the excellence in abandoning [unwholesome states], they do not give rise to weariness, disparagement, or reviling; this is called "not obstructing abandonment.

Furthermore, there is another class who, for the sake of abandoning unwholesome dharmas and for the sake of fulfilling wholesome dharmas, exert themselves with vigor, ardor, and joyful enthusiasm, practicing without ceasing, and think to themselves:
"How may I swiftly realize the wholesome dharmas that accord with reality?"

While he is thus practicing with such fierce diligence, ardent zeal, and joyful application, he has not yet realized the wholesome dharmas that accord with reality; or, although he has realized them, he does not fully understand them. He then thinks:

"As the Blessed One has said, there is no possibility and no occasion for a son of good family who practices the right conduct with diligence not to realize the wholesome dharmas that accord with reality."
Because my practice of correct cultivation has not yet been fulfilled, I have not yet realized the wholesome dharmas that accord with reality.
My cultivation of the meditative absorptions for abandonment should not be empty or vain; it must have fruit and benefit, meaning and flavor, and be truly advantageous.
Because they perceive the benefits in abandoning [unwholesome states], they do not give rise to weariness, revulsion, or disparagement; this is called "not obstructing abandonment.

Furthermore, there is another class who, for the sake of abandoning unwholesome dharmas and for the sake of fulfilling wholesome dharmas, practice with courageous diligence, fervent zeal, and tireless application, thinking to themselves:
"How may I swiftly realize the wholesome dharmas that accord with reality?"
As he thus practices with such fierce diligence, ardent joy, and persistent application, he is able to realize the wholesome dharmas that accord with reality, and he then reflects:
"The abandonment I have cultivated is certainly not empty or vain; it has its fruit and its benefit, its purpose, its savor, and its advantage."
Because he perceives the excellence in abandonment, he does not give rise to weariness, revulsion, or disparagement; this is called "not obstructing abandonment.
Furthermore, there are two further dharmas, namely śamatha and vipaśyanā. What is śamatha?
Answer:
One-pointedness of a wholesome mind is called śamatha. What is vipaśyanā?
Answer:

That which is associated with śamatha, which discriminates, thoroughly discriminates, and most thoroughly discriminates phenomena; which understands, comprehends, closely examines, and pervasively investigates; which is characterized by mental acuity, penetration, scrutiny, and sagacity; and which consists of the practice of awakening, clarity, and wisdom—this is called vipaśyanā.
As the World-Honored One has said:
"There is no concentration without wisdom, nor is there wisdom without concentration;
only when one possesses both concentration and wisdom can one realize nirvana."
"Regarding 'there is no concentration without wisdom': this means that if one possesses such a kind of wisdom, then one will attain such a kind of concentration;
if one lacks such a kind of wisdom, then one will not attain such a kind of concentration. Therefore, it is said that there is no concentration without wisdom."

Regarding "there is no wisdom for one who lacks concentration": this means that if there is wisdom, it is produced by concentration, has concentration as its source, belongs to the category of concentration, and is brought forth by concentration.
If there is such concentration, then there is the attainment of such wisdom;
if there is no such concentration, then there is no attainment of such wisdom. Therefore, it is said that there is no wisdom without concentration.

Regarding the statement that one must possess both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) to realize *nirvāṇa*: the exhaustion of craving, detachment, and cessation is called *nirvāṇa*. One can only realize it by being fully endowed with both concentration and wisdom; if either is lacking, one will certainly be unable to realize it.
For these reasons, it is said that one must possess both concentration and wisdom to realize nirvana.
Furthermore, there may be a person who attains internal tranquility (śamatha) but does not attain the superior wisdom of the observation of phenomena (vipaśyanā).
There may be a person who attains the contemplation of the dharma of superior wisdom but does not attain internal tranquility;
there may also be a person who attains neither internal tranquility nor the contemplation of the dharma of superior wisdom.
There may be a person who attains internal tranquility of mind and also attains the higher wisdom of the contemplation of phenomena.
What kind of person attains internal tranquility of mind but does not attain the higher wisdom of the contemplation of phenomena?
Answer:
If a person (pudgala) attains the four worldly dhyānas but does not attain supramundane noble wisdom (āryaprajñā).
What kind of person attains the practice of higher wisdom (adhiprajñā-dharma-vipaśyanā) but does not attain internal tranquility (citta-śamatha)?
Answer:
If a person (pudgala) has attained supramundane noble wisdom but has not attained the four mundane dhyānas—
what kind of person has neither attained internal calm abiding (śamatha) nor attained the superior wisdom of insight (vipaśyanā)?
Answer:
If a person (pudgala) neither attains the four worldly meditative absorptions (dhyāna) nor attains supramundane noble wisdom (āryaprajñā),
what kind of person attains internal tranquility of mind (śamatha) as well as the dharma-contemplation of higher insight (vipaśyanā)?
Answer:

If a person attains the four mundane dhyānas as well as supramundane noble wisdom—just as it is said that they are associated with the four mundane dhyānas, such that the mind abides, abides equally, abides closely, and abides securely; being undistracted, unconfused, collected, stilled, and concentrated in one-pointedness of mind—this reveals internal śamatha.

As it is said: that which is comprised by supramundane noble wisdom, which discriminates, thoroughly discriminates, and most thoroughly discriminates phenomena; which understands, equalizes, closely examines, and pervasively investigates; which is characterized by mental agility, penetration, scrutiny, and sagacity; and which is the practice of clear awakening and wisdom known as *vipaśyanā*—this reveals the cultivation of the dharma of higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*), which is called *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas, namely, clarity (*vidyā*) and liberation (*vimukti*). What is clarity?
Answer:
The three types of clear knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-vidyā-traya*).
What are the three?

First, the realization by direct knowledge of the recollection of past lives belonging to one beyond training; second, the realization by direct knowledge of death and rebirth belonging to one beyond training;
[and third, the realization by direct knowledge of the destruction of the taints belonging to one beyond training].
Third, the realization through the knowledge of the destruction of outflows belonging to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is called "clarity" (*vidyā*).
What is "liberation" (*vimukti*)?
Answer:
There are three kinds of liberation. What are the three?
The first is the liberation of the mind;
Second is liberation through wisdom;
third is unconditioned liberation.

Regarding "liberation of the mind," it refers to a mind associated with the wholesome root of non-attachment that has already attained, will attain, or is currently attaining resolute conviction; this is called liberation of the mind.

One liberated by wisdom refers to a mind associated with the wholesome root of non-delusion that has already attained, will attain, or is currently attaining resolute conviction; this is called liberation by wisdom.
Unconditioned liberation refers to cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); this is called unconditioned liberation.
Within this, the liberation of the mind may be that of one in training (*śaikṣa*), that of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), or neither that of one in training nor that of one beyond training.
What is training (śaikṣa)?
Answer:
It is the mind associated with the wholesome root of non-attachment that has already resolved, will resolve, or is currently resolving; this is called training.
What is the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
Answer:

It is the mind associated with the wholesome roots of non-attachment belonging to one beyond training, which has already attained resolution, will attain resolution, or is currently attaining resolution; this is called the state of one beyond training.
What is that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Answer:

A mind associated with the wholesome root of non-attachment that is tainted (*sāsrava*), which has already resolved, will resolve, or is currently resolving; this is called neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Liberation through wisdom (prajñā-vimukti) is either of one in training (śaikṣa), or beyond training (aśaikṣa), or neither of training nor beyond training.
What is that which is of one in training? Answer:
When one who is in training possesses a mind associated with the wholesome root of non-delusion, having already resolved, will resolve, or is now resolving, this is called "one in training.
What is "one beyond training"?
Answer: A mind associated with the wholesome root of non-delusion that is beyond training (aśaikṣa), which has already resolved, will resolve, or is currently resolving, is called "beyond training.
What is neither-training-nor-beyond-training?
Answer:

A mind associated with the wholesome root of non-delusion that is tainted (sāsrava), which has already resolved, will resolve, or is currently resolving, is called "neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee" (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
Unconditioned liberation is exclusively neither-learner-nor-non-learner; this is called the liberation of clear knowledge (*vidyā-vimukti*).
Furthermore, there are two dharmas, namely the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). What is the knowledge of exhaustion?
Answer:

It refers to knowing as it truly is: "I have known suffering, I have abandoned its origin, I have realized its cessation, and I have cultivated the path. The knowledge, vision, clarity, awakening, understanding, wisdom, light, contemplation, and insight arising from this is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
What is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*)? Answer: It is the knowledge as it truly is that:

"I have already known suffering and shall no longer know it; I have already abandoned the origin [of suffering] and shall no longer abandon it; I have already realized cessation and shall no longer realize it; I have already cultivated the path and shall no longer cultivate it. The wisdom, vision, clarity, awakening, understanding, insight, light, and contemplation arising from this is called the knowledge of non-arising.

Furthermore, if one knows as it truly is that the outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) have been exhausted, this is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).
If one knows as it truly is that these three exhausted outflows will not arise again, this is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

Furthermore, if one knows as it truly is that all fetters (*saṃyojana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) have been exhausted, this is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).

If one knows as it truly is that all those exhausted fetters, latent tendencies, secondary afflictions, and envelopments shall never arise again, this is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
4. Chapter on the Three Dharmas, Part One of the First Section of the *Saṃgītiparyāya-śāstra*. At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the assembly, saying:

"Venerable ones, you should know that the Buddha, having himself thoroughly mastered three dharmas and realized them through manifest perfect enlightenment, has proclaimed and revealed them to his disciples."

"We should now assemble in harmony to hold a council; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, let there be no discord. We must ensure that the Dharma and Vinaya, which accord with the holy life, endure for a long time, bringing benefit and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, out of compassion for the world of devas and humans, so that they may attain supreme purpose, benefit, and peace."
"What are the three dharmas?
In this regard, there are five summary verses (*uddāna*).
The first summary verse says:"
The first three categories of phenomena comprise ten factors: namely, the faculties (*indriya*), applied thought (*vitarka*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and the elements (*dhātu*).
Of these, the first three each have two types, while the last one has four types.
There are three unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*) and three wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*).
The three unwholesome thoughts and the three wholesome thoughts;
the three unwholesome actions and the three sublime actions;

the three realms of sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty; the three realms of renunciation, non-ill will, and non-cruelty; the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness; and the three realms of form, formlessness, and cessation.
The three unwholesome roots are the unwholesome root of greed, the unwholesome root of hatred, and the unwholesome root of delusion.
Regarding the unwholesome root of greed: what is greed?
Answer:

It refers to all forms of greed and pervasive greed regarding objects of desire—clinging, hoarding, guarding, and firm attachment; fondness and infatuation; indulgence and total indulgence; internal fetters, seeking, and immersion; and that which arises from the accumulation of suffering and is born of the category of greed. All these taken together are termed "greed."
What are the unwholesome roots?
Answer:

This dharma of greed is of an unwholesome nature and can serve as the root for immeasurable unwholesome dharmas. Therefore, this dharma serves as the root of disease, the root of sores, the root of arrows, the root of affliction, the root of suffering, the root of impurity, the root of turbidity, the root of all various defilements, the root of non-purity, and the root of lack of radiance; thus, it is called the unwholesome root of greed.
Regarding the unwholesome root of hatred (*dveṣa-akuśalamūla*):

what is hatred? The answer is: it refers to the desire to cause harm toward sentient beings; harboring a latent resentment within that desires to cause affliction; having hated, will hate, or currently hates; delighting in causing injury and extreme injury; being intensely incensed in mind; and desiring to cause injury toward various sentient beings through mutual opposition and contrariety—having caused injury, will cause injury, or currently causes injury. This, in brief, is called hatred.
What are the unwholesome roots?
Answer:

This phenomenon of hatred (*dveṣa*) is by nature unwholesome and serves as the root for immeasurable unwholesome phenomena. Therefore, this phenomenon acts as the root of disease, the root of abscesses, the root of arrows, the root of affliction, the root of suffering, the root of corruption, the root of turbidity, the root of all defilements, the root of impurity, and the root of lack of radiance; hence it is called the unwholesome root of hatred.
Regarding the unwholesome root of delusion: what is delusion?
Answer:
It refers to ignorance regarding the past, ignorance regarding the future, and ignorance regarding both the past and the future; as well as [ignorance] regarding the internal...
Ignorance regarding the internal, ignorance regarding the external, and ignorance regarding both the internal and external;
ignorance regarding karma, ignorance regarding its maturation, and ignorance regarding both karma and its maturation;

ignorance regarding wholesome actions, ignorance regarding unwholesome actions, and ignorance regarding both wholesome and unwholesome actions; ignorance regarding causes, and ignorance regarding the phenomena produced by causes.
Lacking knowledge of the Buddha, lacking knowledge of the Dharma, and lacking knowledge of the Saṅgha;

lacking knowledge of suffering, lacking knowledge of its origin, lacking knowledge of its cessation, and lacking knowledge of the path; lacking knowledge of wholesome phenomena, lacking knowledge of unwholesome phenomena;
lacking knowledge of blameworthy phenomena, lacking knowledge of blameless phenomena; and lacking knowledge of phenomena that should be cultivated...
Knowing this, one should not practice ignorance regarding phenomena; one should not be ignorant of inferior phenomena or superior and sublime phenomena;
one should not be ignorant of dark phenomena or bright phenomena; one should not be ignorant of phenomena that have adversaries;
one should not be ignorant of dependently arisen phenomena; and one should not be ignorant of the six bases of contact as they truly are.

Thus, this lack of knowledge and lack of vision is not a clear realization; it is darkness, delusion, and the blindness of ignorance; it is a shroud, a net, an entanglement, a state of stupidity, turbidity, and obscuration. It gives rise to blindness, gives rise to ignorance, and gives rise to lack of wisdom; it extinguishes superior insight and obstructs wholesome qualities, preventing one from attaining *nirvāṇa*.

The outflow of ignorance, the flood of ignorance, the yoke of ignorance, the poisonous root of ignorance, the poisonous stem of ignorance, the poisonous branch of ignorance, the poisonous leaf of ignorance, the poisonous flower of ignorance, and the poisonous fruit of ignorance; delusion (*moha*), equal delusion, and extreme delusion; perversion (*viparyāsa*), equal perversion, and extreme perversion; that which arises from the category of delusion and that which arises from the category of perversion—these collectively are termed "delusion."
What are the unwholesome roots?
Answer:

This dharma of delusion is unwholesome by nature and can serve as the root for immeasurable unwholesome dharmas. Therefore, this dharma serves as the root of disease, the root of sores, the root of arrows, the root of affliction, the root of suffering, the root of impurity, the root of turbidity, the root of all various defilements, the root of lack of purity, and the root of lack of brightness; thus it is called the unwholesome root of delusion.
As the Blessed One said:
"Those who are afflicted by evil greed, hatred, and delusion, which torment their own minds, are like a tree whose heartwood is infested with scorpions; its bark, fruit, and all else will wither."
The three roots of goodness are the root of goodness of non-attachment, the root of goodness of non-hatred, and the root of goodness of non-delusion.
Regarding the root of goodness of non-attachment: what is non-attachment?
Answer:

It refers to the absence of greed, the absence of unequal greed, the absence of grasping and hoarding, the absence of guarding and firm attachment, the absence of craving and delight, the absence of mental confusion and delusion, the absence of indulgence and pervasive indulgence, the absence of internal bondage, the absence of desire and seeking, and the absence of immersion, with respect to objects of desire; that which is not the origin of suffering, not of the nature of greed, and not born of greed—this, in brief, is called non-greed (*alobha*).
What are the roots of goodness?
Answer:

They refer to the state of non-attachment, which is wholesome by nature and serves as the root for immeasurable wholesome dharmas. Therefore, this dharma serves as the root of freedom from illness, the root of freedom from abscesses, the root of freedom from arrows, the root of freedom from filth, the root of freedom from turbidity, the root of non-defilement, the root of purity, and the root of brilliant whiteness; for this reason, it is called the wholesome root of non-attachment.
Regarding the wholesome root of non-hatred (*adveṣa*): what is non-hatred? Answer:

It refers to the lack of desire to harm sentient beings, not harboring resentment, and not desiring to disturb or afflict them; it is neither past hatred, nor future hatred, nor present hatred; it is not taking pleasure in causing harm, nor is it excessively causing harm; the mind is not agitated or enraged, and one does not act in opposition toward sentient beings; one does not desire to cause harm, nor has one caused harm, nor will one cause harm, nor is one currently causing harm—this is collectively termed non-hatred.
What is the root of goodness?
Answer:

It refers to the dharma of non-hatred, which is of a virtuous nature and can serve as the root for immeasurable wholesome dharmas. Therefore, this dharma can serve as the root of freedom from illness, the root of freedom from abscesses, the root of freedom from arrows, the root of freedom from filth, the root of freedom from turbidity, the root of non-defilement, the root of purity, and the root of brilliant whiteness; for this reason, it is called the wholesome root of non-hatred.
Regarding the wholesome root of non-delusion: what is non-delusion?
Answer:
It refers to knowledge of the past, knowledge of the future, and knowledge of both the past and the future; it is knowledge of the internal and knowledge of the external.
Knowledge of the internal and external; knowledge of karma, knowledge of maturation, and knowledge of both karma and its maturation;
knowledge of wholesome actions, knowledge of unwholesome actions, and knowledge of both wholesome and unwholesome actions;
knowledge of causes and knowledge of the phenomena produced by causes; knowledge of the Buddha, knowledge of the Dharma, and knowledge of the Saṅgha; and knowledge of suffering.
The knowledge of origination, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path; the knowledge of wholesome phenomena, the knowledge of unwholesome phenomena;
the knowledge of blameworthy phenomena, the knowledge of blameless phenomena; the knowledge of phenomena to be cultivated, the knowledge of phenomena not to be cultivated;
the knowledge of inferior phenomena, the knowledge of sublime phenomena; and the knowledge of dark phenomena and bright phenomena.
Wisdom (*jñāna*) is the knowledge of opposing phenomena, the knowledge of dependently arisen phenomena, and the knowledge of the six bases of contact as they truly are.
Such wisdom, vision, clarity, awakening, understanding, insight, light, and contemplation are collectively termed non-delusion (*amoha*).
What is the root of goodness?
Answer:

It refers to the quality of non-delusion (*amoha*), which is wholesome by nature and serves as the root for immeasurable wholesome dharmas. Therefore, this dharma acts as the root of freedom from disease, the root of freedom from abscesses, the root of freedom from arrows, the root of freedom from filth, the root of freedom from turbidity, the root of non-defilement, the root of purity, and the root of brilliant whiteness; thus it is called the wholesome root of non-delusion.
As the Blessed One said:
"One who is free from greed, hatred, and delusion is called a wise person and is also called a superior person;
such a one does not afflict or harm their own mind."
"Therefore, one should distance oneself from greed, hatred, and ignorance;
by diligently cultivating the light of wisdom, one will swiftly attain the exhaustion of all suffering.
The three unwholesome thoughts are: thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harm.
What is the vitarka of sensual desire?
Answer:

It refers to the searching, thorough searching, and close searching of all minds associated with sensual craving; it is the mind’s manifestation, intense manifestation, and immediate manifestation; its investigation, conceptualization, reflection, and discrimination—all these together are termed the vitarka of sensual desire.
What is the vitarka of ill-will (*vyāpādavitarka*)?
Answer:

It refers to all mental investigations (*paryeṣaṇā*), thorough investigations (*viparyeṣaṇā*), and proximate investigations (*upaparyeṣaṇā*) associated with hatred; it includes the mind’s manifestation, intense manifestation, and immediate manifestation, as well as its estimation, construction, reflection, and discrimination. Collectively, these are termed the vitarka of ill-will.
What is harmful vitarka?
Answer:

It refers to the mental searching, thorough searching, and close searching associated with harmful states; the mind’s manifestation, intense manifestation, and immediate manifestation; its deliberation, conceptual construction, reflection, and discrimination—all these together are termed harmful vitarka.
As the Blessed One said:
"Evil thoughts subdue sentient beings, causing them to see the foul as pure;
they further increase craving and attachment, binding themselves with firm fetters."

Regarding the three wholesome modes of thought (*vitarka*), they are: the thought of renunciation (*nekkhamma-vitarka*), the thought of non-ill will (*avyāpāda-vitarka*), and the thought of non-cruelty (*avihiṃsā-vitarka*).
What is the thought of renunciation?
Answer:

One contemplates the faults of thoughts regarding sensual desires (*kāma-vitarka*), considering that these thoughts of desire are unwholesome dharmas, which base and lowly people believe in, understand, and uphold.

They are collectively censured and loathed by all Tathāgatas, their disciples, and noble, virtuous persons; they can bring harm to oneself, harm to others, and harm to both; they can destroy wisdom, obstruct its counterparts, and hinder *nirvāṇa*. Upholding such dharmas does not give rise to supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), does not lead toward enlightenment (*bodhi*), and does not result in the realization of *nirvāṇa*.

When one thus contemplates the faults and dangers of the pursuit of sensual desires, whatever mental seeking, thorough seeking, and close seeking there is; whatever clarity, extreme clarity, and manifest clarity of mind there is; and whatever measuring, constructing, contemplating, and discriminating there is—this is called the pursuit of renunciation.

Furthermore, in order to abandon thoughts of sensual desire, one contemplates the virtues of thoughts of renunciation (*naiṣkramya-vitarka*). That is to say, thoughts of renunciation are supreme and wholesome dharmas; they are those which the Honored and Exalted Ones have resolved upon and upheld, and which all Tathāgatas, their disciples, and noble virtuous persons (*satpuruṣa*) together praise. They do not bring harm to oneself, nor harm to others, nor harm to both; they do not destroy wisdom, do not obstruct that category [of wholesome states], and do not hinder nirvāṇa. By upholding this dharma, one can give rise to supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), can lead toward enlightenment (*bodhi*), and can realize nirvāṇa.
When one contemplates the virtues of the thought of renunciation (*naiṣkramya-vitarka*) in this manner, all mental seeking up to its conceptualization is called the thought of renunciation.

Furthermore, one contemplates the thought of sensual desire (*kāma-vitarka*) as being like a disease, like an abscess, like an arrow, and a source of affliction; as being impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; as shifting and unstable; as wearisome, debilitated, and gravely ill; as a phenomenon subject to ruin; as rapid and unceasing; as decaying and non-eternal; and as unreliable, a phenomenon subject to transformation and disintegration.
When one thus contemplates the thoughts of sensual desire, all mental seeking up to and including conceptualization is called the thought of renunciation (*naiṣkramya-vitarka*).
Furthermore, in order to abandon the thought of sensual desire, one contemplates that its cessation is true tranquility and contemplates that its path is true renunciation.

When one contemplates in this way the cessation and the path, all mental states ranging from seeking (*paryeṣaṇā*) to discrimination (*vikalpa*) are called the "thought of renunciation" (*naiṣkramya-vitarka*).

Furthermore, when contemplating the meditative absorption of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta-samādhi*) and the path, there are the non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the cessation absorption (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which are associated with the meditative absorption of equanimity.
When one reflects in this manner, all mental investigations up to and including discrimination are called the "thought of renunciation" (*naiṣkramya-vitarka*).

Furthermore, when reflecting upon renunciation and the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with renunciation, as well as the bodily and vocal actions and the formations dissociated from mind that arise from them, all mental investigations up to and including discrimination are called the "thought of renunciation."

What is the absence of ill-will thoughts (*vyāpāda-vitarka*)? Answer: It is the contemplation of the faults and dangers regarding all ill-will thoughts, namely: "These ill-will thoughts are unwholesome states (*akuśala-dharma*), which base and lowly persons believe in, understand, and uphold. They are collectively censured and loathed by all Tathāgatas, their disciples, and noble, virtuous gentlemen. They can cause harm to oneself, harm to others, and harm to both; they can destroy wisdom, obstruct the corresponding category [of wholesome qualities], and hinder *nirvāṇa*. Upholding these states does not give rise to supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), does not lead to enlightenment (*bodhi*), and does not result in the realization of *nirvāṇa*."

When one thus contemplates the faults and disadvantages of various thoughts of ill will (*vyāpāda-vitarka*), whatever mental seeking, thorough seeking, and close seeking there is; whatever mental clarity, extreme clarity, and manifest clarity there is; and whatever measuring, constructing, contemplating, and discriminating there is—this is called "thoughts of non-ill will" (*avyāpāda-vitarka*).

Furthermore, in order to abandon thoughts of ill will (*vyāpāda-vitarka*), one contemplates the virtues of thoughts free from ill will (*avyāpāda-vitarka*). That is to say: thoughts free from ill will are a supreme and wholesome dharma; they are what the noble and eminent ones believe, understand, accept, and uphold; they are praised by all Tathāgatas, their disciples, and virtuous gentlemen. They do not harm oneself, do not harm others, and do not harm both. They do not destroy wisdom, do not obstruct the corresponding category [of wholesome states], and do not hinder *nirvāṇa*. By upholding this dharma, one can give rise to supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), lead toward enlightenment (*bodhi*), and realize *nirvāṇa*.
When one thus contemplates the virtues of non-ill-willful thought (*avyāpāda-vitarka*), all mental seeking up to its full conceptualization is termed non-ill-willful thought.

Furthermore, one contemplates ill-willful thought as being like a disease, like an abscess, like an arrow, and as a source of affliction and harm; as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; as shifting and unstable, weary, debilitated, and incurably afflicted; as a phenomenon subject to ruin and destruction; as rapid and incessant, decaying and non-eternal; and as unreliable, a phenomenon subject to transformation and disintegration.

When one contemplates in this way during moments of ill-will-related thoughts (*vyāpāda-vitarka*), all mental seeking up to conceptualization is called non-ill-will-related thought (*avyāpāda-vitarka*).
Furthermore, in order to abandon ill-will-related thoughts, one contemplates their cessation as true tranquility and contemplates the path to them as true renunciation.
When one contemplates in this way the cessation and the path, all mental states ranging from seeking (*vitarka*) to discrimination (*vikalpa*) are called non-ill-will seeking (*avyāpāda-vitarka*).

Furthermore, one contemplates the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) and its path, as well as the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*), the cessation concentration (*nirodha-samādhi*), and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) associated with the concentration of loving-kindness.
When one reflects in this way, all mental seeking up to and including discrimination is called non-ill-will vitarka.

Furthermore, when reflecting on non-ill-will and the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with non-ill-will, as well as the bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind that arise from them, all mental seeking up to and including discrimination is called non-ill-will vitarka.
What is the thought of harm (*vihiṃsā-vitarka*)? Answer:

It is the contemplation of the faults and resentment inherent in thoughts of harm, namely: "This thought of harm is an unwholesome dharma; it is what base and lowly people believe in, understand, and uphold. It is that which all Tathāgatas and their disciples, as well as noble and virtuous persons, together censure and loathe. It can bring harm to oneself, harm to others, and harm to both; it can destroy wisdom, obstruct its corresponding category, and hinder nirvāṇa. Upholding this dharma does not give rise to supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), does not lead to enlightenment (*bodhi*), and does not result in the realization of nirvāṇa."

When one thus contemplates the faults and disadvantages of harmful thoughts, whatever mental seeking, thorough seeking, and close seeking there is; whatever mental clarity, extreme clarity, and manifest clarity; whatever investigation, conceptualization, contemplation, and discrimination—this is called non-harmful thought.

Furthermore, in order to abandon harmful discursive thought (*vihiṃsā-vitarka*), one contemplates the virtues of non-harming discursive thought (*avihiṃsā-vitarka*). That is to say, non-harming is a supreme and wholesome dharma; it is that which the exalted ones believe, understand, and uphold; it is that which all Tathāgatas and their disciples, as well as noble and virtuous persons, collectively praise. It does not harm oneself, nor harm others, nor harm both; it does not destroy wisdom, it does not obstruct its own category, and it does not hinder *nirvāṇa*. By upholding this dharma, one can give rise to supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), lead toward enlightenment (*bodhi*), and realize *nirvāṇa*.
When one contemplates in this way the virtues of non-harming thought (*avihiṃsā-vitarka*), all mental seeking up to conceptualization is called non-harming thought.

Furthermore, one contemplates harmful thought (*vihiṃsā-vitarka*) as being like a disease, like an abscess, like an arrow, and as an affliction; as being impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, subject to fluctuation; as weariness, exhaustion, and debility; as a phenomenon of destruction and ruin; as rapid and unstable, decaying and non-eternal; and as an unreliable phenomenon of transformation and decay.
When one contemplates in this way regarding all harmful thoughts—including all mental seeking up to conceptualization—it is called non-harmful thought.
Furthermore, in order to abandon harmful thoughts, one contemplates that their cessation is true tranquility, and one contemplates that the path leading to them is true renunciation.
When one contemplates that cessation and the path in this manner, all mental seeking up to and including discrimination is called "harmless inquiry" (*avihiṃsā-vitarka*).

Furthermore, one contemplates the concentration of compassion (*karuṇā-samādhi*) and the path, the non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) associated with the concentration of compassion, the cessation absorption (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
When one reflects in this manner, all mental investigations up to and including conceptualization are called non-harmful investigation (*avihiṃsā-vitarka*).

Furthermore, when reflecting upon non-harmfulness and the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with non-harmfulness, as well as the bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind that arise from them, all mental investigations up to and including conceptualization are called non-harmful investigation.
As the Blessed One said:
"Delight in the cessation of all evil thoughts, Diligently cultivate the contemplation of impurity, Constantly mindfully sever craving and attachment; Thus one can destroy even the most solid bonds."
The three types of unwholesome conduct refer to unwholesome conduct of body, unwholesome conduct of speech, and unwholesome conduct of mind.
What is unwholesome conduct of body?
Answer:
Taking life, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct;
furthermore, taking life, taking what is not given, and unchaste conduct;

furthermore, all unwholesome bodily actions, all bodily actions induced by improper reasoning, and all bodily actions that obstruct meditative concentration—these are collectively termed bodily misconduct (*kāyaduścarita*).
What is verbal misconduct?
Answer:
False speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech.
Furthermore, all unwholesome vocal karma, all vocal karma induced by improper reasoning, and all vocal karma that can obstruct meditative concentration are collectively termed verbal misconduct.
What is unwholesome conduct of the mind?
Answer:
covetousness, ill will, and wrong view.
Furthermore, all unwholesome mental actions, all mental actions induced by improper reasoning, and all mental actions that obstruct meditative concentration are collectively termed mental misconduct.
As the Blessed One said: "If,
having committed misconduct of body, speech, and mind,
one does not cultivate the remedies, one shall fall into hell."
The three types of sublime conduct refer to sublime conduct of body, sublime conduct of speech, and sublime conduct of mind.
What is sublime conduct of body?
Answer:
Abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, and abstaining from sexual misconduct;
furthermore, abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, and abstaining from unchaste conduct.

Furthermore, all bodily actions of those in training (*śaikṣa*), all bodily actions of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and all wholesome bodily actions of those who are neither in training nor beyond training are collectively termed "excellent conduct of body" (*kāyasucarita*).
What is "excellent conduct of speech" (*vāksucarita*)?
Answer:
It consists of abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, and abstaining from frivolous speech.

Furthermore, all verbal actions of those in training (*śaikṣa*), all verbal actions of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and all wholesome verbal actions that are neither of training nor beyond training are collectively termed "excellent verbal conduct" (*vāksucarita*).
What is the sublime mental conduct?
Answer:
Non-attachment, non-hatred, and right view.

Furthermore, all mental actions of those in training (*śaikṣa*), all mental actions of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and all wholesome mental actions that are neither of training nor beyond training are collectively termed "excellent mental conduct" (*manas-sucarita*).
As the Blessed One said:
"If one has cultivated excellent bodily conduct, excellent verbal conduct, and excellent mental conduct..."
"Those who are free from obstructing conditions will be born in the heavens and experience happiness.

Regarding the realm of desire, the realm of ill-will, the realm of harmfulness, as well as the realm of renunciation, the realm of non-ill-will, and the realm of non-harmfulness, these are as explained in the *Dharmaskandha-śāstra*.
The desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm are also as explained in the *Dharmaskandha-śāstra*.
As the Blessed One said:
"Those who are able to fully comprehend The realms of desire, form, and formlessness..."
Because it transcends all bases of dependence, one shall touch the state of no-remainder.
Having personally realized the realm of ambrosia— untainted and inconceivable—
the World-Honored One has taught Nirvana for the benefit of sentient beings.
The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and the realm of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*) are also as explained in the *Dharmaskandha-śāstra*.
As the Blessed One said:
“Sentient beings dwelling in the realm of form, And those dwelling in the formless realm...”
Because one has not realized and known cessation, one will certainly go to a future existence.
If one fully knows the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and does not dwell in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
one proceeds toward ultimate cessation and is later liberated from birth and death.
The second summary verse states:
Two, three, and ten dharmas; Worldly speech, bases, and conduct;
Mental factors, inclinations, and the Elder; Aggregates, exhortation, and the three non-guardings.

There are the three times, the three bases of speech, the three spheres of form, the three types of conduct, the three types of mind, the three types of *pudgala*, the three types of elders, the three groups, the three matters of censuring offenses, and the three things that need not be guarded.
The "three periods of time" refers to the past, the future, and the present.
What is the past? Answer:

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that have already arisen and fully arisen, already been born and fully born, already occurred and fully manifested, already accumulated and fully appeared; which have fallen away into the past, being exhausted, ceased, departed, and transformed; which possess the nature of the past, the category of the past, and are subsumed within the past time—this is called the "past."
What is the future time?
Answer:

Those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that have not yet arisen, have not yet fully arisen; have not yet been born, have not yet fully been born; have not yet occurred, have not yet manifested; have not yet accumulated, and have not yet appeared—possessing the nature of the future, the category of the future, and being subsumed within the future time—this is called the future time.
What is the present time? Answer:

Those formations (*saṃskāra*) that have already arisen and have been fully arisen; that have already been born and have been fully born; that have already evolved and have manifested; that have gathered and appeared; which abide without yet having passed away, without yet having been exhausted or ceased, and without yet having undergone transformation—being present by nature, belonging to the category of the present, and subsumed within the present time—this is called the present time.
Question:
What is the meaning of "world" (loka)?
Answer:
"World" (*loka*) is a designation for all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
The "three bases of speech" (*vāk-āśraya*) refer to the past basis of speech, the future basis of speech, and the present basis of speech.
What is the "verbal basis of the past"?
How is it spoken, and upon what basis is the "verbal basis of the past" explained?
Answer:

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that have already arisen and fully arisen, already been born and fully born, already occurred and fully manifested, already accumulated and fully appeared; which have fallen away into the past, being exhausted, ceased, departed, and transformed—belonging to the nature of the past, the category of the past, and subsumed within the past time—this is called "the past."

Based on such past formations, whatever arises as speech, utterance, discourse, calling, proclamation, manifestation, instruction, vocal path, vocal sound, vocal action, and vocal intimation—this is called "speech."
Furthermore, the aforementioned past formations are also called the "basis of speech.

This is because they serve as the cause, the root, the path, the condition, the origination, the immediate inducer, the productive condition, the collection, and the co-arising [of speech]; and because it is based upon past formations that various forms of speech arise. Therefore, past formations are termed the "past basis of speech."
What is the basis for discourse concerning the future?
How is it that the future is spoken of, and upon what basis is discourse concerning the future expressed?
Answer:

Those formations that have not yet arisen, have not yet fully arisen; have not yet been born, have not yet fully been born; have not yet occurred, have not yet manifested; have not yet accumulated, have not yet appeared; which possess a future nature, belong to the future category, and are subsumed within the future time—these are called the future.

Based on such future formations, whatever arises as speech, utterance, discourse, calling, proclamation, manifestation, instruction, the path of speech, vocal sound, vocal action, and vocal intimation—this is called "speech."
Furthermore, as previously stated, future conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are also called the "basis of speech.

This is because they are the cause, the root, the path, the condition, the origination, the immediate inducer, the producer, the condition for arising, the collection, and the origin; and because it is in dependence upon future conditioned phenomena that discourse regarding speech arises. Therefore, future conditioned phenomena are termed the "basis of speech for the future."
Regarding the "present verbal basis" (*pratyutpanna-vāk-āśraya*): what is the present, what is the speech, and what is the basis such that one speaks of the "present verbal basis"?
Answer:

Those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that have already arisen and have fully arisen, have already been produced and have fully been produced, have already evolved and have currently evolved; which have gathered and appeared, which abide without yet having passed away, without yet having ceased or been extinguished, and without yet having undergone transformation; which are present before one through their conjunction—possessing the nature of the present, the category of the present, and being subsumed within the present time—this is called the "present."

Based upon such presently existing conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), whatever arises as speech, utterance, discourse, calling, proclamation, manifestation, instruction, the path of speech, vocal sound, vocal action, or vocal intimation—this is called "speech."
Furthermore, the aforementioned present formations are also called the "basis of speech.

Because they are the cause, the root, the path, and the condition for the arising of speech—acting as the immediate inducer and the productive conditions for its origination—and because various forms of speech arise in dependence upon present formations, present formations are termed the "present basis of speech."

The statement that there is no fourth or fifth [category] is made in reference to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); that is to say, conditioned phenomena consist of only three types, and no fourth or fifth can be found.
Some say this is stated in reference to all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*): since all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are subsumed under the term "present," no fourth or fifth can be found.
As the Blessed One said:
"Sentient beings delight in verbal designations; They always abide in reliance upon verbal designations.
Without fully understanding verbal designations, They wander through birth and death without end."
If one thoroughly understands words and concepts, saying nothing to others and taking no pleasure in others' speech,
always delighting in the cultivation of meditative concentration;
being diligent in tranquil absorption and seeing the end of birth and death— this is called a true ascetic.
Having vanquished all the hosts of Māras, one reaches the further shore of birth and death.
Regarding the "three bases of form," this means there are three bases that encompass all form.
What are these three?
First, there is that which is material, visible, and resistant;
second, there is that which is material, invisible, and resistant;
third, there is that which is material, invisible, and non-resistant.
What is visible and resistant form?
Answer:
One base.
What is form that is invisible and impinging?
Answer:
Nine bases.
What is non-visible and non-obstructive matter?
Answer:
A small portion of one location.
The three types of formations are: bodily formation, verbal formation, and mental formation.
What is bodily formation?
Answer:

The body is also called bodily formation (*kāyasaṃskāra*); bodily action is also called bodily formation; inhalation and exhalation are also called bodily formations. Within this context, it is intended to refer to inhalation and exhalation as the bodily formations.

Why is this so? Inhalation consists of drawing external air into the interior of the body, while exhalation consists of expelling internal air to the exterior of the body. By the power of these two, the body is moved, becomes supple, and attains tranquility; therefore, inhalation and exhalation are called bodily formations (*kāyasaṃskāra*).
What is vocal activity?
Answer:

Speech is called vocal activity; vocal karma is also called vocal activity; and vitarka and vicāra are also called vocal activity. In this context, the intention is to refer to vitarka and vicāra as vocal activity.

Why is this so? It is because one must first engage in vitarka and vicāra before being able to produce speech; it is not the case that speech occurs without vitarka and vicāra. Therefore, vitarka and vicāra are said to be the mental formations of speech.
What, then, are the mental formations of mind?
Answer:

The mind is also called mental formation (*manas-saṃskāra*); mental action (*manas-karman*) is also called mental formation; and perception (*saṃjñā*) and volition (*cetanā*) are also called mental formations. Within this context, it is perception and volition that are intended by the term "mental formation."

Why is this so? Because perception (*saṃjñā*) and volition (*cetanā*) are mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*); they rely upon the mind, are bound to the mind, evolve in dependence on the mind, and assist the mind. Therefore, perception and volition are called mental formations (*manosaṃskāra*).
The three minds are: first, the mind likened to a leaking sore;
second, the mind likened to a flash of lightning;
and third, the mind likened to a vajra.
What is the analogy of the ulcer for the mind?
Answer:
As the Blessed One said:

"Monks, you should know that there is a certain class of persons (pudgala) in the world who are by nature violent and evil, delighting in coarse and harsh speech; they become greatly incensed at even a slight provocation, harboring resentment with stubborn malice, and their speech is fierce and aggressive."
Just as a malignant, discharging ulcer, upon being touched by even a slight object, immediately exudes copious pus and blood that will not cease, so too is that mind:
when encountering even a minor adverse condition, it immediately becomes enraged and harbors resentment that does not subside.
Question:
For what reason is that mind compared to a festering sore?
Answer:

When that mind, intellect, and consciousness briefly encounter adverse conditions, it immediately and swiftly gives rise to various kinds of foul and evil states; therefore, it is called "the mind likened to a leaking sore.
*Abhidharma-sarvāstivāda-saṃgīti-paryāya-pāda-śāstra*, Fascicle Three.
*Abhidharma-sarvāstivāda-saṃgīti-paryāya-pāda-śāstra*, Fascicle Four.
Spoken by the Venerable Śāriputra;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Four, Part Two: The Three Dharmas. What is the simile of the lightning flash regarding the mind?
Answer:
As the Blessed One said:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that there is a certain type of person who dwells in the forest, or at the foot of a tree, or in a secluded place. Through diligent application and frequent cultivation, they realize such a state of tranquil mental concentration. Relying on this concentrated mind, they are able to permanently sever the five lower fetters and attain the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmi). They undergo a superior birth by transformation and abide in the higher realms, attaining parinirvāṇa there without returning again to be born in the desire realm."
Just as when the summer season has passed and the early autumn arrives, a flash of lightning issues from a great cloud-palace, momentarily manifesting a form and color before swiftly vanishing;
likewise, for a certain class of *pudgala* who dwells in the forest hermitage (*araṇya*)—as described at length—the mind they attain is called "the simile of lightning."
Question:
For what reason is that mind called "the simile of lightning"?
Answer:

That mind-consciousness realizes the fruit of non-returning; it is able to illuminate [the truth] for a moment, but then quickly vanishes again. For this reason, it is called the "mind like a flash of lightning.
What is the "diamond-like mind"?
Answer: As the Blessed One said:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that there is a certain type of person who dwells in the forest, or at the foot of a tree, or in a secluded place. Because he has diligently practiced and cultivated [the path] extensively, he realizes such a state of tranquil mental concentration. Relying on this concentrated mind, he is able to exhaust all outflows (āsravas) and realize the untainted liberation of mind and wisdom. In this very life, through supreme direct knowledge and insight, he personally realizes and experiences the perfection of his virtues, namely: 'I have realized for myself that birth is exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence.'"
For example, there is no small thing that a vajra cannot cut, pierce, or shatter—whether it be iron, ivory, or shell; horn, pearl, or jade and stone.

In this way, there is a certain class of individuals who dwell in the forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*), and so forth, as extensively described; the mind they have attained is called "diamond-like" (*vajropama*).
Question:
For what reason is that mind called "diamond-like"?
Answer:

That mind, consciousness, and mentation realize the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*); because it cannot be destroyed by fetters, bonds, and the like, it is therefore called the "diamond-like mind" (*vajropama-citta*).

As for the three types of persons (*pudgala*): the first is the person whose wisdom is obscured; [the second is the one whose wisdom is unobscured; and the third is the one whose wisdom is both obscured and unobscured].
Second, the person of obscured wisdom;
third, the person of extensive wisdom.
What is the person of obscured wisdom?
Answer:
As the Blessed One said:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that there is a certain type of person in the world who sits before a bhikṣu for the sake of hearing the Dharma. Out of compassion, the bhikṣu preaches the essentials of the Dharma to him, revealing that which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with skillful and elegant phrasing and meaning—a pure, singular, perfect, and stainless holy life. Yet, while seated upon the Dharma-seat, he is unable to understand any part of the Dharma taught—neither the beginning, the middle, nor the end."
Having risen from their seats, they were likewise unable to comprehend the beginning, middle, or end of the Dharma that was taught. Why is this?
Because they possess no wisdom at all;
they are like overturned vessels or inverted jars, which, though much water be poured upon them, ultimately receive and retain nothing.

In this way, a certain class of person sits before a bhikṣu for the sake of hearing the Dharma; as has been explained at length, they possess no wisdom at all—such a person is called one whose wisdom is obscured.
Question:
For what reason is such a person called one whose wisdom is obscured?
Answer:

He possesses such wisdom that, while seated upon the Dharma-seat, although he desires to know every part of the teaching—the beginning, middle, and end—he is unable to know them all because he lacks [the necessary] wisdom.

Although such a person possesses this wisdom, once they have risen from their seat, even though they wish to comprehend the beginning, middle, and end of the Dharma taught, because they lack [true] wisdom, they are unable to comprehend it; therefore, they are called a person of obscured wisdom (*āvṛtaprajña-pudgala*).
What is a person of "knee-wisdom" (jānu-prajña)?
Answer:
As the Blessed One said:

“Bhikṣus, you should know that there is a certain class of persons who sit before the bhikṣus for the sake of hearing the Dharma. Out of compassion, the bhikṣus preach the essentials of the Dharma to them, revealing that which is virtuous in the beginning, virtuous in the middle, and virtuous in the end—whose phrasing and meaning are exquisite, pure, complete, and the pristine holy life.”

While he was on the Dharma-seat, although he was able to understand all parts of the teaching—the beginning, middle, and end—he was unable to comprehend any part of the teaching once he rose from his seat; though he had previously received it, he subsequently forgot it.
For example, suppose a person obtains exquisite food and drink and places it upon their lap; yet, due to a lapse in mindfulness, they suddenly rise from their seat and cause it all to fall.

In the same way, a certain type of *pudgala* sits before a *bhikṣu* to listen to the Dharma, and after having explained it at length, subsequently forgets it. Such a person is called a *pudgala* with "knee-wisdom."
Question:
For what reason is such a person called one of "knee-wisdom" (jānumātra-pañña)?
Answer:

When he possesses this wisdom while seated upon the Dharma-seat, because he possesses this wisdom, he is able to know all parts of the teaching—the beginning, middle, and end—exactly as he wishes to know them;
yet when he rises from his seat, although he still wishes to comprehend all parts of the teaching—the beginning, middle, and end—he is unable to do so because he lacks that wisdom.
Although one has previously received [the teachings], they are later forgotten; therefore, such a person is called one of "stunted wisdom" (khila-prajña).
What is a person of "vast wisdom" (vipula-prajña)?
Answer:
As the Blessed One said:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that there is a certain class of persons who sit before the bhikṣus for the sake of hearing the Dharma. Out of compassion, the bhikṣu preaches the essentials of the Dharma to them, revealing that which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; its phrasing and meaning are exquisite, it is pure, unified, complete, and the pristine holy life."

While seated upon the Dharma-seat, he is able to fully understand the beginning, middle, and end of the Dharma he teaches; having risen from his seat, he likewise fully comprehends the beginning, middle, and end of the Dharma taught, and is further able to skillfully understand the underlying meaning and intent of what has been said.

It is like a daughter of the kṣatriya caste, or a daughter of the brāhmaṇa caste, or a daughter of a householder, or a daughter of a lay devotee, who has bathed in clear water, anointed her body with exquisite perfumes, combed and trimmed her hair and nails, polished her brows and face, donned fresh and clean garments, put on various necklaces, and adorned herself with bracelets and bangles, yet remains with only a single flower garland not yet placed upon her head.
There were certain venerable ones who held exquisite flower garlands—such as those of the *utpala* and *campaka*—and bestowed them upon them according to their preferences.
At that time, the women were filled with joy and exultation; they respectfully received them and placed them upon their heads, cherishing them with deep devotion and never letting them go.

In this way, a certain class of individuals sits before a bhikṣu for the sake of hearing the Dharma, and so forth, until they thoroughly understand the meaning and intent of what is taught; these are called individuals of extensive wisdom.
Question:
For what reason is one called a person of extensive wisdom (prabhūtaprajña-pudgala)?
Answer:

He possesses such wisdom that, while seated upon the Dharma-seat, regarding the teachings he expounds, he is able to know—according to his desire—the beginning, middle, and end of those teachings; because he possesses this wisdom, he is able to know them all completely.

Possessing such wisdom, once he has risen from his seat, he can understand, according to his desire, the beginning, middle, and end of the Dharma taught; because he possesses this wisdom, he is able to comprehend it all and further skillfully discern the intended meaning of what was taught; therefore, he is called a person of extensive wisdom (*pudgala*).
