As the Blessed One said:
"One whose wisdom is obscured lacks intelligence; though they have heard the Dharma many times, lacking wisdom, they cannot comprehend it, just like pouring water into an overturned vessel."
Those of limited wisdom are superior to those before them;
though they may understand while sitting and listening, they forget everything once they have risen, like food dropped from one's lap.
Those of vast wisdom are most excellent; even when rising from their seat in the Dharma assembly, [they do not lose what they have heard].
Fully understanding both the words and their meaning, like a woman wearing a flower garland;
possessing mindfulness, retention, and eloquence, delighting in the cultivation of pure deeds and detachment;
severing arrogance and negligence, one is able to abandon all evil destinies.
Regarding the "three types of elders," these are the elder by birth, the elder by worldly convention, and the elder by the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
What is the elder by birth?
Answer:
Those who are senior by birth—venerable elders and those of advanced age—are called "seniors by birth.
What is a "worldly elder"?
Answer:
Suppose there were a wealthy and noble elder who knew the Dharma, and he established a rule with others, saying:

"To all those who know the Dharma and possess greater wealth, higher status, more distinguished lineage, greater power, larger retinues, and more numerous followers than we do, we shall all recommend them as the senior seat (upādhyāya), and we shall provide for them with offerings, reverence, respect, and praise."

For this reason, even if one is only twenty or twenty-five years of age, if they are able to know the Dharma and have attained great wealth, status, noble lineage, and great power, and possess a large retinue and many followers, everyone should harmoniously unite to recommend them as the *sthavira* (elder), making offerings to them, honoring, respecting, and praising them.

Just as in various lands, cities, and royal capitals, those who possess great learning, excellent understanding of calculation, eloquence in writing and seals, or who excel others in any particular craft or field of work, are all united in harmony to elect them as the presiding elder (*sthavira*), providing for them with offerings, respect, honor, and praise.

Just as among a caravan of merchants, one who possesses great wealth is unanimously elected by the group as the presiding elder (sthavira), being provided with offerings, honored, revered, and praised;
or just as when one becomes a king or a high minister, all people together provide him with offerings, honor, reverence, and praise.

For example, when King Nanda, of the lineage of Long-Haired Kings, desired to incite war, he summoned King Aśvajit of the Kṣatriya caste, bestowed upon him abundant wealth and jewels, and commanded him to demonstrate various skills.
Having recognized his superiority, he said to the minister:
"Lord of the Realm, you should know that I wish to pay homage at the feet of King Aśvajit of the Kṣatriya caste.
The minister replied:
“Your Majesty should not pay homage at the feet of the Kṣatriya King Aśvājita. Why is this?
He is a minister and counselor;
a sovereign should not pay homage at the feet of a minister or counselor.”
There are countless such matters of this kind; what is intended here is the worldly elder during the time of King Nanda of the Long-Haired royal lineage.
What, then, is the Dharma-nature elder?
Answer:
Those who have received full ordination and are elderly and long-standing are called *dharmatā-sthaviras*.
Some say that these are also *sthaviras* by birth year.
Why is this? Because the Buddha has taught that one who has gone forth and received full ordination is called "truly born.

If there is a bhikṣu who has attained arhatship—whose taints are forever exhausted, who has done what was to be done and accomplished what was to be accomplished, who has laid down the heavy burden and attained his own benefit, whose fetters of existence are destroyed and who is liberated through right knowledge, and whose mind is well-mastered—it is with reference to such a person that the term "Elder of the Dharma-nature" (dharmatā-sthavira) is used here.
As the World-Honored One spoke in the verses of the Elder:
"With a mind wavering and much idle chatter, With a defiled intent and distracted thoughts,
Though one has long dwelt in secluded groves, One is not a true Elder."
"Endowed with precepts, wisdom, and right mindfulness, With a mind tranquil and liberated,
One who can thus contemplate the Dharma Is called a true Elder.
The three groups refer to the group fixed in wrongness, the group fixed in rightness, and the indeterminate group.
What is the group fixed in wrongness?
Answer:
The five deeds of immediate retribution.
What is the group of those fixed in the right nature?
Answer: The dharmas of those in training and those beyond training.
What is the indeterminate group?
Answer:
It consists of all other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), excluding the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya-karma*).

Regarding the three matters of accusing another of an offense: these are the matter of accusing based on what was seen, the matter of accusing based on what was heard, and the matter of accusing based on suspicion.

As for the matter of accusing based on what was seen: what constitutes "seeing," what constitutes "accusing," and what constitutes the "matter" such that one speaks of the matter of accusing based on what was seen?
Answer:

"Seeing" refers to seeing a bhikṣu intentionally take the life of a living being, taking what is not given, engaging in unchaste sexual conduct, knowingly speaking false speech, intentionally emitting semen, eating at improper times, drinking various intoxicants, digging the earth with one's own hands, destroying living plants and trees, or engaging in singing, dancing, music, wearing flower garlands, and indulging in heedless dissipation; this is called "accusing by seeing."
This refers to five ways of charging with an offense:

first, charging based on observation; second, charging based on recollection; [third, charging based on suspicion; fourth, charging based on what has been heard; fifth, charging based on what has been seen].
Third, one should formally announce the *karmavācanā* when raising a charge;
fourth, establishing the raising of a charge at the time of the *poṣadha*;
fifth, establishing the raising of a charge at the time of the *pravāraṇā*.
What is the accusation based on observation?
Answer:
It refers to one who observes.
The other bhikṣu said:
"Venerable one, you have committed such and such an offense; you should confess it and not conceal it. To confess brings peace, whereas by not confessing, the offense becomes even more grave."
This is called "accusation based on observation.
What is "accusation based on recollection"?
Answer:
This refers to having another person instruct them to bring it to mind, saying:
"Venerable one!
You have already committed such-and-such an offense; you should confess it and not conceal it. To confess brings peace, whereas to fail to confess causes the offense to become even more grave."
This is called the formal accusation based on recollection.
What is the formal accusation through a *karmavācanā* (procedural motion)?
Answer:
One should say:
"Venerable one, you should not depart silently from this dwelling place without having alerted me; I have something of little importance to say to you."
This is called the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the accusation of an offense.
What is the procedure for establishing the accusation during the *poṣadha* ceremony?
Answer:
This refers to one who has been appointed during the *poṣadha* ceremony and speaks as follows:
"This community of bhikṣus is sitting together in harmony to perform the *poṣadha*; I, the bhikṣu named so-and-so, have been appointed by this *poṣadha* assembly."
This is called the formal establishment of an accusation during the *pravāraṇā*.
What is the formal establishment of an accusation during the time of the *pravāraṇā*?
Answer:
This refers to when those appointed to conduct the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) speak as follows:

"The community of bhikṣus is sitting together in harmony to perform the rite of *pravāraṇā*; I, the bhikṣu named so-and-so, have been appointed by this assembly for the purpose of conducting the *pravāraṇā*."
This is called establishing the formal accusation (*ukkhepana*) at the time of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.

This is called "accusation" (*ukkhepa*). "Matter" (*vatthu*) refers to the very offense previously seen; this is called the "matter. Thus, these combined are termed the "matter of an accusation based on what was seen" (*diṭṭhena ukkhepaka-vatthu*).

Regarding "hearing of the matter of accusing another of an offense": what is meant by "hearing," what is meant by "accusing," and what is meant by "matter" such that one speaks of "hearing of the matter of accusing another"?

Answer: "Hearing" refers to hearing that a bhikṣu has intentionally taken the life of a living being; has taken what was not given; has engaged in unchaste conduct, the practice of sexual desire; has knowingly spoken false speech; has intentionally emitted semen; has eaten at improper times; has drunk various liquors; has dug the earth with his own hands; has destroyed living plants and trees; or has engaged in singing, dancing, music, wearing flower garlands, and other forms of dissipation and self-indulgence. This is called "hearing of the accusation."

That is to say, the five kinds of formal accusation (codanā) as previously described are called "accusation" (codanā); the matter (vastu) refers to the specific offense heard as mentioned above, which is called "matter"; thus, these combined are termed "the matter of hearing an accusation."

Regarding the matter of raising a charge based on doubt: what is doubt, what is raising a charge, and what is the matter, such that one speaks of "the matter of raising a charge based on doubt"? Answer: Doubt arises from five conditions: [1] seeing, [2] hearing, [3] suspecting, [4] recollecting, and [5] being deluded. These are called the five conditions for the arising of doubt. What is meant by "seeing"? It refers to seeing with the eye a person who has committed an offense, or seeing them commit a transgression, or seeing them engage in improper conduct. This is called "seeing. What is meant by "hearing"? It refers to hearing with the ear that a person has committed an offense, or hearing them commit a transgression, or hearing them engage in improper conduct. This is called "hearing. What is meant by "suspecting"? It refers to suspecting that a person has committed an offense, or suspecting them to have committed a transgression, or suspecting them to have engaged in improper conduct. This is called "suspecting. What is meant by "recollecting"? It refers to recollecting that a person has committed an offense, or recollecting them to have committed a transgression, or recollecting them to have engaged in improper conduct. This is called "recollecting. What is meant by "being deluded"? It refers to being deluded regarding a person who has committed an offense, or being deluded regarding them committing a transgression, or being deluded regarding them engaging in improper conduct. This is called "being deluded. These are the five conditions for the arising of doubt. What is meant by "raising a charge"? It refers to accusing another of an offense, accusing them of a transgression, or accusing them of improper conduct. This is called "raising a charge. What is meant by "the matter"? It refers to the basis upon which the charge is raised—namely, the offense itself, the transgression, or the improper conduct. This is called "the matter. Thus, one speaks of "the matter of raising a charge based on doubt."
First, by way of form;
second, by way of sound;
third, by way of fragrance.
Fourth, by way of flavor; fifth, by way of touch.

Regarding "by way of form," it refers to seeing a bhikṣu entering a village at an improper time or leaving a village at an improper time; or entering or leaving a grove with a woman; or being intimate with non-Buddhists; or being intimate with *śaṇḍhas* or *paṇḍakas*; or being intimate with bhikṣuṇīs; or being intimate with prostitutes; or being intimate with young boys; or being intimate with grown women; or being intimate with widows.
Having seen such suspicious matters as these, he conceived a doubt:

"Observing this venerable one's current conduct, which is so impure, unbecoming of a śramaṇa, and inconsistent with his practice, it is certain that this venerable one must have already committed an act contrary to the celibate life."
This is called the arising of doubt due to visible forms (*rūpa*).

Regarding [doubt] due to sounds (*śabda*), it refers to hearing that a bhikṣu has entered a village at an improper time or departed from a village at an improper time; or hearing that he has entered or departed from a grove with a woman; or hearing that he is intimate with non-Buddhists, intimate with *ṣaṇḍhas* or *pandakas*, intimate with bhikṣuṇīs, intimate with courtesans, intimate with young boys, intimate with adult women, or intimate with widows.
Having heard such doubtful matters as these, he conceived a doubt:

"I have heard that this venerable one currently practices such impure conduct, which is neither the way of a śramaṇa nor a practice in accordance with it; therefore, this venerable one must certainly have already committed the offense of unchaste conduct."
This is called the arising of doubt due to sound. Regarding that which arises due to odor:

suppose there is a bhikṣu who, for the purpose of washing his hands, or washing his face, or drinking water, or for some other reason, enters the dwelling place of another bhikṣu and smells various defiled odors—namely, the scent of women, or the scent of wine and meat, or the scent of ointments and incense, or any other scent associated with sexual indulgence. Having smelled these odors, he then gives rise to a doubtful thought:
"Since such impure, un-Sramanic, and un-conformable odors are present in this venerable one’s dwelling place, he must certainly have violated the practice of celibacy."
This is called the arising of doubt due to fragrance. Regarding that which arises due to taste:

suppose there is a bhikṣu who, for the purpose of washing his hands, washing his face, or drinking water, or for some other reason, enters the dwelling place of another bhikṣu and sees that bhikṣu chewing various flavored substances in his mouth—namely, *tambūla*, camphor, nutmeg, or any other such sensual flavor.
Having seen that bhikṣu taste such flavors, he conceived this doubt:
"Now, since this venerable one’s tongue has tasted such impure, un-monastic, and non-conforming flavors, he must certainly have already committed an act contrary to the holy life."
This is called the arising of doubt through taste. Regarding that which arises from contact:

suppose there is a bhikṣu who, for the purpose of washing his hands, washing his face, drinking water, or for some other reason, enters the dwelling place of another bhikṣu. There he sees the bed and seat where that bhikṣu resides, adorned with precious incense and decorated with fine, soft, multicolored fabrics; it is furnished with brocade, embroidery, and silk, and at both ends of the bed are placed vermilion pillows covered with kāliṅga cloth. Furthermore, in that dwelling place, he sees a woman—beautiful and young—either sitting or lying down.
Having seen this, he immediately conceived a doubt:

"Now, the body of this venerable one has such impure contact; it is neither that of a śramaṇa nor contact consistent with the path. He must certainly have already committed an act contrary to the holy life."
This is called the arising of doubt through contact.
This is called "accusation based on doubt," referring to the five types of accusation as previously explained.
This is called the "matter of the accusation," meaning that the very matter of the offense previously doubted is what constitutes the matter.
These are collectively termed the matters of raising charges based on doubt.

Regarding the "three non-guardings," it means that the three types of action (trikarma) of all Tathāgatas are free from error; because there is nothing to conceal for fear of being discovered by others, they are called "non-guardings."
What are the three?

First, all bodily actions (*kāyakarman*) of the Tathāgata are pure in their manifestation; there are no impure manifestations of bodily action that he must conceal or guard for fear of being perceived by others.

Second, all verbal actions of the Tathāgata are pure in their manifestation; there are no impure verbal actions manifested such that he would need to conceal or protect them for fear of being perceived by others.
Third, all mental actions of the Tathāgata are pure in their manifestation; there are no impure mental actions that he would need to conceal or guard from others' perception.
What is the Tathāgata’s pure manifestation of bodily action?
Answer:
The pure manifestation of bodily action refers to abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, and abstaining from sexual misconduct.
Furthermore, it consists of abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, and abstaining from unchaste conduct.

Furthermore, all instances of the manifestation of pure bodily action belonging to those in training (*śaikṣa*), all instances of the manifestation of pure bodily action belonging to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and all instances of the manifestation of pure bodily action that are wholesome but belong to neither those in training nor those beyond training, are collectively termed the manifestation of pure bodily action.

In this context, the meaning intended is the pure manifestation of all the bodily actions of the Tathāgata that are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as the pure manifestation of all his bodily actions that are neither [beyond] training nor [still] in training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
Because the Tathāgata has fully and perfectly accomplished such pure conduct of bodily action, it is said that all the Tathāgata’s bodily actions are pure in their manifestation.
What is the Tathāgata’s lack of impure manifest bodily action?
Answer:
Impure manifest bodily action refers to taking life, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct.
Furthermore, taking life, taking what is not given, and unchaste conduct;

furthermore, all unwholesome bodily actions, all bodily actions induced by improper reasoning, and all bodily actions that obstruct meditative concentration—these are collectively termed impure manifest bodily actions.

Regarding these impure manifestations of bodily action, the Tathāgata has already severed them and fully understood them; like cutting the root of a grass or the crown of a *tāla* tree, he has rendered them such that they will never arise again in the future.

For this reason, the Tathāgata has nothing to conceal, hide, or shield, lest others see this impure bodily karma of his; therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata has no impure manifestation of bodily karma.
What is the Tathāgata’s pure engagement in vocal action?
Answer:
Pure engagement in vocal action means being free from false speech, free from divisive speech, free from harsh speech, and free from frivolous speech.

Furthermore, all instances of the pure manifestation of the speech-activity of those in training (*śaikṣa*), all instances of the pure manifestation of the speech-activity of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and all instances of the pure manifestation of the wholesome speech-activity of those who are neither in training nor beyond training, are collectively termed the "pure manifestation of speech-activity."

In this context, the meaning intended is that all the pure manifestations of the Tathāgata’s post-learner (aśaikṣa) vocal karma, as well as all the pure manifestations of his wholesome vocal karma that is neither learner nor post-learner (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa), are present.
Because the Tathāgata has fully and perfectly accomplished such pure conduct of vocal action, it is said that all the Tathāgata’s vocal actions are pure in their manifestation.
What is the Tathāgata’s lack of impure verbal conduct?
Answer:
Impure verbal conduct refers to false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech.

Furthermore, all unwholesome verbal karma, all verbal karma induced by improper reasoning, and all verbal karma that can obstruct meditative concentration are collectively termed impure verbal karma in its actual manifestation.

Regarding these impure verbal actions in their active manifestation, the Tathāgata has already severed them and fully understood them; like cutting the root of a grass or the crown of a tāla tree, he has rendered them such that they will never arise again in the future.

Because there is nothing in the Tathāgata that must be concealed, obscured, or guarded against—lest others see this karma of his impure speech—it is said that the Tathāgata has no unwholesome verbal conduct in manifestation.
What is the Tathāgata’s pure manifestation of mental action?
The answer is: the pure manifestation of mental action refers to non-attachment, non-hatred, and right view.

Furthermore, all instances of the manifestation of pure mental action belonging to those in training (*śaikṣa*), all instances of the manifestation of pure mental action belonging to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and all instances of the manifestation of pure mental action that is wholesome yet belongs neither to those in training nor to those beyond training—these together are termed the manifestation of pure mental action.

In this context, the meaning is intended to refer to the pure manifestation of all the Tathāgata’s mental actions that are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as the pure manifestation of all his wholesome mental actions that are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
Because the Tathāgata has fully and perfectly accomplished such pure conduct of mental karma, it is said that all the Tathāgata’s mental karma is pure conduct.
What is the Tathāgata’s lack of impure mental activity in its manifestation?
Answer:
Impure mental activity in its manifestation refers to greed, hatred, and false views.

Furthermore, all unwholesome mental karma, all mental karma induced by improper reasoning, and all mental karma that can obstruct meditative concentration are collectively termed impure manifest mental karma.

The Tathāgata has already severed and fully understood these impure mental actions in their active manifestation; like cutting the root of a grass or the crown of a tala tree, he has rendered them such that they will never arise again in the future.

For this reason, the Tathāgata has nothing to conceal, hide, or shield from view, lest others perceive these defiled mental actions of his; therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata has no impure manifestation of mental action.
The third summary verse states:
There are nine sets of three dharmas, namely: the three types of craving, outflows, and seeking;
as well as darkness, the body, fear, suffering, and the categories of pride.
There are three cravings, three outflows, three searches, three modes of existence, three dark bodies, three fears, three feelings, three natures of suffering, and three types of conceit.
The three cravings are: first, craving for sensual pleasures;
second, craving for form;
and third, craving for the formless.
What is sensual craving?
Answer:

Among all sensual desires, it is the various forms of greed and pervasive greed, the grasping and hoarding, the guarding and protecting, the indulgence and attachment, and the defiled passion; this is called sensual craving.

Furthermore, among the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates of phenomena associated with the desire realm, all forms of greed, pervasive greed, grasping and hoarding, guarding and protecting, indulgence and attachment, and passionate defilement—these are called "desire-craving" (*kāmatṛṣṇā*).

Furthermore, from the Avīci Great Hell below up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven above, within all these encompassed phenomena of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, whatever constitutes greed, pervasive greed, grasping and storing, guarding and protecting, indulgence and attachment, and passionate defilement—this is called sensual craving (*kāmatṛṣṇā*).
What is craving for form (*rūparāga*)?
Answer:

Among all forms, it is the various types of greed and pervasive greed, the grasping and hoarding, the guarding and protecting, the indulgence and attachment, and the defiled passion; this is called craving for form.

Furthermore, among the fourteen elements, ten bases, and five aggregates that are bound to the form realm, all forms of greed, pervasive greed, grasping, hoarding, guarding, attachment, and defiled craving—these are called "craving for form."

Furthermore, from the Heaven of the Retinue of Brahmā below up to the Heaven of Ultimate Form above, within all phenomena comprised therein—form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—the various forms of greed, pervasive greed, grasping, hoarding, guarding, attachment, and defiled craving are called "craving for form."
What is craving for the formless?
Answer:
It is the various forms of greed and pervasive greed toward the formless realms, including grasping, hoarding, guarding, attachment, and defiled craving; this is called craving for the formless.

Furthermore, among the phenomena associated with the formless realm—namely, those belonging to the three realms, two bases, and four aggregates—the various forms of greed, pervasive greed, grasping, hoarding, protection, indulgence, and stained attachment are called "craving for the formless."

Furthermore, just as in the desire realm and the form realm there are fixed locations with distinct upper and lower levels that do not intermingle, such a thing does not exist within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Nevertheless, one may speak of "lower" and "upper" based on the superiority or inferiority of meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and rebirths (*upapatti*). That is to say, from the lower level of the Heaven of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) up to the highest level of the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), regarding all phenomena—feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—contained therein, whatever craving, intense craving, grasping, hoarding, guarding, indulgence, and passionate attachment there is, this is called "craving for the formless" (*ārūpyatṛṣṇā*).
As the Blessed One said:
“Those persons possessed of craving Wander through the long course of time;
Repeatedly undergoing the suffering of the womb, They come and go among the various realms of existence.”

“Sentient beings who have severed craving, because the torrential floods have been cut off and there is no longer the moisture of craving to sustain rebirth, do not transmigrate into future existence.
Furthermore, there are three types of craving: first, craving for sensual desire; [second, craving for existence; third, craving for non-existence].
2. craving for existence;
3. craving for non-existence.
What is craving for sense-desires?
Answer:
Among all desires, whatever constitutes greed, pervasive greed, grasping, hoarding, guarding, attachment, and passionate defilement—this is called craving for sense-desires (*kāmatṛṣṇā*).
What is craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*)?
Answer:

The various forms of craving and pervasive craving for the realms of form and formlessness—characterized by grasping, concealing, guarding, indulgence, and defiled attachment—is called craving for existence (*bhavarāga*).
What is craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*)?
Answer:

For one who delights in non-existence, the various forms of craving, intense craving, grasping, hoarding, guarding, indulgence, and passionate attachment toward that state of non-existence are called *vibhavatṛṣṇā* (craving for non-existence).
Furthermore, how is this so?

Suppose there is a certain class of people who are oppressed by fear, tormented by fear, oppressed by sorrow and suffering, and tormented by sorrow and suffering; because they are touched by painful sensations, they form this thought:
"How wonderful it would be if, after my body has died, it were cut off and destroyed, never to exist again, and all illnesses were forever severed—would that not be bliss?"

He delights in non-existence; regarding that non-existence, he experiences various forms of craving and intense craving, grasping at it, guarding it, and becoming attached to it with passionate longing—this is called craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*).
As the Blessed One said:
"Sentient beings gripped by craving, Their minds greedy for existence and non-existence,
Bound by the yoke of Māra, Their bodies are never at peace."
"Flowing through the various realms of existence, Once born, one returns to old age and death;
Like a calf longing for its mother's milk, It follows her, never leaving.
As for the three outflows (*āsrava*): first, the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*); [second, the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*); third, the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*)].
2. The outflow of sensual desire;
3. the outflow of ignorance.
What is the outflow of sensual desire?
Answer:

With the exception of ignorance bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-avidyā*), all other fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) bound to the desire realm are called the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*).
What is the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*)?
Answer:

With the exception of ignorance bound to the realm of form and the formless realm, all other fetters, bonds, latent tendencies, secondary afflictions, and entanglements bound to the realm of form and the formless realm are called "with outflows" (sāsrava).
What is the outflow of ignorance?
Answer:
Lack of wisdom regarding the three realms; this is called the outflow of ignorance.
As the Blessed One said:
"If a bhikṣu has already severed the outflows of sensual desire, existence, and ignorance,
then because all outflows are eternally exhausted, he attains parinirvāṇa without shadow."
The three types of seeking are: first, the seeking of sensual desire;
second, the seeking of existence;
and third, the seeking of the holy life.
What is the pursuit of sensual desire (*kāma-paryeṣaṇā*)?
Answer:

For one who dwells in the realm of sensual existence (*kāmadhātu*), the various pursuits for the sake of attaining those sensual-dharma teachings not yet attained—namely, the pursuit, the conforming pursuit, the equal conforming pursuit, the longing pursuit, the eager pursuit, the seeking pursuit, and the diligent pursuit—this is called the pursuit of sensual desire.
What is the seeking of existence (*bhava-paryeṣaṇā*)?
Answer:

For one who dwells in the realms of form or formlessness, the various seekings up to diligent seeking for the sake of attaining those dharmas of the realms of form and formlessness that have not yet been attained—this is called the seeking of existence.
What is the pursuit of the holy life (*brahmacarya*)?
Answer:
Abstinence from the two types of sexual union is called the holy life; the Noble Eightfold Path is also called the holy life.
In this context, the "holy life" (brahmacarya) refers to the Noble Eightfold Path.
The "search for the holy life" (brahmacaryaiṣaṇā) is defined as all seeking, up to and including diligent striving, by those who have not yet attained this Noble Eightfold Path and seek to attain it.

Furthermore, as for the "search for sensual desires" (*kāma-paryeṣaṇā*): it is not a search for being reborn in various states of existence after death; rather, it refers to the seeking, even the diligent seeking, for the sake of obtaining—among present things that are agreeable to one's mind—the objects of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, as well as clothing, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for illness. This is called the search for sensual desires.
There is that which is sought; "that which is" refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandhāḥ*). What are the five?

They are the aggregate of clinging to form (*rūpa-upādānaskandha*), the aggregate of clinging to feeling (*vedanā-upādānaskandha*), the aggregate of clinging to perception (*saṃjñā-upādānaskandha*), the aggregate of clinging to formations (*saṃskāra-upādānaskandha*), and the aggregate of clinging to consciousness (*vijñāna-upādānaskandha*).
Suppose there is a certain class of people who think to themselves:
"How may I obtain such a kind of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness in a future life?

After death, they will be born into the various realms of existence; their seeking for the five aggregates, such as form and so forth—even their diligent seeking—is called "craving for existence" (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*).

Regarding the seeker of the holy life (*brahmacarya*): when one proceeds from the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) toward the "receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), there is a seeking of the holy life, yet it is not yet the possession of the holy life. Why is this so?
The Noble Eightfold Path is called the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
At that time, it has not yet been attained nor nearly attained; it does not yet exist nor is it currently present.

However, from the moment one proceeds from the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) toward the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), there is both the seeking of the holy life and the holy life itself.
Why is this? The Noble Eightfold Path is called the "holy life" (brahmacariya); at that time, he has already attained it, has nearly attained it, possesses it, and it is present before him.

In this manner, one proceeds from the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) to the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvayajñānakṣānti*); from the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering to the subsequent knowledge of suffering;

from the subsequent knowledge of suffering to the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of origination (*samudaya-dharmajñānakṣānti*); from the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of origination to the dharma-knowledge of origination;

from the dharma-knowledge of origination to the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvayajñānakṣānti*); and from the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of origination to the subsequent knowledge of origination.

Wisdom proceeds from the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvaya-jñāna*) toward the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñānakṣānti*); from the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of cessation toward the knowledge of the dharma of cessation;

from the knowledge of the dharma of cessation toward the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñānakṣānti*); from the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of cessation toward the subsequent knowledge of cessation;

from the subsequent knowledge of cessation toward the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharmajñānakṣānti*); and from the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of the path toward the knowledge of the dharma of the path.
When wisdom proceeds from the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*) toward the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*),

from the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path toward the subsequent knowledge of the path, from the subsequent knowledge of the path toward the subsequent knowledge of the path, or when proceeding toward other untainted knowledges (*anāsravajñāna*),
there is both the quest for the holy life (*brahmacaryaiṣaṇā*) and the holy life itself.
Why is this? The Noble Eightfold Path is called the "holy life" (brahmacariya); at that time, he has already attained it, has nearly attained it, possesses it, and it is present before him.

Furthermore, when one realizes the fruit of a Once-returner or a Non-returner by means of the mundane path, there is a seeking of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) that is not [itself] the holy life. Why is this so?
The Noble Eightfold Path is called the "holy life" (*brahmacarya*). At that time, it has not been attained, nor has it been nearly attained; it has not existed, nor is it currently present.

However, when one realizes the fruit of stream-entry through the untainted path, or realizes the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, or arhatship, there exists both the seeking of the holy life and the holy life itself.
Why is this? The Noble Eightfold Path is called the "holy life" (brahmacariya); at that time, he has already attained it, has nearly attained it, possesses it, and has it manifest.
As the Blessed One said:
"Endowed with mindfulness, concentration, and clear comprehension,
the true disciples of the Buddhas seek the noble path with clear comprehension, and never seek after anything else."
"If craving has already ceased, one shall proceed toward the exhaustion [of suffering] via the Noble Path;
because the bhikṣu seeks this exhaustion, he attains shadowless parinirvāṇa. Regarding the "three existences" (trai-dhātuka):
first, the existence of desire (kāma-bhava); [the others being the existence of form and the existence of the formless].
2. Form existence; 3. Formless existence.
What is sensual existence?
Answer:

If karma bound to the desire realm takes grasping as its condition and is intended to bring about future existence (*bhava*), that maturation of such karma is called "existence in the desire realm" (*kāma-bhava*).
What is "existence in the form realm" (*rūpa-bhava*)?
Answer:
If karma bound to the form realm takes grasping as its condition and is intended to bring about future existence, that maturation of such karma is called "form-existence" (rūpa-bhava).
What is "formless-existence" (arūpya-bhava)?
Answer:

If karma bound to the formless realm takes grasping as its condition and is intended to bring about future existence, the maturation of that karma is called "existence in the formless realm" (ārūpyabhava).
Regarding the three bodies of darkness: first, the body of darkness of the past; [second, the body of darkness of the present; third, the body of darkness of the future].
2. The dark body of the future;
3. The dark body of the present. Regarding the dark body of the past:
what is the past, what is darkness, and what is the body, such that they speak of it as the "dark body of the past"?

Answer: The past refers to those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that have already arisen and have been fully arisen; that have already been produced and have been fully produced; that have already evolved and have been fully manifested; that have already accumulated and have appeared; that have fallen away, passed, ceased, vanished, and transformed. Being of a past nature, belonging to the past category, and subsumed within the past time—this is called the past.

"Darkness" refers to the various forms of speculative inquiry and divergent wisdom initiated regarding past formations, extending in detail up to the arrow of doubt and hesitation; this is called darkness.
Regarding "body" (*kāya*): some say that ignorance associated with doubt is called "body.
Within this context, it is precisely doubt that is named "body. Why is this so?
"Black" refers to a lack of wisdom; because it is black, it is dark, and is thus called "darkness," which is itself doubt.
This very darkness is called the "body"; therefore, it is termed the "past body of darkness."
Regarding the phrase "the dark body of the future": what is the future, what is darkness, and what is the body, such that one speaks of "the dark body of the future"? Answer:

The "future" refers to those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that have not yet arisen, have not yet fully arisen; have not yet been produced, have not yet fully been produced; have not yet occurred, have not yet fully occurred; have not yet manifested, have not yet fully manifested; have not yet accumulated, and have not yet appeared. Being of the nature of the future, belonging to the category of the future, and subsumed within the future time—this is called the future.

"Darkness" refers to the various forms of analytical inquiry and divergent wisdom initiated regarding future formations, ranging extensively up to the arrow of doubt and hesitation; this is called darkness.
Regarding "body" (*kāya*): some say that ignorance associated with doubt is called "body.
Within this context, it is precisely doubt that is named "body. Why is this so?
"Black" refers to a lack of wisdom; because it is black, it is dark, and is thus called "darkness," which is to say doubt.
This very darkness is called the "body"; therefore, it is termed the "future body of darkness."

Regarding the phrase "the present dark body" (*pratyutpanna-tamaskāya*): what is meant by "present," what is meant by "dark," and what is meant by "body" such that one speaks of "the present dark body"?

Answer: "Present" refers to those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that have already arisen and have fully arisen; have already been born and have fully been born; have already evolved and have manifested as having evolved; which have gathered, appeared, and remain; which have not yet passed away, have not yet ceased or been extinguished, and have not yet departed from their combination but are manifest before one. Being of the nature of the present, belonging to the category of the present, and included within the present time—this is called "present."

"Darkness" refers to the arising of various forms of divergent wisdom seeking understanding regarding present activities, ranging extensively up to the arrow of doubt and hesitation; this is called darkness.
Regarding "body" (*kāya*): some say that the ignorance associated with doubt is called "body.
Within this context, it is precisely doubt that is termed "body. Why is this so?
"Black" refers to a lack of wisdom; because it is black, it is dark, and is thus called "black darkness," which is precisely doubt.
This very black darkness is termed the "body," and is therefore called the "present body of black darkness."
The three fears are: first, the fear of illness;
second, the fear of old age;
and third, the fear of death.
Regarding "fear of illness," what is illness?
Answer:
Headaches and so forth, as explained in detail in the *Dharmaskandha-śāstra*; this is called illness.
What is fear (*bhaya*)?
Answer:

Suppose there is a certain person who, having seen another’s illness, develops a deep sense of revulsion and aversion, thinking to himself: "My own body also possesses this portion, possesses this nature, possesses this quality, and has not transcended this condition. Because of this, he gives rise to alarm, terror, dread, and horripilation; this is called fear.
Because fear arises from illness, it is called "fear of illness.
Regarding the "fear of old age," what is old age?
Answer:
The falling out of hair and so forth, as explained in detail in the *Dharmaskandha-śāstra*, is called old age.
What is fear?
Answer:
For instance, there is a certain class of people who, upon seeing others aged, give rise to deep revulsion; as described at length, they become so terrified that their hair stands on end.
This is called "fear. Because fear arises from aging, it is termed "the fear of aging."
Regarding the fear of death: what is death?
Answer:

It is the transition, dissolution, and disappearance of various sentient beings from their respective groups of sentient beings; as explained at length in the *Dharmaskandha-śāstra*, this is called death.
What is fear? Answer:
It is when a certain class of persons, having seen another die, gives rise to deep revulsion and distress, and so forth, up to being terrified with their hair standing on end; this is called fear.
Because fear arises from death, it is called "fear of death.
As the Blessed One said:
"Though ordinary worldlings are able to feel revulsion for the phenomena of sickness, old age, and death,"
Yet, unable to see it as it truly is, one does not grow weary of this dependent body.
I am able to grow weary of this body;
having deeply understood this Dharma, I take no pleasure in dwelling long, but shall swiftly enter the realm of nirvana without remainder.
I observe every aspect: the life of the healthy youth is destroyed by sickness, old age, and death; only renunciation brings peace and security.
I have exerted myself with diligence and attained mastery of the ultimate path.
"Though not practicing among the various desires, he abandons them and cultivates the holy life.

Chapter Four: The Three Dharmas, Part Three. Regarding the three types of feeling (*vedanā*): first, pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).
2. painful feeling;
3. neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
What is pleasant feeling?
Answer:

That which is comprised within the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*)—arising from contact conducive to pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanīya-sparśa*) and consisting of bodily pleasure and mental pleasure—is called pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).

Furthermore, when practicing the first, second, and third dhyānas, that which is comprised within the feeling of equanimity—arising from contact conducive to pleasant feeling and consisting of bodily pleasure and mental pleasure—is called pleasant feeling.
What is the feeling of suffering?
Answer:

It is the bodily and mental pain, the unbalanced feeling, and that which is comprised within feeling, produced by contact conducive to the feeling of suffering; this is called the feeling of suffering.
What is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?
Answer:

It is the bodily equanimity and mental equanimity produced by contact conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; it is a feeling that is categorized as feeling, being neither balanced nor unbalanced. This is called neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
As the Blessed One said:
"Endowed with mindfulness, concentration, and clear comprehension,
the true disciples of the Buddhas are able to correctly understand all feelings, thereby preventing greed and other defilements from arising."
"Regarding all sensations and the path, may they both be gradually extinguished; because the monk has exhausted sensation, he attains shadowless parinirvāṇa.

As for the nature of the three types of suffering: first, the nature of the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā); [second, the nature of the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā); and third, the nature of the suffering of conditioned formations (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā)].
2. the nature of suffering as change (vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā);
3. the nature of suffering as conditioned formations (saṃskāraduḥkhatā).
What is the nature of suffering as suffering (duḥkhaduḥkhatā)?
Answer:
The conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are suffering by way of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
What is the nature of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*)?
Answer:

The conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are suffering by virtue of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*). What is the nature of the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*)?
Answer:
The formations (*saṃskāra*) of the formless realm are suffering by virtue of the suffering inherent in formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).

Furthermore, disagreeable formations are suffering by virtue of the suffering of pain (*duḥkha-duḥkha*); agreeable formations are suffering by virtue of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*); and formations conducive to equanimity are suffering by virtue of the suffering inherent in formations.

Furthermore, whether it be painful feelings, their associated phenomena, or their co-existent phenomena—whether arising from them or being of their same nature—the undesirable ripening fruit is suffering by virtue of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*).

Whether it be pleasant feelings, the mental factors associated with them, the phenomena coexistent with them, those arising from them, or their desirable ripened fruits of that same category—all these are suffering by virtue of the suffering inherent in change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*).

Whether it be a sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant, or the mental factors associated with it, or the phenomena co-arising with it, or those produced from them, or their subsequent types—such neutral ripened fruits (vipāka-phala) that are neither desirable nor undesirable—are suffering by virtue of the nature of conditioned suffering (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā).
Furthermore, what is the nature of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*)?
Answer:
It is that which pertains to all bodies and is suffering by virtue of the suffering of suffering.
Why is this? Because it is upon the basis of the body that various sufferings such as old age, sickness, and death arise.
What is the nature of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*)?
Answer:

As the Blessed One has said, when pleasing friends, pleasing associates, or pleasing objects undergo change and deterioration, or when one encounters slander, contempt, and so forth, sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and despair arise; at that time, one suffers by virtue of the suffering inherent in change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
What is the nature of suffering as conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*)? Answer:

With the exception of the nature of suffering as pain (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) and the nature of suffering as change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), all other contaminated conditioned phenomena (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*) are suffering by virtue of being suffering as conditioned existence.
Regarding the three types of pride: first, the type of pride thinking "I am superior";
second, the type of pride thinking "I am equal";
and third, the type of pride thinking "I am inferior."
What are the types of pride regarding superiority?
Answer:
For example, there is a certain class of people who think as follows:

Regarding my lineage, physical appearance, occupation and craft, wealth and status, lifespan, strength, and so forth—whether collectively or individually—all these are superior to theirs; from this arises pride, past pride, or future pride, a loftiness of mind and a haughty disregard for others: this is called the class of pride known as "I am superior."
What is the category of the pride of "I am"?
Answer:
It is when a certain class of persons thinks as follows:

Regarding my lineage, physical appearance, occupation and craft, wealth and status, lifespan, strength, and so forth—whether collectively or individually—if, due to specific causes and conditions, one gives rise to pride, has given rise to pride, or will give rise to pride, such that the mind is uplifted and the mind is conceited and disdainful, this is called the category of pride of equality (*sammāna-māna*).
What is the type of inferiority-conceit (*ūnamāna*)?
Answer:
It is when a certain class of persons thinks as follows:

Whether collectively or individually, my lineage, physical appearance, occupation and craft, wealth and status, lifespan, strength, and so forth, are all inferior to theirs; yet, due to various causes and conditions, I give rise to pride—past, present, or future—characterized by mental exaltation and self-conceited disdain. This is called the type of pride regarding one's own inferiority (*hīnātmābhimāna*).
The fourth summary verse says:
There are ten [sections] on four groups of three dharmas, namely:
fire, merit, desire, pleasure, as well as wisdom, faculties, eyes, and reliance; six [sections] on fire and two on wisdom.
There are three fires, three bases of meritorious action, three births through desire, three births through pleasure, three types of wisdom, three faculties, three eyes, and three supports.
Of these, fire and wisdom each have two categories; the remaining six each have one.
The three fires of the first three days are: first, the fire of greed;
second, the fire of hatred;
and third, the fire of delusion.
What is the fire of greed?
Answer:

It refers to all forms of greed and equal greed regarding objects of desire; it is characterized by grasping and hoarding, guarding and protecting, firm attachment, fondness, and delight; it involves delusion and confusion, indulgence and pervasive indulgence, internal fetters, seeking and craving, and the arising of greed from the category of greed that constitutes the accumulation of suffering. Taken together, these are termed "greed."

Those who are thus obscured and overwhelmed by craving give rise to various kinds of bodily fever, mental fever, and both bodily and mental fever; bodily burning, mental burning, and both bodily and mental burning; as well as bodily affliction, mental affliction, and both bodily and mental affliction.

Furthermore, because craving as an entangment serves as a condition, one experiences for a long night the ripening fruit that is undesirable, unpleasant, unenjoyable, and disagreeable; this is called the fire of craving.
What is the fire of hatred? Answer:

It refers to the desire to cause harm toward sentient beings; harboring internal resentment with the intent to disturb and afflict them; having been angry, being about to be angry, or currently being angry; delighting in faults and extreme faults; the mind being intensely enraged; and desiring to cause harm to sentient beings through mutual opposition and contrariety—whether such harm has already occurred, will occur, or is occurring at present—all this is collectively termed "hatred."

One who is thus obscured and overwhelmed by hatred gives rise to various kinds of bodily heat, mental heat, and both bodily and mental heat; bodily burning, mental burning, and both bodily and mental burning; bodily affliction, mental affliction, and both bodily and mental affliction.

Furthermore, because one is conditioned by the obsession of malice, one experiences for a long night the ripening fruits that are unlovely, unpleasant, disagreeable, and contrary to one's will; this is called the fire of malice.
What is the fire of delusion (*moha*)?

The answer is: ignorance regarding the past, ignorance regarding the future, and ignorance regarding both the past and the future; explained at length, it includes everything from the category of delusion and that which arises from delusion, up to the category of transformation and that which arises from transformation—collectively, this is termed delusion.

Overwhelmed and suppressed by this ignorance, they give rise to various kinds of fever of body, fever of mind, and fever of both body and mind; burning of body, burning of mind, and burning of both body and mind; and affliction of body, affliction of mind, and affliction of both body and mind.

Furthermore, because it takes the entanglement of delusion as its condition, one experiences for a long night the ripening fruit that is undesirable, unpleasant, unpleasing, and disagreeable; this is called the fire of delusion.
As the Blessed One said:
"Those who are of the class of fools, burned by the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion,
respectively indulge in sensual objects, harm living beings, and harbor animosity toward the noble Dharma."
If one does not know, as it truly is, the blazing fires of the three poisons,
one will remain attached to the existence of a self and be unable to proceed toward nirvana.
By this, one treads upon the wrong path and falls into the three evil realms.
Suffering intense agony and transmigrating in saṃsāra, they remain unable to untie the bonds of Māra.
The disciples of the Perfectly Awakened One, always diligent day and night,
extinguish the three fires respectively through foul contemplation, loving-kindness, and wisdom.
"From this one enters the noble path, subdues the armies of Māra, and realizes the two types of nirvāṇa—cool, tranquil, and free from grasping and outflows.
As for the latter three fires: first, the fire to be served and honored; [the second, the fire of the afflictions; and the third, the fire of wisdom.]
2. One should provide offerings to the fire;
3. one should make sacrifices to the fire.
What is meant by "one should serve the fire"?
Answer:
Parents are those whom a child ought to serve and honor.
As the Blessed One said when addressing the brahmin Ujjaya: "What is meant by 'one who should serve the fire'?"
It means that worldly parents ought to receive various articles of pleasure from their children, being served correctly at all places and times.
How, then, should a child serve the sacrificial fire with various articles of pleasure, being correct in its service at all places and times?

It means that a son of noble family, by the power of diligence, the strength of his hands and feet, or the labor of his sweat and blood, uses wealth and articles of enjoyment acquired in accordance with the Dharma to serve and make offerings to his parents appropriately and at the proper times, without error.
Why is it called "the fire that should be served"?
It is because a son of noble family is born from them, nurtured by them, and thereby brought to completion; for this reason, the Buddhas declare that parents are the fire that should be served.
What is it that should be given as alms?
Answer:
Wives, children, slaves, servants, and kinsmen—these are what the head of the household ought to provide.
As the Blessed One said when teaching the brahmin Ujjaya: "What is meant by 'one who should be given offerings to the fire'?

It refers to one's wife, children, servants, laborers, and various kinsmen and friends, to whom the head of the household should appropriately provide various articles of enjoyment at the proper place and time."
How does a householder provide various articles of enjoyment to those to whom they ought to be given—namely, the sacrificial fires—at the proper place and time without error?

It means that a son of noble family, by means of the power of diligence, the strength of his hands and feet, or the labor of his sweat and blood, provides wealth and articles of enjoyment acquired in accordance with the Dharma to his wife, children, slaves, servants, laborers, and friends at the proper place and time without error.
Why is he called "One to Whom Fire Should Be Offered"?

It is because this son of noble family lives at home in accordance with the Dharma; his wife and others serve him without error, performing for him as instructed whatever tasks are to be done, so that he lacks nothing and his aims are swiftly accomplished.
Therefore, the Buddhas have taught that one’s wife, children, slaves, servants, and all kinsmen and friends should be regarded as fuel to be given to fire.
How should one provide offerings to this fire?
Answer:
True śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are those who should be venerated by all donors.
As the Blessed One said when addressing the brāhmaṇa Ujjaya: "What is meant by 'the fire that should be venerated'?"

This refers to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who have already abandoned greed or are practicing the discipline of subduing greed; who have already abandoned hatred or are practicing the discipline of subduing hatred; and who have already abandoned delusion or are practicing the discipline of subduing delusion. Such śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas should receive from donors various articles of comfort, provided with correct offerings at the appropriate place and time.
How does a donor provide offerings of various requisites for enjoyment to the fire worthy of worship, in accordance with the proper place and time, and without error?

It means that a son of noble family, by means of the power of diligence, the power of his hands and feet, or the power of sweat and blood—using wealth and requisites for enjoyment acquired in accordance with the Dharma—provides offerings in accordance with the proper place and time, and without error.
Regarding the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas mentioned previously, for what reason are they called "fires to be honored"?

It is because when members of noble families honor arhats and those in training (śaikṣas), these individuals are the true fields of merit (puṇyakṣetra) in the world; they enable the donor to plant merit therein, thereby bringing about the most excellent ripening of wealth and happiness in this life and future lives, as well as the fruit of liberation. For this reason, the Buddhas declare that true śramaṇas and true brāhmaṇas are fires to be honored.
Other worldly fires are not to be honored, served, or offered to, for they cannot cause sentient beings to attain superior fruits.
As the Blessed One said:
"The wise, according to the Dharma, perform sacrifices to the three fires."
"Born into a world of happiness, one realizes the liberation that is free from suffering.
Regarding the three types of meritorious actions: first, the meritorious action consisting of giving; second, the meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline;
[and third, the meritorious action consisting of cultivation].
Third, the meritorious activities consisting of cultivation.

Regarding the meritorious activity consisting of giving: what is "consisting of giving," what is "merit," what is "activity," and what is "matter" such that it is called a "meritorious activity consisting of giving"?
Answer:

Regarding the category of giving (*dāna*), it refers to a donor bestowing upon śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, those practicing the path, and beggars such as food, drink, medicinal decoctions, clothing, flower garlands, and various scents for anointing and scattering.
Dwellings, bedding, seats, lamps, candles, and such items are called the category of giving.
Furthermore, there may be giving by means of the body—namely, giving the body itself or giving bodily action;
or there may be giving by means of speech—namely, giving speech itself or giving vocal action.

Either by giving away material objects or by giving through the mind—meaning either giving the mind itself, or giving mental action (*manas-karman*), or giving the mind of relinquishment (*tyāga-citta*)—this is called the category of giving.
Merit refers to bodily restraint, verbal restraint, and purity of livelihood that accompany giving; this is called merit.

Action refers to the various volitions accompanying giving—including initial volition, sustained volition, subsequent volition, and the category of volition—as well as the mental and physical acts performed by the mind; this is called action.
"Entity" (vastu) refers to the donor, the recipient, and the object given; these are called the entity.
Within this context, the category of giving is termed the "category of giving," and it is also termed merit (puṇya), action (karman), and entity (vastu).
In this context, merit (puṇya) is called "merit," and it is also called "action" (karma), "matter" (vastu), and "the category of giving" (dāna-varga).
In this context, action is called "action," and it is also called "matter," "the category of giving," and "merit."
In this context, "matter" refers solely to the matter of names.

Regarding the "basis of meritorious action consisting of the class of morality": what is the class of morality, what is merit, what is action, and what is the basis, such that it is described as the "basis of meritorious action consisting of the class of morality"?
Answer:

As for the category of ethical discipline (*śīla*), it refers to abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from sexual misconduct, abstaining from false speech, and abstaining from drinking *sura*, *maireya*, *madhya*, and intoxicating liquors that lead to negligence; this is called the category of ethical discipline.
"Merit" refers to bodily restraint, verbal restraint, and purity of livelihood that accompany ethical discipline; this is called merit.

"Karma" refers to the various volitions that accompany ethical discipline—including initial volition, sustained volition, subsequent volition, and the category of volition—as well as the mental and vocal actions performed by the mind; this is called karma.
"Action" refers to guarding against, ceasing, warding off, or abstaining from the act of taking life; this is the act of abstaining from taking life.
It refers to guarding against, ceasing, warding off, or abstaining from the act of taking what is not given; this is the act of abstaining from taking what is not given.
To guard against, to cease, to obstruct, or to abstain from sexual misconduct is the abstention from sexual misconduct.
To guard against, to cease, to obstruct, or to abstain from false speech is the abstention from false speech.

If one guards against, ceases, obstructs, or abstains from the consumption of *surā*, *maireya*, and *madana*—the intoxicants that are the basis for heedlessness—this is the act of abstaining from all fermented and distilled liquors.
This is called the "matter."
In this context, the category of morality is called the "category of morality," and it is also called merit, action, and matter.
In this context, merit is called "merit," and it is also called action, matter, and the category of morality.
In this context, what is called "action" (*karman*) is termed action, and is also termed a "matter" (*vastu*), a "category of morality" (*śīla-nikāya*), and "merit" (*puṇya*).
In this context, what is called a "matter" is termed a matter, and is also termed a category of morality, merit, and action.

Regarding the "bases of meritorious action consisting in cultivation" (*bhāvanā-maya-puṇya-kriyā-vastu*): what is cultivation, what is merit, what is action, and what is the basis, such that they are called "bases of meritorious action consisting in cultivation"?

Answer: Regarding the category of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it refers to the four immeasurables—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; these are called the category of cultivation.
Regarding merit (*puṇya*), it refers to the bodily restraint, verbal restraint, and purity of livelihood that accompany the immeasurables; these are called merit.

Karma refers to volitions (cetanā) that proceed in conjunction with the immeasurables, including the categories of volition, equal volition, manifest volition, completed volition, and the nature of volition; these constitute the mental and vocal actions of the mind, which are termed karma.
Regarding "the basis" (*vastu*): it refers to the objective basis (*ālambana-vastu*) upon which the four immeasurables arise;
this is called the "basis. In this context, the category of cultivation is termed "category of cultivation," and it is also called merit, action, and basis.
In this context, merit is called "merit," and it is also called "action" (*karman*), "matter" (*vastu*), and "the category of cultivation.
In this context, action is called "action," and it is also called "matter," "the category of cultivation," and "merit."
In this context, "phenomena" (dharma) refers solely to named phenomena.
As the Blessed One said:
"The wise, relying upon the Dharma, Diligently train in generosity, ethical discipline, and cultivation."
"Born into a world free from suffering, one experiences the fruits of three kinds of happiness.

Regarding the first type of birth through desire: there are sentient beings who delight in experiencing the various excellent objects of desire present before them, and they exercise sovereign mastery over these present excellent objects of desire. This refers to humans in their entirety and a portion of the devas; this is the first birth through desire.

There are sentient beings who delight in experiencing various exquisite sensory objects created by themselves; they exercise sovereign power over these self-created exquisite sensory objects. These are the gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati), which is the second birth within the realm of desire.

There are sentient beings who delight in experiencing the various exquisite objects of desire provided by others; they exercise sovereign mastery over these exquisite objects of desire provided by others, namely the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Creations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), which is the third birthplace of the desire realm.

Regarding the phrase "therein exist sentient beings": these sentient beings are, in truth and in the ultimate sense, unapprehendable and unattainable; they do not exist, nor do they manifest as existing. They are merely designated by the conventional expressions of "notion" (*saṃjñā*) and "conceptualization" (*prajñapti*) upon the aggregates, elements, and bases—referring to them as a "sentient being," a "man" (*nara*), a "mind-born" (*manuja*), a "young brahmin" (*māṇava*), a "life-principle" (*jīva*), a "born one" (*jantu*), a "nourisher" (*poṣa*), a "person" (*puruṣa*), or an "individual" (*pudgala*). It is for this reason that it is said there exist sentient beings for whom pleasant feeling is present.

Regarding "the objects of various exquisite desires," this refers to those sentient beings who constantly delight in enjoying, guarding, accumulating, entrusting, and depositing the objects of desire that appear before them according to their original mode of birth.

Regarding "the mastery and sovereignty over the various excellent objects of desire present before them," this means that those sentient beings, with respect to the objects they enjoy—whether stored, guarded, accumulated, entrusted, or deposited—possess power and attain sovereignty over the objects of desire present before them according to their original birth, and thus enjoy them as they wish.
"Those who are complete as humans" indicates all human beings.
"One part of the devas" indicates the four lower heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
"This is the first" means that, according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and successive order of calculation, this occupies the first position.
"Those who desire birth" refers to those born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Furthermore, "there are sentient beings" means that sentient beings cannot be apprehended in terms of their reality, ultimate meaning, or supreme truth; this is explained in detail as previously stated.

Regarding "those who delight in the various exquisite objects of desire created by themselves," this refers to the gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*nirmāṇarati*), who perform such types of karma that bring about transformation and increase. By means of this karma, they create various things—such as men and women—according to their own desires and enjoy them; that is to say, if a goddess creates a god-man and enjoys herself, or if a god-man creates a goddess and enjoys himself.

Regarding their sovereign mastery over the rich and wondrous objects of desire they themselves emanate: this refers to the gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*), who perform such superior karma; by virtue of that karma, they emanate various things such as men and women according to their own inclinations, and they possess the power and sovereignty to enjoy these things as they wish.
"Those who are the gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati)" refers to all the gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations.
"This is the second" means that, according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and successive order of calculation, this occupies the second position.
"Those who desire birth" refers to those born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, "there are sentient beings" means that sentient beings are not to be found in terms of reality, ultimate truth, or the highest meaning; this is explained in detail as previously stated.

Regarding "those who delight in the various exquisite objects of desire created by others": this refers to those in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Creations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*) who perform and cultivate such types of karma; by virtue of that karma, although they share the same class of body, the same realm, the same birth, and the same destiny as the other inhabitants of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Creations, there are nevertheless distinctions of high and low, superior and inferior among them.
The inferior devas manifest various objects of the five sensory pleasures—forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles—and cause the superior devas to enjoy them therein.

As for their sovereignty over the wealth of these manifested sensory pleasures of others, it means that the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas perform and accumulate such types of karma that, by virtue of this karma, they cause the inferior devas to manifest various objects of the five sensory pleasures according to their own desires; thus, those superior devas possess the power and mastery to enjoy these sensory objects at will.

For example, although the gods of the Brahma realm share the same class, the same destiny, the same birth, and the same mode of progression, there are distinctions of high and low, superior and inferior; namely, the gods of the Brahma-pāriṣadya heaven are inferior while the Brahma-purohita gods are superior, and the Brahma-purohita gods are inferior while the Mahābrahmā gods are superior.

The Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods are also like this; they perform and increase such types of karma, and by virtue of that karma—explained at length as before—they are called Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods, which signifies all those who possess mastery over the transformations created by others.
"This third one" refers to its position as the third according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and successive order of calculation.
"Born in the desire realm" means that it arises within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Regarding the three types of birth through joy: there are sentient beings who, with this very body, are moistened, thoroughly moistened, gladdened, thoroughly gladdened, filled, and thoroughly filled by the joy and bliss born of seclusion; having been moistened and even thoroughly filled, they dwell in peace and happiness—namely, the gods of Brahma’s Retinue (Brahmapārisadya). This is the first birth through joy.

There are sentient beings who, with this very body, are thoroughly moistened, thoroughly saturated, thoroughly gladdened, and thoroughly suffused by the joy and bliss born of concentration; being thus thoroughly moistened and even thoroughly suffused, they dwell in happiness—namely, the Ābhāsvara devas. This is the second realm of rebirth through bliss.

There are sentient beings who, with this very body, are moistened, thoroughly moistened, gladdened, thoroughly gladdened, filled, and thoroughly filled by the joy born of detachment from rapture; having been moistened and even thoroughly filled, they dwell in bliss—namely, the gods of the Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna), which is the third rebirth in bliss.

Regarding the phrase "therein exist sentient beings": these sentient beings are, in truth and in the ultimate sense, unapprehendable, unattainable, non-existent, and not presently manifest. They exist merely as designations, conventions, and verbal expressions based upon the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases—such as "sentient being," "man," "mind-born," "mortal," "life-principle," "creature," "nourisher," "person," and "individual. It is for this reason that it is said, "therein exist sentient beings."

Regarding this very body: "body" is called *kāya*; bodily action is also called *kāya*; the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is also called *kāya*; the five material faculties are also called *kāya*; and the aggregate of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) is also called *kāya*. In the present context, the intended meaning refers to the body as the aggregate of the four great elements; therefore, it says, "this very body."
"Joy and happiness born of seclusion" refers to the pleasure obtainable within the first dhyāna, which is comprised of the feeling of equanimity; this is called joy and happiness born of seclusion.

"Moistening and thoroughly moistening, refreshing and thoroughly refreshing, filling and thoroughly filling" means that the gods of the Brahma-purohita realm obtain this joy and happiness born of seclusion according to their desire, without hardship or difficulty. That is to say, this very joy and happiness born of seclusion arises, fully arises, is produced, fully produced, accumulates, and manifests, thereby causing this body—a collection of the four great elements—to be moistened and thoroughly moistened, refreshed and thoroughly refreshed, and filled and thoroughly filled.

"Having been moistened and even completely filled, he dwells in ease" means that at that time, through the joy and bliss born of seclusion, his body and mind dwell in ease, free from suffering and affliction.
As the Blessed One said in the *Vibhaṅga-jāti-sūtra*:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that just as a practitioner of meditative concentration, passing away from this place, is born among the Brahmakāyika devas and frequently experiences the joy and happiness born of seclusion."
Having previously dwelt here and entered the first dhyāna, he also frequently experienced the joy and bliss born of seclusion;
the joy and bliss born of seclusion he experienced before and after were no different and no distinct, because they were based on equal concentration.
This means that because one first practices, cultivates, or frequently performs [the meditative work] regarding the first dhyāna in this world, one is subsequently born in that Brahmakāyika heaven.
Second, the category of the joy and bliss born of seclusion experienced by both is similar; that is to say, the "Brahmakāyika devas" indicates the first dhyāna.
The Heaven of the Brahma-multitude (*Brahmakāyika*) is the first; that is to say, according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and successive order of enumeration, this occupies the first place.

As for "Birth in Joy" (*Sukhopapatti*), it refers to the fact that in this place of birth one experiences peaceful and secure joy for a long duration; being free from suffering and joy, one experiences pleasant sensations, and is thus called "Birth in Joy."
Furthermore, regarding "there are sentient beings": it means that sentient beings cannot be apprehended in terms of their reality or ultimate meaning, as explained at length previously.
Regarding "this very body": "body" is called "body," and so forth, as explained at length.

Regarding "the joy and bliss born of concentration": this refers to the pleasure obtainable within the second dhyāna, which is comprised within the category of equanimous feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*); this is called the joy and bliss born of concentration.

That which moistens, thoroughly moistens; gladdens, thoroughly gladdens; fills, thoroughly fills—this refers to how the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, within this meditative absorption, obtain the joy and bliss born of concentration at will, without hardship or difficulty.
