Furthermore, regarding clothing—namely, outer robes, upper garments, undergarments, single-layered skirts, double-layered skirts, single-layered armpit-covers, and double-layered armpit-covers—whatever greed, excessive greed, grasping, hoarding, protection, firm attachment, and defiled craving one has toward such various types of clothing is called the arising when it should arise, the abiding when it should abide, and the grasping when it should be grasped, due to the craving for clothing by bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and others.
How is it that bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and others, due to craving for food and drink, arise when they should arise, abide when they should abide, and grasp when they should grasp?
Answer: In this context, "food and drink" refers to the five kinds of edible foods and the five kinds of consumable foods.
The five kinds of things that should be chewed are: first, roots; second, stalks; third, leaves; fourth, flowers; and fifth, fruits.
The five kinds of things that should be eaten are: first, cooked rice; second, congee; third, cakes and parched grain flour; fourth, fish and meat; and fifth, soups and stews.

Regarding such various foods and drinks, the various forms of greed, intense greed, grasping, hoarding, guarding, firm attachment, and defiled craving—these are what is meant by the monks and nuns giving rise to craving for food and drink when it ought to arise, abiding in it when it ought to abide, and grasping at it when it ought to be grasped.

How is it that monks, nuns, and others, out of attachment to bedding and furniture (*śayanāsana*), arise when they ought to arise, remain when they ought to remain, and grasp at them when they ought to grasp?
Answer:

In this context, "bedding and furniture" refers to courtyards, houses, halls, pavilions, towers, and palaces; long corridors, circular rooms, grottoes, caves, courtyards, and verandas; as well as huts made of grass and leaves, and dwellings made of earth or stone.

Furthermore, regarding bedding and requisites (*śayanāsana*): this refers to beds, seats, woolen rugs, mattresses, single-layered mats, quilts, *karpāsa* cotton, *kambala* wool, pillows, coarse hair-cloths, and small stools.

With respect to such various kinds of bedding and requisites, whatever greed, excessive greed, grasping, hoarding, guarding, firm attachment, and defiled craving there may be—this is called the greed of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs for bedding and requisites, which arises when it ought to arise, persists when it ought to persist, and is grasped when it ought to be grasped.

How is it that bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and others, due to craving for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*) and craving for non-existence (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*), arise when they ought to arise, abide when they ought to abide, and grasp when they ought to grasp?
Answer:
Herein, "existence" refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandhāḥ*), namely, the aggregates of clinging of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"Non-existence" refers to the future cessation of these five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
For example, there is a certain class of people who think:
"May the five aggregates arise for me in the future."
Furthermore, there is another class who thinks:
"May my five aggregates be severed and extinguished after death.

Regarding existence and non-existence, they harbor craving, pervasive craving, attachment, concealment, protection, firm clinging, and defiled love. This is called the craving for existence and non-existence that arises when it should arise, persists when it should persist, and grasps when it should grasp, belonging to monks, nuns, and others.
Regarding the four types of improper conduct that one nevertheless engages in: first, engaging in what should not be done out of desire;
second, engaging in what should not be done out of hatred;
third, engaging in what should not be done out of delusion.
4. One should not engage in what ought not to be done out of fear.
How is it that one engages in what ought not to be done out of desire?
Answer:

Suppose there is a certain person—whether it be a preceptor, a teacher, a co-preceptor, a co-teacher, or any of their respective associates and friends—who, when a dispute arises within the Saṃgha, [acts as follows].
He thinks to himself:
"If I form a faction with my teacher and his peers, I fall into unrighteousness; if I do not form a faction with my teacher and his peers, I fall into injustice."
Although one forms such a thought, because one is obscured and overcome by desire, one gives rise to unwholesome physical and verbal actions; this is called "acting inappropriately due to desire."
What is meant by "acting out of malice when one ought not to act"?
Answer:
It is as when a certain person harboring resentment encounters a dispute arising within the Saṃgha.
He thought to himself:
"If I assist those who harbor resentment and enmity, it would be contrary to my feelings;
yet if I act in opposition to them, it would violate the principles of propriety."
Although they form this thought, because they are obscured and overcome by anger, they give rise to evil physical and verbal actions; this is called "acting inappropriately due to anger."
What is meant by "acting out of delusion when one ought not to act"?
Answer:

It is as when there is a certain class of person who is by nature dull-witted, and either his preceptor (*upādhyāya*), or his instructor (*ācārya*), or a fellow disciple of the preceptor, or a fellow disciple of the instructor, or any of his personal friends with whom he associates, has a dispute arise within the Saṃgha.
He thinks to himself:
"I do not now know what is right or wrong, or good or bad; I must simply support my preceptor and others.
Because he is overwhelmed and obscured by delusion, he initiates unwholesome physical and verbal actions. This is called acting inappropriately due to delusion.
What is meant by "engaging in conduct that should not be engaged in out of fear"?
Answer:
Suppose there is a certain person who is a friend of a king, a friend of a minister, or a friend of a powerful bandit, and a dispute arises within the Saṃgha.
He thought to himself:

"If I do not assist those who possess power, because of this cause and condition, I may lose my reputation and profit, or my robes and bowl, or even my life. Therefore, I must certainly now side with and support those who possess power."
Because he is overwhelmed and subdued by fear, he engages in unwholesome bodily and verbal actions; this is called "acting what should not be done out of fear.
As the Blessed One said:
"Those who possess greed, hatred, and delusion, and who violate the Dharma out of fear..."
"He has fallen away from fame and profit, Just like the waning moon.
Regarding the four ways of answering questions: first, there are questions that should be answered categorically;
second, there are questions that should be answered analytically.
Third, questions to be answered by counter-interrogation;
fourth, questions to be set aside.
What is a question to be answered categorically?
Answer:
If someone were to ask:

"Is the Blessed One a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Bhagavān?"
Is the Dharma taught by the Buddha well-expounded, directly visible, free from feverish affliction, timely, leading onward, to be personally realized by the wise within?

Is the Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples endowed with wondrous conduct, upright conduct, reasoned conduct, conduct in accordance with the Dharma, harmonious and respectful conduct, and conduct that follows the Dharma?
Are suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path noble truths?
Are all conditioned phenomena impermanent?
Are all phenomena selfless?
"Is nirvāṇa tranquil?
There are immeasurable such modes of questioning, to which one should give a categorical response (*ekāṃśavyākaraṇa*):
"The Blessed One is a Tathāgata, an Arhat," and so on, up to "nirvāṇa is tranquil. This is called a question to be answered categorically.
Why should this question be answered categorically? Answer:

Because if this question is answered categorically, it can lead to meaningful benefit, lead to wholesome qualities, lead to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), give rise to supernormal knowledge and wisdom (*abhijñā-prajñā*), produce perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and realize *nirvāṇa*; therefore, this question should be answered categorically.
How should a question be answered by means of analysis? Answer:
If someone were to ask:
"What is meant by 'dharma'? When asked this question, one should answer by means of analysis:

dharmas are of many kinds—whether past, future, or present; whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate; whether bound to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; whether of the learner (*śaikṣa*), the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), or neither learner nor non-learner; or whether to be abandoned by vision, abandoned by cultivation, or not to be abandoned.
There are immeasurable gateways to such dharmas that should be explained through analysis; this is called "that which should be explained through analysis.
Question:
Why should this question be explained through analysis?
Answer:

Because, regarding this question, if one were to provide an analytical answer (vibhajya-vyākaraṇa), it would lead to benefit, lead to wholesome qualities, lead to the holy life (brahmacarya), give rise to supernormal knowledge (abhijñā), produce perfect enlightenment (sambodhi), and lead to the realization of nirvana; therefore, this question should be answered analytically.
How should a question be answered by means of counter-interrogation? Answer:
If someone were to ask:
When asked, "Please teach me the Dharma," one should respond with a counter-question:
"The Dharma is of many kinds; which Dharma do you ask about?"

Are they past, future, or present? Are they wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate? Are they bound to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm? Are they of the learner (*śaikṣa*), the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), or neither learner nor non-learner? Are they to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*), abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), or not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*)?
Such dharmas as these have immeasurable modes; they should be answered by means of counter-interrogation, and this is called "answering by counter-interrogation.
Question:
For what reason should this question be answered by counter-interrogation?
Answer:

Because, regarding this question, if one were to answer by means of a counter-interrogation, it would lead to meaningful benefit, lead to wholesome qualities, lead to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), give rise to supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), produce perfect awakening (*sambodhi*), and bring about the realization of *nirvāṇa*; therefore, this question should be answered by means of a counter-interrogation.
What is the question that should be set aside?
Answer: If someone asks:
“Is the world eternal, or is it non-eternal, or both eternal and non-eternal, or neither eternal nor non-eternal?
Is the world finite, or is it infinite, or both finite and infinite, or neither finite nor infinite?”
Is the life-principle identical to the body, or is the life-principle different from the body?
Does the Tathāgata exist after death, or does he not exist, or does he both exist and not exist, or does he neither exist nor not exist?
Regarding such questions that are illogical, one should set them aside without providing an answer.
That is to say, one should respond by stating:
"The Buddha declared that this question is not to be answered, because [categories such as] permanence and impermanence are illogical."
This is called a question to be set aside.
Question:
For what reason should this question be set aside?
Answer:

Because, regarding this question, if one sets it aside without providing a categorical answer, it can lead to meaningful benefit, lead to wholesome qualities, lead to the holy life, give rise to supernormal knowledge and wisdom, produce perfect enlightenment, and bring about the realization of nirvana; therefore, this question should be answered by setting it aside.
As the Blessed One said:
"First, one should answer categorically; second, one should answer analytically;
third, one should answer with a counter-question; fourth, one should set it aside."
Regarding these four questions, one who knows how to answer them in sequence brings forth the benefit of meaning,
wholesome dharmas, and the utterly pure holy life (brahmacarya).
Profound and difficult to subdue, they know both what is meaningful and what is meaningless.
"Abandoning what is non-beneficial and taking up what is beneficial, one who observes with discernment is called a wise person.
Regarding the four kinds of giving: first, there is giving where the giver is pure but the recipient is impure;
second, there is giving where the recipient is pure but the giver is impure.
Third, there is giving where both the giver and the recipient are pure;
fourth, there is giving where both the giver and the recipient are impure.
What is the case where there is giving, the giver is pure, but the recipient is impure?
Answer:
As the Blessed One said:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that if there is a donor who possesses pure ethical discipline and abides in restraint, who holds views based on [the law of] dependence and views regarding the fruits [of action], and who, relying on such views, speaks these words:"
"There certainly exists giving, and there certainly exists the ripening of its fruit.

Yet, one who receives such gifts lacks pure ethical discipline and does not abide in the vows; being without reliance on the view [of causality] and without the view that there is a result, they rely on such a view and speak these words:
"There certainly is no giving, and there certainly is no ripening of its fruit."
This is called a gift where the giver is pure and the recipient is impure.
Why is this gift one where the giver is pure and the recipient is impure?
Answer:
All the constituent factors and all the provisions should be cultivated and accumulated by the giver.
Those constituent factors and those provisions are accomplished by the giver.
Regarding the various factors and requisites, the recipient should cultivate and accumulate them;
yet those factors and those requisites are not accomplished by the recipient.
Therefore, in this giving, the giver is pure while the recipient is impure.
What is the case where there is giving in which the recipient is pure but the giver is impure?
Answer:
As the Blessed One has said:

"Monks, you should know that if there is a donor who does not possess pure ethical discipline and does not abide in the restraint of the Vinaya, who lacks the view of reliance and lacks the view of the results [of actions], and who, relying on such a view, speaks these words:
'There is certainly no giving, and no ripening of results.'"

The recipient of the gift is one who possesses pure ethical discipline and abides in restraint; they possess the view of dependence and the view of results, and based on such views, they speak these words:
"There definitely exists giving, and there exists the ripening of its fruit."
This is called a gift where the recipient is pure, but the giver is impure.
Why is this gift such that the recipient is pure while the giver is impure?
Answer:
The various factors and the various requisites should be cultivated and accumulated by the giver;
yet those factors and those requisites are not accomplished by the giver.
The recipient should cultivate and accumulate all the constituent factors and requisites;
when those factors and those requisites are accomplished by the recipient,
this gift is pure for the recipient but impure for the giver.
What is the gift in which both the giver and the recipient are pure?
Answer:
As the Blessed One said:

"Monks, you should know that if there is a donor who possesses pure ethical discipline and abides in restraint, who holds the view of [karmic] dependence and the view of results, and based on such a view makes this statement:
'There is certainly giving; there is the ripening of results.'"

The recipient of the gift is likewise endowed with pure ethical discipline and abides in the vows; possessing the view of dependence and the view of the fruit, based on such a view, they speak these words:
"There is certainly giving, and there is the ripening of its fruit."
This is called a gift where both the giver and the recipient are pure.
Why is this gift one in which both the giver and the recipient are pure?
Answer:
The various factors and various requisites should be cultivated and accumulated by the giver;
those factors and those requisites are accomplished by the giver.
The various factors and various requisites should be gathered by the recipient.
With those factors and those provisions, the recipient is also accomplished.
Therefore, this gift is pure for both the giver and the recipient.
What kind of gift is it where both the giver and the recipient are impure?
Answer:
As the Blessed One said:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that if there is a donor who is not endowed with pure ethical discipline and does not abide in the code of restraint, who lacks the view of reliance and the view of karmic fruit, and who, relying on such a view, speaks these words:"
"There is certainly no giving and no ripening of results.

Furthermore, those who receive such gifts do not possess pure ethical discipline nor abide in the vows; they lack the view of reliance and the view of results, and based on such views, they speak these words:
"There is certainly no giving and no ripening of results."
This is called a gift where both the giver and the recipient are impure.
Why is this gift one where both the giver and the recipient are impure?
Answer:
The various factors and the various provisions should be cultivated and accumulated by the giver;
yet those factors and those provisions are not accomplished by the giver.
The various factors and requisites should be cultivated and accumulated by the recipient;
yet those factors and those requisites are not accomplished by the recipient.
Therefore, this gift is impure for both the giver and the recipient.
As the Blessed One said:
"One who possesses the precepts gives to one deficient in precepts, being pure and realizing the Dharma,
and having faith in the ripening of karmic results— it is only such a giver who is pure."
Giving to one deficient in precepts who possesses full precepts, though impure and leading to what is not Dharma,
results in the ripening of the fruit of karma for the donor alone; giving to one deficient in precepts who is also deficient in precepts,
being impure and leading to what is not Dharma, [results in the ripening of the fruit of karma for both].
I say that for one who slanders the ripening of karmic results, there is no great fruit.
But for one who gives to those endowed with precepts, who is pure and has realized the Dharma,
and who has faith in the ripening of karmic results— I say that for such a person there is great fruit.
One who has faith in the ripening of the fruits of karma, and gives to those they respect—
such as parents, servants, and others— is praised by all the wise. With body, speech,
and mind free from attachment, such a one practices the sublime conduct of a bhikṣu.
Not seeking wealth and honor for oneself, yet able to bestow extensively upon others;
when one who is already free from desire gives to another who is free from desire—
I say that such a gift is the most supreme among all material gifts.
The Saṃgītiparyāya-pāda-śāstra of the Sarvāstivādins, Volume Eight;
The Abhidharma-saṃgītiparyāya-pāda-śāstra, Volume Nine,
spoken by the Venerable Śāriputra.

Chapter Five, Part Four: The Four Means of Integration. The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) are: first, the means of integration through giving (*dāna*);
second, the means of integration through kind speech (*priyavāditā*).
Third, the means of attraction through beneficial conduct;
fourth, the means of attraction through cooperation.
What is the means of attraction through generosity?
Answer:

In this context, "giving" refers to when various donors give to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, those practicing the path, and beggars food, drink, medicinal decoctions, clothing, flower garlands, unguents and powdered incense, dwellings, bedding, lamps, candles, and other such items; this is called giving.
Furthermore, as the Blessed One said to the householder Hatthaka:
"Householder,
you should know that among all forms of giving, the gift of Dharma is supreme."
This is called generosity (*dāna*).

As for the "means of integration" (*saṃgrahavastu*), it means that by means of this generosity, one integrates others equally, draws them near, sustains them closely, and causes them to become affectionately attached.

Thus, giving to other sentient beings is able to gather them equally, to gather them closely, to sustain them closely, and to cause them to become attached; for this reason, it is called the "means of gathering through giving."
What is the means of integration through kind speech (*priyavāditā-saṃgrahavastu*)?
Answer:

Herein, "kind speech" refers to pleasant speech, speech that is flavorful, speech with a relaxed countenance and level gaze, speech free from frowning, speech preceded by a smile, speech of greeting and consolation offered first, lovely speech, and words of welcome—namely, speaking as follows:
"Welcome, Venerable One!
Are you able to endure the affairs of the world? Are you able to cross over them? Do you dwell in peace and happiness?
May you lack nothing in food, drink, clothing, bedding, or other necessary requisites."
Various expressions of this kind, such as words of consolation and inquiry after one's well-being, are called "words of welcome.
These, together with what was previously explained, are collectively termed "loving speech" (*priyavāditā*).
Furthermore, as the Blessed One said to the householder Hatthaka:
"Householder!

You should know that among all forms of pleasant speech, the most excellent is this: skillfully exhorting sons and daughters of good family to listen to the Dharma with attentive ears, preaching the Dharma at the proper times, instructing them at the proper times, and providing definitive analysis at the proper times—this is called pleasant speech."

Regarding the "basis of gathering through kind speech": it means that by means of this kind speech, one equally gathers others, gathers them closely, holds them close, and causes them to become intimate.
Thus, because such kind speech is able to equally gather, gather closely, hold close, and cause intimacy among other sentient beings, it is called the "basis of gathering through kind speech."
What is the means of attraction consisting of beneficial conduct?
Answer:

In this context, beneficial conduct refers to when sentient beings encounter serious illness, or face calamities, hardships, and distress without rescue, one goes to their side and, giving rise to a mind of compassion, provides service and relief through skillful means by means of bodily and verbal actions; this is called beneficial conduct.
Furthermore, as the Blessed One said to the householder Hatthaka:

"Householder, you should know that among all beneficial actions, the most excellent is this: to skillfully exhort, discipline, and establish those who lack faith, so that their faith becomes perfected."
If there are those who have broken their precepts, they skillfully exhort, guide, tame, and establish them so that their precepts become complete.
If there are those who are stingy and greedy, they skillfully exhort, guide, tame, and establish them so that their generosity becomes complete.
If one uses skillful means to exhort, guide, discipline, and establish those with impaired wisdom so that their wisdom becomes perfected—
such instances as these are called beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*).
As for the "inclusion of matters" (*vastusaṃgraha*), it refers to how, by means of this beneficial conduct, one [acts] toward others.
It gathers, gathers closely, holds closely, and causes [beings] to become intimate.

In this way, beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*) is able to gather equally, gather closely, hold closely, and cause intimacy toward other sentient beings; therefore, it is called the "means of gathering through beneficial conduct."
What is the means of integration through cooperation?
Answer:
In this context, "cooperation" refers to acting as a virtuous companion for one who feels deep revulsion toward taking life, so as to lead them away from taking life.
If one is deeply weary of and detached from taking what is not given, they act as a virtuous companion to lead them away from taking what is not given.
If one is deeply weary of and detached from sexual misconduct, they act as a virtuous companion to lead them away from sexual misconduct.
If one is deeply weary of and seeks detachment from false speech, they should act as a virtuous companion to help them abandon false speech.
If one is deeply weary of and seeks detachment from drinking various intoxicants, they should act as a virtuous companion to help them abandon the drinking of various intoxicants.
All such things as these are called "common purpose" (samānārthatā).
Furthermore, as the Blessed One said to the householder Hatthaka:
"Householder!"

One should know that among all forms of "sameness of purpose" (samānārthatā), the most excellent are those involving Arhats, Non-returners (anāgāmin), Once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin), and Stream-enterers (srotāpanna).
To engage in sameness of purpose with Arhats, Non-returners, Once-returners, and Stream-enterers is what is called "sameness of purpose."

Regarding the "means of integration through common purpose" (*samānārthatā-saṃgrahavastu*): it means that by means of this common purpose, one equally integrates, closely integrates, closely sustains, and causes others to become intimately attached.

In this way, through common purpose toward other sentient beings, one is able to equally integrate, closely integrate, closely sustain, and cause them to become intimately attached; therefore, it is called the "means of integration through common purpose."
As the Blessed One said:
"Generosity and kind speech, Beneficial conduct and cooperation—
These are taught as appropriate in various places To universally gather all the world."
If these four means of integration did not exist in the world,
even a son would have no desire to provide filial support to his parents.
Because these means of integration exist, those who possess the Dharma follow and practice them.
Therefore, those who have attained the great essence observe with increasing insight and establish [the teachings].
As for the four modes of birth: first, egg-birth; second, womb-birth; [third, moisture-birth;
fourth, transformation-birth].
Third, moisture-born;
fourth, transformation-born.
What is egg-born?
Answer:
If sentient beings are born from eggs, it means that while within the eggshell they are first enveloped by the eggshell, and only after breaking through the eggshell do they emerge.

What, then, are these? They are such as geese, swans, peacocks, mynas, parrots, *cāṣa* birds, *kalaviṅka* birds, *jīvajīvaka* birds, and so forth; as well as certain classes of nāgas, certain classes of garuḍas, and certain classes of humans.

Furthermore, there are other classes of sentient beings who are born from eggs; that is to say, those who are first enveloped by an eggshell and only later emerge after breaking through the shell are all termed "egg-born."
What is birth from a womb?
Answer:

It refers to those sentient beings who are born from a womb; that is to say, while in the fetal sac, they are first enveloped by the fetal sac, and only after breaking through the fetal sac do they emerge.

What, then, are these? They are such as elephants, horses, camels, oxen, donkeys, sheep, deer, water buffaloes, and pigs; as well as certain classes of nāgas, certain classes of garuḍas, certain classes of pretas, and certain classes of humans.

Furthermore, there are other classes of sentient beings who are born from a womb; that is to say, those who are first enveloped within a fetal membrane while in the womb and are subsequently born after breaking through that membrane are all called "womb-born."
What is birth from moisture?
Answer:

It refers to those sentient beings who, through mutual warmth, mutual moisture, and mutual aggregation, take birth upon heaps of excrement, or upon drainage ditches, or upon filthy latrines, or upon putrid flesh, or upon stale gruel, or upon thickets of grass, or upon dense forests, or upon grass huts, or upon leaf-caves, or upon ponds, or upon lakes, or upon marshes, or upon rivers, or upon the great ocean, and other such moist grounds.

What, then, are these? They are such as crickets, moths, mosquitoes, gadflies, midges, and gnats; insects born from hemp; certain classes of nāgas; certain classes of garuḍas; and certain classes of humans.

Furthermore, all other classes of sentient beings who are mutually warmed, and so forth, up to those who can only be born by depending on the moisture of the great ocean, damp ground, and the like, are all called moisture-born (*saṃsvedaja*).
What is birth by transformation (*upapāduka*)?
Answer:
When sentient beings are born instantaneously, complete with all limbs and without deficiency in their faculties, and without any physical support or basis.

What, then, are these? They are all devas, all hell-beings, all intermediate state beings (*antarābhava*), as well as a portion of nāgas, a portion of garuḍas, a portion of pretas, and a portion of humans.

Furthermore, there are other classes of sentient beings who possess complete limbs and unimpaired faculties, and who arise suddenly without any support; all such beings are called "apparitional" (upapāduka).
Regarding the four ways of obtaining a self-body (*ātmabhāva*): first, there is the acquisition of a self-body that can only be harmed by oneself and not by another;
second, there is the acquisition of a self-body that can only be harmed by another and not by oneself;
third, there is the acquisition of a self-body that can be harmed by both oneself and another.
4. There are those who have attained a self-body that is incapable of being harmed by either themselves or others.
What is it like for one who has attained a self-body that can only be harmed by oneself and not by others?
Answer:
If sentient beings possess the power themselves to end their own lives, yet others lack the power to end their lives, how is this so?

It refers to the gods of the Desire Realm known as the *krīḍā-pramada* (those who forget through play). At times, while engaged in extreme amusements and play for a long duration, they become physically exhausted and lose mindfulness; by virtue of these conditions, they then pass away.

Furthermore, there are gods in the desire realm who are prone to mental anger and resentment; at times, they become so extremely furious and agitated that they stare at one another with glaring eyes for a long duration, and by reason of this, they immediately perish.

Furthermore, there are other classes of sentient beings who possess the power to terminate their own lives, yet lack the power for others to terminate their lives; these are said to have acquired a physical existence that can only be harmed by themselves and not by others.
What is it that possesses a self-substance which can only be destroyed by another and not by oneself?
Answer:
It refers to those sentient beings who lack the power to sever their own lives, yet others possess the power to sever their lives.

What, then, is this? It refers to being within the eggshell or the mother’s womb, whether in the stage of the kalala, the arbuda, the peśī, the ghana, or the praśākhā, when the sense faculties are not yet complete and have not yet matured.

Furthermore, there are other classes of sentient beings who lack the power to terminate their own lives, yet others possess the power to terminate their lives; these are said to have obtained a physical existence that can only be harmed by another and not by themselves.
What is it that possesses a self-substance which can be harmed by both oneself and others?
Answer:
It refers to those sentient beings who possess the power themselves to sever their own lives, and for whom others also possess the power to sever their lives.
What, then, are these? They refer to elephants, horses, camels, oxen, donkeys, sheep, deer, water buffaloes, pigs, and so forth.

Furthermore, there are other classes of sentient beings who possess the power to take their own lives, and others who also possess the power to take their lives; these are said to have acquired a physical existence that can be harmed by both themselves and others.
What is it that possesses a self-substance which cannot be harmed by either oneself or others? Answer:
It refers to those sentient beings who lack the power to sever their own lives, and whom others likewise lack the power to sever their lives.

What, then, are these? They are: all gods of the form and formless realms; sentient beings dwelling in the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), or the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*); sentient beings dwelling in their final existence (*caramabhavika*); those sent by the Buddha and those prophesied by the Buddha; universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) and the mothers who conceive them while carrying their embryos; the Bodhisattva in his final birth and the mother who conceives him while carrying his embryo; and all those in the hells, such as the *kaṅkīra*, *uttara*, the son of the elder of Vārāṇasī, the son of the elder of Rājagṛha, the youth Yaśas, the Naga King Elāpattra, the Naga King Supratiṣṭhita, the horse-king Balahaka, and King Yama.

Furthermore, there are other classes of sentient beings who lack the power to take their own lives, nor do others have the power to take their lives; these are said to possess a physical existence that is incapable of being harmed by either themselves or others.
The fifth summary verse says:
Five, four, eight dharmas; namely, the flow, the destination, and suffering;
the four types of speech, and the two types of conduct—bad and sublime; and the four non-noble and noble utterances.

There are four types of persons (pudgala) who follow the current and so forth; four types of persons characterized by conduct for their own benefit and so forth; four types of persons who go from darkness to darkness and so forth; four types of persons who undergo suffering for themselves and so forth; the four types of verbal misconduct; the four types of verbal good conduct; the four types of non-noble speech; and the four types of noble speech.
Regarding the four types of persons (pudgala) such as those who flow with the current: first, the person who flows with the current;
second, the person who flows against the current;
third, the person who abides in themselves; [and fourth, the person who has gone beyond].
4. The person who has reached the other shore.
What is the person who flows with the current?
Answer:
As the Blessed One said:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that there is a certain class of persons (pudgala) in the world who, being habituated to various sensual desires, commit unwholesome deeds; these are called persons who go with the flow."
Question:
For what reason is one called an individual who goes with the flow?
Answer:

Craving is the stream of birth and death; this person (pudgala) flows along with it, and as they approach that state, this is their path and this is their track. Therefore, such a person is called one who "flows with the current."
What is a person who goes against the stream?
Answer:
As the Blessed One said:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that there is a certain class of persons (pudgala) in the world whose nature is characterized by intense greed, hatred, and delusion; they repeatedly experience mental distress and suffering through the application of attention (manasikāra) born of their weariness toward greed, hatred, and delusion."

Through the mental application of revulsion toward suffering and grief, he constantly and diligently cultivates the pure, unified, perfect, and stainless holy life until the end of his life; such a person is called an individual who goes against the stream.
Question:
For what reason is one called a person who goes against the stream?
Answer:

Craving is the stream of birth and death; this person, regarding the dharma for severing craving, conforms to it, inclines toward it, and approaches it—that is their path, that is their track—therefore they are called a person who goes against the stream.
What is a person who abides in themselves?
Answer:
As the Blessed One said:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that there is a certain class of persons who dwell in the forest, or beneath a tree, or in a secluded place; through practice, cultivation, frequent application, and right reflection, they realize such a state of tranquil mental concentration."

Following this concentrated mind, one severs the five lower fetters (pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni) and is destined for apparitional birth (upapāduka); attaining parinirvāṇa in that very place, one does not return again to be born in this desire realm. Such a person is called an "autonomous" (svastha) pudgala.
Question:
For what reason is one called a "person who abides in themselves" (svastha-pudgala)?
Answer:

This person, abiding in the realm of transformation-birth (nirmāṇarati), attains parinirvāṇa and does not return again to be born in this desire realm; therefore, they are called a person who abides in themselves (svastha-pudgala).
What is a person who has reached the other shore?
Answer:
As the Blessed One said:

Bhikṣus, you should know that there is a certain class of persons who dwell in the forest, or under a tree, or in a secluded place; through practice, cultivation, frequent application, and right reflection, they realize such a state of tranquil mental concentration.

Following this concentrated mind, one brings all outflows (*āsrava*) to permanent cessation and realizes the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom that are free from outflows. In this very life, through direct knowledge and realization, one fully experiences and correctly understands: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence. Such a person is called an individual who has reached the further shore (*pāraga*).
Question:
For what reason is one called a *pudgala* who has reached the other shore?
Answer:

The existence of a body within birth and death is called this shore; the eternal extinction of *nirvāṇa*, characterized by the exhaustion of craving and freedom from defilement, is called the other shore.

Because this *pudgala* is able to attain, acquire, touch, and realize that other shore—the eternal extinction of *nirvāṇa* through the exhaustion of craving and freedom from defilement—he is called a *pudgala* who has reached the other shore (*pāramitā-gata*).
As the Blessed One said:
"One who has not subdued or abandoned desire, and who is submerged in the craving of the desire realm—
I call such a person one who follows the current, repeatedly undergoing birth and death."
If one dwells securely in right mindfulness, Unstained by the habituation of desire and evil,
And having grown weary of and abandoned desire, grief, and suffering— I call such a person one who flows against the current.
Training to sever the five afflictions, One fulfills the five qualities of non-retrogression.
Having attained the faculty of supreme concentration, I call this "dwelling in oneself.
Regarding all phenomena, whether superior or inferior, one is liberated with nothing remaining;
the wise person reaches the end of the world—this I call "reaching the further shore."

Regarding the four types of persons (pudgala) based on their practice for self-benefit and so forth: first, there is the person who practices for self-benefit but does not practice for the benefit of others;
second, there is the person who practices for the benefit of others but does not practice for self-benefit;
third, there is the person who practices both for self-benefit and for the benefit of others.
4. There are persons who possess neither the practice for their own benefit nor the practice for the benefit of others.
What is the person who possesses the practice for their own benefit but lacks the practice for the benefit of others?
Answer:
As the Blessed One said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that there is a certain class of persons in the world who possess swift discerning patience regarding all wholesome dharmas."

Although such a person, for the sake of knowing the meaning and knowing the Dharma among all phenomena, diligently practices the practice in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*), harmonious and respectful conduct (*sāmīcīpratipatti*), and conduct following the Dharma (*anudharmapratipatti*), their speech is not refined, their mastery of eloquent language is incomplete, and they do not achieve preeminent speech, beautiful speech, clear speech, intelligible speech, independent speech, or inexhaustible speech. Furthermore, regarding the meaning, they are unable to demonstrate it, instruct others, encourage them, comfort them, or praise it so that others may understand; nor can they diligently teach the Dharma to the fourfold assembly to inspire those who cultivate virtue through demonstration, instruction, encouragement, and consolation. Such a person is called an individual who possesses practice for their own benefit but lacks practice for the benefit of others.
What is the person who possesses conduct for the benefit of others but lacks conduct for their own benefit?
Answer:
As the Blessed One said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that there is a certain class of persons who lack swift discernment and patience regarding the various wholesome dharmas."

Regarding all phenomena, such a person does not seek to know their meaning nor to know the teachings themselves; they do not diligently practice the "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*), the "harmonious and respectful practice," or the "practice following the Dharma. Nevertheless, their speech is well-modulated and their verbal expression is perfect; they also achieve preeminent speech, beautiful speech, clear speech, intelligible speech, independent speech, and inexhaustible speech. Furthermore, for the sake of making others understand the meaning, they are able to demonstrate, instruct, encourage, console, and praise; they demonstrate, instruct, encourage, console, and praise those who cultivate virtue. Moreover, they diligently preach the Dharma to the fourfold assembly. This is called a person who possesses conduct for the benefit of others but lacks conduct for their own benefit.
What is the person who possesses both conduct for their own benefit and conduct for the benefit of others?
Answer:
As the Blessed One has said:
"Monks, you should know that there is a certain type of person who possesses swift discernment and acceptance regarding all wholesome phenomena."

For the sake of knowing the meaning and for the sake of knowing the Dharma, he diligently practices the practice in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*), the practice of harmony and respect (*sāmīcīpratipatti*), and the practice following the Dharma (*anudharmapratipatti*). His speech is refined and his eloquence is perfected; he further achieves preeminent speech, beautiful speech, clear speech, intelligible speech, independent speech, and inexhaustible speech. Furthermore, for the sake of making the meaning known to others, he is able to demonstrate, instruct, encourage, and console them; he is also able to praise those who have demonstrated, instructed, encouraged, and consoled the cultivation of virtue. He is also able to diligently preach the Dharma to the fourfold assembly. This is called a person who possesses both practice for their own benefit and practice for the benefit of others.
What is the person who possesses neither conduct for their own benefit nor conduct for the benefit of others?
Answer:
As the Blessed One has said:
"O bhikṣus, you should know that there is a certain class of persons (pudgala) in the world who lack swift discernment and patience regarding their own wholesome qualities."

Regarding all phenomena, such a person does not seek to understand their meaning nor to understand the teachings themselves; they do not diligently practice the "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*), nor the "harmonious and respectful practice," nor the "practice following the Dharma. Their speech is unrefined, their mastery of eloquent expression is incomplete, and they fail to achieve preeminent speech, beautiful speech, clear speech, or intelligible speech. Furthermore, for the sake of making the meaning known to others, they are unable to demonstrate, instruct, or encourage; they cannot console, nor can they praise those who demonstrate, instruct, encourage, console, and inspire the cultivation of virtue. They do not diligently preach the Dharma to the fourfold assembly. This is called a person who possesses neither the practice for their own benefit nor the practice for the benefit of others.
Regarding the four types of persons (pudgala) who proceed from darkness to darkness and so forth: first, there is the person who proceeds from darkness to darkness;
second, there is the person who proceeds from darkness to light;
third, there is the person who proceeds from light to darkness; [and fourth, the person who proceeds from light to light].
4. There are individuals who proceed from light to light.
What kind of individual proceeds from darkness to darkness?
Answer:
As the Blessed One said:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that there is a certain class of *pudgala* born into a lowly and impoverished family—namely, a family of *caṇḍālas*, *puṣkasas*, artisans, musicians, or any other such defiled, poor, and destitute lineage lacking food and clothing, where one is of ugly appearance, despised by others, and conscripted for labor by the multitude. This is called 'darkness.'"
Relying on this darkness, he commits unwholesome actions of body, unwholesome actions of speech, and unwholesome actions of mind.
Due to the causes and conditions of such unwholesome conduct, at the dissolution of the body after death, he falls into a perilous and evil destination and is reborn in hell.

It should be understood that such a person is like one who goes from darkness to darkness, falls from a foul latrine into a foul latrine, enters a violent torrent from a violent torrent, moves from one prison to another prison, or washes with foul blood in foul blood; likewise, one who relies on a base and lowly body to perform evil deeds is also like this, and is called a person who "goes from darkness to darkness."
What is the person who proceeds from darkness to light?
Answer:
As the Blessed One has said:
"O bhikṣus, you should know that there is a certain class of persons (pudgala) born into a low and destitute family—namely, a family of caṇḍālas—and so forth, up to what is called 'darkness.'"
Relying on this darkness, he performs wholesome deeds of body, wholesome deeds of speech, and wholesome deeds of mind.
By reason of such wholesome conduct, at the breaking up of the body after death, he transcends the lower realms and is reborn in a happy destination, among the devas.

It should be understood that such a person is like someone who ascends from the ground to a staircase, from the staircase to a seat, from the seat to a palanquin, from the palanquin to a horse, from the horse to an elephant, and from the elephant enters a palace; likewise, one who performs sublime deeds while relying on a base and lowly body is also like this, and is called a person who proceeds from darkness toward light.
What is the person who proceeds from light to darkness?
Answer:
As the Blessed One has said:

“Bhikṣus, you should know that there is a certain class of persons (pudgala) born into wealthy and noble families—namely, into great kṣatriya clans, or great brāhmaṇa clans, or great clans of householders (śreṣṭhin), or great clans of lay devotees (gṛhapati), or other such great clans.”

In his household, there were many kinds of precious jewels, clothing, food and drink, male and female slaves and laborers, elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep; his storehouses were filled with wealth, grain, and all other necessities, none of which were lacking.
Having been born into this family, his physical appearance is upright and dignified, and his speech is majestic and solemn; he is respected and loved by all—this is called "clarity.
Relying on this clarity, he commits unwholesome actions of body, unwholesome actions of speech, and unwholesome actions of mind.
Due to such causes and conditions of unwholesome conduct, at the dissolution of the body after death, he falls into a perilous and evil destination and is reborn in hell.

It should be known that such a person is like someone who descends from a palace to mount an elephant, descends from the elephant to mount a horse, descends from the horse to mount a carriage, descends from the carriage to sit upon a seat, descends from the seat to stand on a step, and finally falls from the step to the ground. In the same way, one who commits evil deeds while relying on a body of wealth and nobility is just like this; such a person is called "one who goes from light to darkness."
What is the person who proceeds from light to light?
Answer:
As the Blessed One has said:

Bhikṣus, you should know that there is a certain class of persons born into wealthy and noble families—namely, great kṣatriya clans—and so on, as described at length, up to what is called "knowledge."
Relying on this illumination, he performs sublime deeds of body, sublime deeds of speech, and sublime deeds of mind.
By reason of such sublime conduct, he transcends the lower realms and is reborn among the devas in the higher realms.

It should be understood that such a person is like someone who goes from step to step, from seat to seat, from carriage to carriage, abandons a horse to mount another horse, abandons an elephant to mount another elephant, or goes from palace to palace; likewise, one who performs sublime deeds while relying on a body of wealth and nobility is also like this, and is called a person who "goes from light to light."
As the Blessed One said:
"Those who are poor and lowly, Lacking faith and full of anger and resentment,
Greedy, stingy, and delighting in evil deeds, Who take pleasure in false imaginings and wrong views."
Seeing śramaṇas and brahmins who are endowed with precepts and great learning,
one does not show them respect but reviles and disparages them, saying, "I have nothing to give.
By thus disparaging the giver, the gift, and the recipient, they will, upon death, be reborn according to their karma.
Falling into the realms of evil destinies and hells, they go from darkness to darkness. Yet those who are poor and lowly,
who possess faith and are free from anger and resentment,
who are endowed with shame and dread of blame and hold right view, and who delight in giving while remaining free from stinginess and greed— [they proceed toward light].
Seeing śramaṇas and brahmins who are endowed with precepts and great learning,
one should welcome them with joy and provide equal offerings and respect.
Praising the giver and the recipient of the gift, they will, upon death, be reborn according to their karma.
Ascending to the celestial realms of the happy migrations, one passes from darkness to light.
Yet those who possess wealth and status, lacking faith and filled with anger and resentment,
who are stingy, greedy, and delight in committing evil, and who take pleasure in false imaginings and wrong views— [they do not].
Seeing śramaṇas and brahmins who are endowed with precepts and great learning,
one does not show them respect but reviles and disparages them, saying, "I have nothing to give.
By thus disparaging the giver, the gift, and the recipient, when they die, they will be reborn according to their karma.
Falling into the realms of evil destinies and hells, they go from light into darkness.
Those who are wealthy and noble, possessing faith and free from anger and resentment,
endowed with a sense of shame, modesty, and right view, delight in giving and are free from stinginess and greed.
Seeing śramaṇas and brahmins who are endowed with precepts and great learning, one should welcome them with joy and serve them;
one should provide equal offerings and respect, praising both the giver and the recipient. When they die, they will be reborn according to their karma.
"Ascending to the celestial realms of the higher destinies, this is the passage from light to light.

Regarding the four types of individuals (*pudgala*) who undergo suffering and so forth: first, there is the individual who torments himself and exerts himself in torment, but does not torment others nor exert others in torment;
second, there is the individual who torments others and exerts others in torment, but does not torment himself nor exert himself in torment.
Third, there are persons who afflict themselves and exert themselves in self-affliction, and likewise afflict others and exert others in affliction;
fourth, there are persons who neither afflict themselves nor exert themselves in self-affliction, and neither afflict others nor exert others in affliction.
What is the person who torments themselves and exerts themselves in torment, yet does not torment others nor exert others in torment?
Answer:
As the Blessed One said:

"O bhikṣus, you should know that there is a certain class of persons (pudgala) in the world who practice asceticism and maintain themselves through harsh means: they remain naked without clothing, do not dwell in houses, and receive food and drink with their bare hands without using vessels or utensils. When receiving food and drink, it must not be separated by swords or staves, nor by cauldrons or pots, nor by basins or jars; it must not be food received while a dog stands at the door, nor food upon which flies have settled, nor food that is mixed with filth, nor food that is cut into pieces, nor food that is wrapped or covered."
The one who serves food and drink does not say "come forward," nor does he say "go back," nor does he say "stay.
The food is not from one who is pregnant, nor from one who has recently given birth, nor is it food obtained by nursing an infant.
It was not intentionally prepared for him, nor is it spoiled; it contains no meat, no fish, and no dried or salted meats.
One does not drink alcohol, nor does one drink fermented grain-drink;
one may either abstain entirely, or partake of food once, twice, thrice, four times, five times, six times, or seven times;
or one may beg from one household, two, three, four, five, six, or seven; or one may eat a single morsel, two, three, four, five, or six.
Or once every seven days; or eating once every two, three, four, five, six, or seven days;

or once every half-month, or once every month; or eating grass and vegetables, or eating barnyard millet and weeds, or eating cow dung, or eating fruits and gourds, or eating husks and chaff, or eating the bran of rice, or...
They eat the hearts of wild barley, or eat uncultivated beans; they dwell in the wilderness eating various roots and fruits, even down to eating scattered grains and fallen leaves.

There are those who, though clothed, wear garments of hemp or *xiǎi* grass; some wear *fú* or *zhù* fabrics, some wear *máo* or *pú* grass, some wear *shā* or *bó* grass, some wear coarse wool, some wear felt or woolen cloth, some wear animal skins, some wear bird feathers, some wear bamboo tablets, and some wear tree bark. Some have disheveled hair, some have unkempt hair, some wear small topknots, some wear large topknots; some shave their beards but keep their hair, some shave their hair but keep their beards, some keep both, and some shave both; some pluck out only their hair, some pluck out only their beards, and some pluck out both beard and hair. Some constantly hold up both hands, some perpetually stand on one foot, some delight in standing constantly, some renounce beds and seats, and some delight in squatting while practicing asceticism.

Some lie on beds of thorns, some on beds of ashes, some on beds of pestles, or on beds of wooden planks; some lie upon ground smeared with cow dung; some delight in tending the sacrificial fire, even performing it three times a day; some delight in entering water, even entering it three times a day; or they walk about with one foot raised, turning their gaze to follow the movement of the sun.

Such immeasurable practices as diligent suffering, equal suffering, pervasive suffering, and self-inflicted suffering are called the person who undergoes self-suffering and self-diligent suffering, but does not cause suffering to others nor diligent suffering to others.
Question:
For what reason is such a person called one who "afflicts himself and exerts himself in affliction, but does not afflict others nor exert others in affliction"?
Answer:

Because they sustain their lives through self-inflicted suffering, they are called persons who inflict suffering upon themselves and exert themselves in self-torment, but do not inflict suffering upon others or exert themselves in tormenting others.
What is a person who inflicts suffering upon others and exerts themselves in tormenting others, but does not inflict suffering upon themselves or exert themselves in self-torment?
Answer:

If one slaughters sheep, slaughters chickens, or slaughters pigs; if one captures birds, captures fish, or hunts wild animals; if one commits robbery, acts as an executioner, binds dragons, serves as a jailer, cooks dogs, or sets snares and traps—such a person is called an individual who causes others suffering and inflicts diligent suffering upon others, yet does not cause suffering for themselves and does not inflict diligent suffering upon themselves.
Question:

For what reason is such a person called "one who causes others suffering and exerts effort to cause others suffering, but does not cause himself suffering nor exert effort to cause himself suffering"?
Answer:

Because one sustains one's own life by causing suffering to others, such a person is called a "person who causes suffering to others and exerts effort toward causing suffering to others, but does not cause suffering to themselves nor exert effort toward causing suffering to themselves.

What is a person who both causes suffering to themselves and exerts effort toward causing suffering to themselves, and also causes suffering to others and exerts effort toward causing suffering to others?
Answer:

It is like when a royal priest wishes to perform a sacrifice; he first establishes a sacrificial altar within the city, smears his limbs with various clarified butters and oils, lets his hair hang loose and leaves his head uncovered, dons a black deerskin, holds a deer horn in his hand to rub his limbs, and at times sacrifices to fire or worships the heavens.

Within the sacrificial altar, he starved himself and subjected himself to austerity; he placed a golden calf and its mother cow before him, first milking one teat to offer to the Fire God (Agni), the second for the King, the third for the Queen, the fourth for the Prime Minister, and the remainder for his other loved ones.

Within the sacrificial altar, one slaughters various types of bulls, water buffaloes, cows, calves, chickens, pigs, sheep, and other such classes of animals; furthermore, one punishes and terrifies one's relatives and attendants, causing them to weep, grieve, suffer, and lament. This is called a person who both torments themselves and exerts themselves in torment, and likewise torments others and exerts others in torment.
Question:
For what reason is such a person called one who torments himself and exerts himself in tormenting himself, and also torments others and exerts others in tormenting them?
Answer:

Because they live their lives by inflicting suffering upon themselves and also inflicting suffering upon others, they are called persons who inflict suffering upon themselves and exert themselves in self-torment, and who also inflict suffering upon others and exert themselves in tormenting others.
What is the person who neither afflicts themselves nor exerts themselves in self-affliction, and neither afflicts others nor exerts others in affliction?
Answer:

It refers to those Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugatas, World-Knowers, Unsurpassed Leaders of Men to be Tamed, Teachers of Gods and Humans, Buddhas, Bhagavans, who appear in the world and proclaim the True Dharma—revealing the practice that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with excellent phrasing and meaning, pure, singular, complete, and the pristine holy life.
When those sons or daughters of good family have heard this Dharma, they give rise to profound pure faith. Having given rise to pure faith, they reflect thus:
"Living at home is cramped and full of many defilements, like a prison; leaving the home life is vast and spacious, free from all clamor and confusion, like empty space."

Those who remain stained by household life are unable to maintain, throughout their entire lifespan, a pure, unified, perfect, and stainless holy life (brahmacarya) through diligent practice; therefore, I should now, with right faith, shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, renounce the ways of the household, and go forth into the homeless state.
Having reflected thus, they renounce their wealth, status, and kin—whether small or great—in their entirety.
Having so renounced them, with right faith, they shave off their hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and leave the household life to enter the homeless state.

Having gone forth, he upholds the pure precepts and diligently guards the prātimokṣa discipline; his conduct and manners are entirely perfect, he perceives even the slightest transgression with deep dread, and he is able to fully undertake and train in all the points of training.

Abstaining from taking life and discarding all weapons and staves, possessing a sense of shame and dread of blame, endowed with loving-kindness and compassion, they feel deep pity even for the smallest sentient beings down to the eggs of ants, never harming them, and ultimately remain far removed from the practice of taking life.

Abstaining from taking what is not given, he is able to give and delights in giving; when receiving pure gifts, he knows the proper measure and does not give rise to defiled attachment toward any possessions. He maintains a pure and blameless self-nature, ultimately remaining far removed from the practice of taking what is not given.

Abstaining from unchaste conduct, they constantly practice the holy life; their journey is that of sublime conduct and their minds are pure. They remain far removed from the foul-smelling, defiled dharma of sensual desire, ultimately distancing themselves from all unchaste practices.

Free from false speech, he always delights in truthful speech, sincere speech, trustworthy speech, acceptable speech, and speech that causes no worldly dispute; he is ultimately and completely removed from the nature of false speech.

He abstains from divisive speech; he does not destroy others, nor does he repeat what he has heard from one person to another for the purpose of causing division, nor does he repeat what he has heard from another to the first for the purpose of causing division.

They always delight in reconciling those who have already been estranged; they praise those who are at peace and cause their harmony to be firm; they always delight in proclaiming words that bring others together and words that do not cause division, being ultimately and completely free from the practice of divisive speech.

One abstains from harsh speech; the words one utters are neither coarse nor abrasive, nor are they bitter enough to cause others resentment. Furthermore, they do not cause many people to feel unloved, unhappy, displeased, or joyless, nor do they obstruct the cultivation of meditative equipoise (*samāpatti*) and concentration (*samādhi*).
Regarding such harsh and evil speech, he is able to completely eradicate it.

The speech he utters is harmonious, gentle, pleasing to the ear, delightful, perfect, pure, and beautiful; it is clear and easy to understand, a joy for others to hear, independent, and inexhaustible. It causes many sentient beings to find it lovely, desirable, joyful, and pleasing, and it enables them to cultivate meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) and concentration (*samādhi*).

One should always delight in initiating such excellent and beautiful speech, and ultimately remain far removed from the practice of harsh and evil speech. One should abstain from frivolous and impure speech;

whatever words one utters should be timely and appropriate to the occasion, consistent with the Dharma and the meaning, truthful and genuine, capable of bringing peace and tranquility, orderly and purposeful, rational and decorous, free from confusion or defilement, and conducive to benefit and profit—thus remaining ultimately far removed from the practice of frivolous and impure speech.

He stays far removed from buying and selling false scales, false bushels, false measures, or containers; he never keeps elephants, horses, oxen, donkeys, chickens, pigs, dogs, or other such animals; nor does he keep male or female slaves, laborers, men, women, friends, or relatives; he never accepts or stores grain, wheat, beans, or the like, nor does he accept or store gold, silver, or other treasures.
He does not eat at improper times, or eats but a single meal; he never wanders about at the wrong time or in improper places.

Whether speaking or remaining silent, he avoids generating frivolous or contentious discourse. He is content with clothing, obtaining merely enough to cover his body; he is content with food, taking only what is necessary to dispel hunger and thirst.
Wherever he travels or dwells, his robes and alms bowl follow him, just as a bird, whether flying or perching, does not abandon its throat or wings.

By means of this, he accomplishes the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*); he closely guards the doors of the sensory faculties and abides in right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*). Through the power of right mindfulness, he defends his mind: when seeing forms with the eye, hearing sounds with the ear, smelling odors with the nose, tasting flavors with the tongue, feeling tangibles with the body, or cognizing phenomena with the mind, he does not grasp at their signs (*nimitta*) nor cling to their secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*). In these various spheres, he abides in the restraint of the faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*), guarding against covetousness, distress, and evil unwholesome states, ensuring that they never arise or grow within the mind.

By means of the aggregate of ethical discipline, he closely guards the doors of the sense faculties; whether looking ahead or behind, going or coming, bending or stretching, or looking down or up, and even when putting on his robes or holding his alms bowl, he dwells in constant clear comprehension.

Having thus accomplished the aggregate of pure ethical discipline, closely guarding the doors of the sense faculties with right mindfulness and clear comprehension, he goes at the first part of the day to the cities and villages where he resides, carrying his robe and bowl, guarding his sense faculties, dwelling in right mindfulness, and practicing the alms-round with dignified and composed deportment.

Having received the food, he returns to his original dwelling; when he has finished eating, he puts away his robes and bowl, washes his feet, takes up his sitting mat, and proceeds to an araṇya, a wilderness, a mountain forest, or a remote place, abandoning all bedding and furniture.

That place was inhabited only by non-human beings; dwelling in empty spaces or beneath trees, they sat cross-legged with their bodies held upright, abandoning external objects of attachment and abiding in mindfulness directed toward the present. Their minds were constantly focused, remaining far removed from greed, hatred, lethargy, drowsiness, restlessness, regret, doubt, and hesitation—those secondary afflictions that obstruct wholesome qualities, weaken the power of wisdom, and prevent the realization of nirvāṇa while causing one to dwell in the cycle of birth and death. Through this, they became free from sensual desires and unwholesome states, and eventually attained the fourth *dhyāna*.

By means of such a sublime state of meditative concentration—pure, stainless, free from secondary afflictions, supple, wieldy, and established in imperturbability—his mind inclines toward the realization of the knowledge and vision of the exhaustion of the outflows; he is able to know and see things as they truly are: "This is the noble truth of suffering; this is the noble truth of the origin; this is the noble truth of cessation; this is the noble truth of the path."
Through such knowledge and such vision, the mind is liberated from the outflow of desire (*kāmāsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyāsrava*).

Having been liberated, one knows and sees according to reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence. This is called the person who neither torments themselves nor exerts themselves in self-torment, and who neither torments others nor exerts others in torment.
Question:

For what reason is such a person called one who neither inflicts suffering upon himself nor exerts himself to inflict suffering upon himself, and who neither inflicts suffering upon others nor exerts himself to inflict suffering upon others?
Answer:

Because he maintains his life neither by afflicting himself nor by afflicting others, he is called a person who neither afflicts himself nor exerts himself in self-affliction, and neither afflicts others nor exerts them in affliction.
The Saṃgītiparyāya-pāda-śāstra of the Sarvāstivādins,
Volume Nine. The Abhidharma-saṃgītiparyāya-pāda-śāstra,
Spoken by the Venerable Śāriputra, Volume Ten.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Five, Part Four: The Four Unwholesome Verbal Actions. First, false speech; second, divisive speech;
[third, harsh speech; fourth, idle chatter.]
3. Harsh speech; 4. Frivolous speech.
What is the misdeed of false speech?
Answer:
As the Blessed One said:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that there may be one who speaks falsely, whether before a person of integrity, or in the midst of a great assembly, or in the royal court, or in the court of legal officials, or in the home of a kinsman or friend; for the purpose of providing testimony, he makes such an inquiry as follows:"
“O son of good family, you should reflect within yourself; if you know, speak; if you do not know, do not speak. If you have seen, speak; if you have not seen, do not speak.”
Having received this question, he does not know yet claims to know, or knows yet claims not to know; he has not seen yet claims to have seen, or has seen yet claims not to have seen.
Whether for his own sake, for the sake of another, or for the sake of material gain, he knowingly utters false speech and does not refrain from false speech.

In this context, "one who possesses false speech" refers to one who does not abandon false speech, does not sever false speech, does not feel revulsion toward false speech, abides in false speech, and is established in false speech; such a person is called "one who possesses false speech."

"Or in the presence of witnesses" means: whether it be witnesses from a village, witnesses from a town, or witnesses from a kingdom—when such witnesses are encountered, assembled, or standing before one, this is called "being in the presence of witnesses."

"Or among a great assembly" means: whether it be an assembly of kṣatriyas, an assembly of brahmins, an assembly of householders, or an assembly of śramaṇas—encountering, joining, or being present before such various great assemblies is called "or among a great assembly."

"Or being in a royal household" means that there is a king surrounded by his ministers; whether one encounters them, associates with them, or stands before them, this is called "being in a royal household."

"Or being in a court of law" means that when a group of legal experts has gathered for deliberation—whether they have met together, are assembled, or are present before one—it is called "being in a court of law."

"Or being in the home of relatives and friends" means: when various relatives and friends gather for conversation, whether they have met, are assembled, or are present before one; this is called "being in the home of relatives and friends."

"To cause [the witness] to testify, one asks this question" means that one exhorts them to speak words of truth, desiring to resolve what is right and what is wrong, and thus inquires together with them.

"You, son of good family, should reflect upon it yourself: if you know it, speak; if you do not know it, do not speak; if you have seen it, speak; if you have not seen it, do not speak. This means causing them to recall the objects previously experienced and to speak according to reality so as to serve as clear evidence; this is an exhortation.
If you have seen, heard, sensed, or known this matter, you may then proclaim, establish, and reveal it;

if you have not seen, heard, sensed, or known this matter, do not falsely proclaim, establish, or reveal it. Therefore, I say this: "O son of good family, you should reflect for yourself: if you know it, speak; if you do not know it, do not speak. If you have seen it, speak; if you have not seen it, do not speak."

Regarding the statement that he, having received this question, says he knows when he does not know, or says he does not know when he knows; or says he has seen when he has not seen, or says he has not seen when he has seen: herein, "saying one knows when one does not know" means that what is experienced by the ear-consciousness and understood by the ear-consciousness is called "that which is heard. Yet, in reality, it has not been heard or understood by the ear-consciousness. One conceals this perception (*saṃjñā*), this acceptance (*kṣānti*), this view (*dṛṣṭi*), and this matter of straightforwardness, saying, "I have already heard it. These are called "saying one knows when one does not know."

Regarding "knowing but saying one does not know": this refers to when the ear-consciousness has already received and understood [an object], yet one conceals this perception, this acceptance, this view, and this honest fact by saying, "I did not hear it. These instances are called "knowing but saying one does not know."

Regarding "claiming to have seen what was not seen": that which is received by the eye-consciousness and cognized by the eye-consciousness is called "seen. If one conceals this perception, this acceptance, this view, and this honest fact—that the eye-consciousness has not actually received or cognized it—and says, "I have already seen it," this is called claiming to have seen what was not seen.

Regarding "saying one has not seen what was actually seen": this refers to a case where the visual consciousness has already experienced and cognized an object, yet one conceals this perception, this acceptance, this view, and this honest fact by saying, "I did not see it. This is called "saying one has not seen what was actually seen."

Whether for his own sake, for the sake of another, or for the sake of material gain, he speaks words of falsehood with full awareness. In this context, "for his own sake" refers, for example, to a certain person who, having committed robbery himself, is seized and brought before the king; the king personally interrogates him:
"Ho there, man! [What have you done?]"
"Did you actually commit theft with another's property?
He thought to himself:

"If I answer truthfully, the King will surely become enraged and inflict severe punishment upon me—whether by beating, binding, banishing from the country, confiscating my wealth, or even taking my life."

"I shall conceal myself, thoroughly conceal myself; I shall hide myself, thoroughly hide myself; I shall protect myself, thoroughly protect myself, so that by speaking a falsehood I may escape punishment.
Having had this thought, he addressed the king, saying:
"I have never stolen the property of others."
"I pray that Your Majesty will examine me and see that I am truly not a thief.
This is what is meant by "either acting for oneself or for another.

For example, suppose there is a certain friend who has committed a robbery and is arrested and brought before the king. The king personally interrogates him but cannot obtain the truth; therefore, in order to establish the evidence, he pursues and interrogates [the friend's accomplice], saying:
"Is it true that your friend committed the theft?
He thought to himself:

"If I answer the King truthfully, he will surely become enraged and cause my friend to suffer severe punishment—whether by flogging, binding, banishing from the country, confiscating his wealth, or even taking his life."

"I am a kinsman and friend; I ought to cover for him as one would cover, conceal him as one would conceal, and protect him as one would protect, by uttering a falsehood so that he may escape punishment.
Having formed this thought, he addressed the king, saying:
"My kinsman has never plundered or stolen the property of others; I pray that Your Majesty will examine the matter and see that he is truly not a thief."
This is what is meant by "either for the sake of another" or "for the sake of material gain.
For example, there is a certain class of people who, harboring covetousness in their minds, think:

"I shall employ deceptive and false speech as a skillful means to seek out desirable objects of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, as well as clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other resources."

Having formed this thought, he immediately went in search [of the object]. On account of this cause and condition, he uttered false speech; thus it is said that [false speech may be spoken] "for the sake of wealth and profit.

To speak false speech with full awareness means that, having reached a definitive conclusion, one repeatedly proclaims, expounds, and expresses false words; this is called speaking false speech with full awareness.
