"I am currently afflicted and entangled by the suffering of illness; my physical strength is weak and inferior, and I am unable to advance in the sublime practices I am cultivating. For now, I should lie down and rest myself."

Having formed this thought, he consequently fails to apply himself with diligence to attain what has not yet been attained, to reach what has not yet been reached, or to realize what has not yet been realized; this is called the seventh matter of indolence.
Furthermore, Venerable One, suppose there is a certain person who, though recently recovered from being afflicted by the suffering of illness, thinks to himself:

"I have been afflicted by the suffering of illness; although I have not long been recovered, my physical strength is weak and inferior, and I am unable to apply myself to the sublime practices that ought to be cultivated. For now, I should lie down and rest myself."

Having formed this thought, he consequently fails to apply himself with diligence to attain what has not yet been attained, to reach what has not yet been reached, or to realize what has not yet been realized; this is called the eighth matter of indolence.
These eight types are called the matters of indolence.
Question:
For what reason are these eight termed "matters of indolence"?
Answer:
Laziness refers to indolence.

Through these eight matters, that which has not yet arisen comes into being, and that which has already arisen increases and expands further; for this reason, they are called the "matters of laziness."
Regarding the eight matters of diligence, what are the eight?

Venerable sir, you should know that there is a certain person who, residing in dependence upon a city or a village, puts on his robes and takes up his bowl at the first part of the day to enter the city or village and wander for alms.
When he goes for alms, he thinks:
"May I obtain abundant and exquisite food and drink.
If his wish is not fulfilled, he then thinks:
"Although my food is meager, my body is light and agile, and I am capable of advancing in the cultivation of the sublime practices.

Having formed this thought, he applies himself with fervent diligence to attain what has not yet been attained, to reach what has not yet been reached, and to realize what has not yet been realized; this is called the first matter of diligence.

Furthermore, venerable ones, suppose there is a certain person who, dwelling in dependence upon a city or a village, puts on his robes and takes up his bowl at the first part of the day to enter the city or village and wander for alms.
When he goes for alms, he forms this thought:
"May I obtain abundant and exquisite food and drink.
If he succeeds in obtaining what he desires, he then forms this thought:
"Since my food is abundant and my physical strength is robust, I am capable of advancing in the cultivation of the sublime practices.

Having formed this thought, he applies himself with blazing diligence to seek what has not yet been attained, to reach what has not yet been reached, and to realize what has not yet been realized; this is called the second matter of diligence.
Furthermore, venerable one, suppose there is a certain person who, having engaged in business during the day, thinks to himself:

"Since I have been occupied with business during the day, I have had no leisure to study the Noble Teaching of the Great Master; now, during this night, I should exert myself to make up for my previous neglect."

Having formed this thought, he applies himself with fervent diligence to seek what has not yet been attained, to reach what has not yet been reached, and to realize what has not yet been realized; this is called the third matter of diligence.
Furthermore, venerable one, suppose there is a certain person who, having planned to perform various tasks tomorrow, thinks to himself:

"Since I must attend to my tasks tomorrow, I will have no leisure to study and train in the Noble Teacher’s holy instruction; therefore, during this night, I should apply myself with diligence in advance to make up for those deficiencies."

Having formed this thought, he applies himself with fervent diligence to attain what has not yet been attained, to reach what has not yet been reached, and to realize what has not yet been realized; this is called the fourth basis of diligence.
Furthermore, Venerable One, suppose there is a certain person who, while traveling on a road during the day, reflects thus:

"Since I have been traveling on the road during the day, I have had no leisure to study and practice the Noble Teaching of the Great Master; now, during this night, I should exert myself with diligence to make up for what was previously neglected."

Having formed this thought, he exerts himself with fervent diligence to attain what has not yet been attained, to reach what has not yet been reached, and to realize what has not yet been realized; this is called the fifth matter of diligence.
Furthermore, Venerable One, suppose there is a certain person who, having resolved that he must travel on a road tomorrow, thinks to himself:

"Since I must travel on a road tomorrow, I will have no leisure to study the Noble Teaching of the Great Master; therefore, during this night, I should apply myself with diligence in advance to make up for what I may miss."

Having formed this thought, he applies himself with fervent diligence to attain what has not yet been attained, to reach what has not yet been reached, and to realize what has not yet been realized; this is called the sixth matter of diligence.
Furthermore, venerable friend, suppose there is a certain person who is afflicted and entangled by the suffering of illness, and he thinks to himself:

"Since I am afflicted and entangled by the suffering of illness, it is possible that because of this affliction by illness, I shall lose my life, resulting in nothing gained from the Great Teacher’s teaching."

Having formed this thought, he applies himself with fervent diligence to seek what has not yet been sought, to reach what has not yet been reached, and to realize what has not yet been realized; this is called the seventh matter of diligence.
Furthermore, venerable one, suppose there is a certain person who, though recently recovered from being afflicted by the suffering of illness, thinks to himself:

"Although I have recently been freed from the affliction of illness that once beset me, it is possible that the suffering of illness may arise again; because of such illness, I might lose my life and find nothing at all gained from the Great Teacher’s teaching."

Having formed this thought, he applies himself with fervent energy to seek what has not yet been attained, to reach what has not yet been reached, and to realize what has not yet been realized; this is called the eighth matter of diligence.
These eight kinds are called the matters of diligence (*vīrya-vastu*).
Question:
For what reason are these eight called the matters of diligence?
Answer:
Diligence refers to exertion.

By means of these eight matters, that which has not yet arisen is brought into being, and that which has already arisen increases, grows, and expands further; for this reason, they are called the "bases of diligence" (*vīrya-vastu*).
Regarding the eight types of birth resulting from merit, what are these eight?

Venerable one, you should know that there is a certain class of person who gives to various śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, to the poor, to those who practice the path, and to mendicants who practice austerities—namely, clothing, food and drink, as well as perfumes, flowers, dwellings, bedding, and requisites such as lamps and other articles for sustaining life.
Upon seeing a wealthy and noble person, one should form this thought:
"By virtue of the roots of goodness accumulated through this act of giving, may I, in a future life, attain such wealth and nobility as this person."

If he practices, cultivates, and frequently applies himself to this mind, then through that practice, cultivation, and frequent application, although he previously took pleasure in the inferior and the clamorous, he subsequently comes to delight in seeking the superior, the sublime, and the tranquil.

There is such a possibility: when his body breaks up and his life ends, he is reborn among humans as one who attains wealth and nobility. Although he experiences the sovereignty, peace, and happiness of wealth and nobility, he is endowed with ethical discipline (*śīla*) and pure intentions; because the ethical discipline of his previous human existence was pure, this is called the first production of merit.

Just as one who wishes to be born among humans obtains a class of wealth and nobility, it should be known that the same applies to those who wish to be born among the Cāturmahārājakāyika, Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, and Brahmakāyika devas.
However, regarding the distinctions among the Brahmakāyika devas, one should speak of their freedom from desire.
As for the statement "herein these are named the first through the eighth," they are numbered as the first through the eighth in a gradual, sequential, continuous, and successive order.
Regarding the term "Source of Merit" (*puṇyotpāda*):
Question—Why is this called the Source of Merit?
Answer:
Because they have gathered the fruits of merit and are born in this place, it is called "Birth of Merit" (Puṇyaprasava).
Regarding the eight classes of beings, what are the eight?
Answer:
First, the assembly of kṣatriyas;
second, the assembly of brahmins;
third, the assembly of householders.
4. the assembly of śramaṇas;
5. the assembly of the Cāturmahārājakāyika devas;
6. the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa devas;
7. the assembly of the Māras;
8. the assembly of the Brahmās.
What is the assembly of the kṣatriyas?
Answer:
Those who display that form, display those aggregates, and display those divisions are called the kṣatriya assembly.
This applies extensively to the assemblies up to the Brahmā assembly as well.
Regarding the eight worldly dharmas, what are the eight?
Answer:
First, gain; [and so forth].
Second, not obtaining;
third, disparagement;
fourth, praise.
5. Praise; 6. Blame; 7. Suffering;
8. Joy (sukha).
What is meant by "attainment" (prāpti)?
Answer:

If, regarding pleasant forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites for illness—whether they have been obtained, separately acquired, already possessed, or are yet to be obtained—this is called "acquisition."
What is meant by "not obtaining"?
Answer:

If, with regard to desirable forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles; clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites for illness; or various articles of daily life—one does not obtain them, obtains them separately, has already obtained them, or ought to obtain them—this is called "not obtaining."
What is meant by "defamation"?
Answer:

When one turns their back on others and does not appear before them, failing to praise, extol, laud, or celebrate them, and instead stating that their faith, ethical discipline, learning, generosity, wisdom, and so forth are all incomplete—this is called defamation.
What is meant by "renown"?
Answer:

When one is not present before others, but they praise, extol, and laud them, saying that such a person is fully endowed with faith, ethical discipline, learning, generosity, wisdom, and so forth—this is called renown.
What is meant by "praise" (saṃstuti)?
Answer:

When one does not turn away from others, but rather faces them directly; when one does not revile, disparage, scold, or humiliate them, but instead commends, extols, and lauds them, saying, "You are fully endowed with faith, ethical discipline, learning, generosity, wisdom, and so forth"—this is called praise.
What is meant by "reviling"?
Answer:

When one does not remain hidden but appears before others, and speaks with censure, reproach, abuse, and insult—neither praising, nor commending, nor extolling, nor lauding, nor glorifying them—saying, "Your faith, precepts, learning, generosity, wisdom, and so forth are all incomplete," this is called reviling.
What is called suffering?
Answer:
Because one is touched by contact conducive to painful feeling, bodily and mental suffering arise; that which is comprised within the category of feeling as an uneven experience is called suffering.
What is called pleasure?
Answer:

Because it is touched by contact conducive to pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanīya-sparśa*), there arises physical and mental pleasure; this is a type of feeling subsumed under the category of equanimity (*upekṣā*), and it is what is called pleasure.
The Blessed One spoke these verses on this occasion:
"Gain and loss, dispraise and praise, Fame and infamy, suffering and pleasure— These arise from the mind’s desire for the impermanent;
They are subject to change and decay, difficult to preserve."
The wise one knows things as they truly are; seeing them directly, he subdues birth and death.
Toward phenomena that are pleasant or unpleasant, his mind gives rise to neither delight nor anger.
Though he encounters what is favorable or adverse, he is able to abandon, subdue, and extinguish it.
"Regarding all liberations, one reaches the further shore at the limit of the world.
What are the eight liberations?
Answer:
Possessing form, one perceives forms; this is the first liberation.
With the internal perception of formlessness, one perceives external forms; this is the second liberation.
Realizing the liberation of purity through bodily witness and dwelling therein fully; this is the third liberation.

Transcending all perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of sensory resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, one enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space, having fully attained the perception of infinite space; this is the fourth liberation.
Transcending the sphere of infinite space, one enters and dwells in the fulfillment of the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is the fifth liberation.
Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters and dwells in the fulfillment of the sphere of nothingness; this is the sixth liberation.
Transcending the sphere of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the fulfillment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the seventh liberation.

Transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the fulfillment of the cessation of perception and feeling, having realized it through bodily witness; this is the eighth liberation.

Regarding "one possessing form who perceives forms," this means that with respect to internal individual perceptions of form, one has not yet distanced oneself from them, nor distinguished oneself from them; one has not yet subdued them, nor distinguished oneself in subduing them; one has not yet extinguished them, nor destroyed them.

Because he has not yet distanced himself from, nor individually distanced himself from; has not yet subdued, nor individually subdued; and has not yet extinguished or destroyed the internal perceptions of individual forms, he contemplates external forms through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), visualizing them as either livid (*vinīlaka*), festering (*vipūyaka*), disintegrating (*vipaṭumaka*), scattered (*vikṣiptaka*), being devoured (*vikhāditaka*), mottled red (*vilohitaka*), skeletal (*asthi*), or a chain of bones (*asthisaṃkalika*). This is called "possessing form while contemplating forms."
"First" means that among all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), it is counted as the first in terms of gradual, sequential, continuous, and successive order.
"Liberation" (*vimokṣa*) refers to the wholesome form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness present within this concentration; these are called liberation.

Regarding "having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms": this means that with respect to internal, individual perceptions of form, he has already distanced himself from them, has individually distanced himself from them; he has already subdued them, has individually subdued them; he has already caused them to vanish and has destroyed them.

Because he has already distanced himself from internal perceptions of individual forms, having distanced himself individually, tamed them individually, caused them to subside, and destroyed them; by the power of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), he contemplates external forms as either livid, or festering, or disintegrating, or scattered, or being devoured, or bloody, or skeletal, or a chain of bones. This is called "having no perception of internal form, one contemplates external forms."
The second refers to that which is counted as the second within the various meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) by way of gradual, sequential, continuous, and successive order.
As for "liberation" (*vimokṣa*), it refers to all wholesome form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness present within this absorption; these are called liberation.
Regarding "attaining and dwelling in the full realization of the pure liberation with one’s own body," it is asked:
What is the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for this pure liberation?
By what means does the practitioner of meditation enter the meditative absorption of pure liberation?
Answer:

When a beginner first practices meditation, they take up the sign of a green tree—namely, its green trunk, green branches, green leaves, green flowers, and green fruit—or they take up the sign of green garments or green ornaments, or they take up various other kinds of green signs.

Having thus apprehended these various blue signs, by the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), one contemplates, recollects, examines, and establishes the conviction that "this form is such-and-such a blue sign."

Since he has thus, by the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), reflected upon, attended to, examined, and established the conviction that "this form is this particular blue," his mind then becomes distracted and flows toward various signs, unable to focus one-pointedly on a single object to reflect that "this form is blue and nothing else."

Because that mind is distracted and flows toward various signs, it cannot be focused one-pointedly on a single object to contemplate that "this form is certainly blue"; thus, he is unable to settle the mind and enter the meditative absorption of the pure liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa*).
In order to collect the mind that is distracted, wandering, and flowing, one binds the attention to a single blue sign and contemplates it, thinking: "This is blue; it is not a non-blue sign.

One contemplates this sign with diligence and vigor until the mind remains in continuous succession for a long duration; through such preparatory application (*prayoga*), one enters the meditative absorption of the pure liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa-samādhi*).

Having diligently and repeatedly practiced this preliminary application (*prayoga*), one further advances in the cultivation of the means for this meditative concentration (*samādhi*); that is, one repeatedly practices, repeatedly cultivates, and repeatedly performs the path induced by that preliminary application.

Having repeatedly practiced, repeatedly cultivated, and repeatedly performed the path induced by the preparatory stage, the mind then becomes settled, thoroughly settled, and closely settled; it flows in a continuous stream toward a single direction and binds mindfulness to a single object, contemplating that this form is certainly the sign of blue.

By means of the mind abiding, abiding closely, abiding near, continuing in a single flow, and binding its attention to a single object, one contemplates the sign of blue as non-dual and unchanging, and is thus able to realize and enter the meditative absorption of the pure liberation.
Just as one contemplates the sign of blue, so too should one contemplate yellow, red, and white, according to what is appropriate.
As for the "third," this refers to that which is counted as the third within the various meditative absorptions (dhyāna) by way of gradual, sequential, continuous, and successive order.
"Liberation" refers to all wholesome form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness within this meditative concentration; these are called liberation.
Regarding "transcending all perceptions of form," what are perceptions of form?
Answer:

All perceptions, conceptualizations, and states of perception associated with the group of eye-consciousness—whether currently perceived, already perceived, or yet to be perceived; whether presently manifesting, already manifested, or yet to be manifested—are called the perception of form.
Furthermore, some say that the various perceptions and conceptualizations associated with the five groups of consciousness, and so forth as explained at length, are called "perception of form.

In this present context, however, the various perceptions and conceptualizations associated with the visual consciousness group, and so forth as explained at length, are what are called "perception of form."

When entering this meditative absorption, one is able to transcend all perceptions of form, transcend them equally, and transcend them most thoroughly; therefore, it is said that "all perceptions of form are transcended and ceased."
Regarding "perception of resistance" (*sappaṭighasaññā*): what is perception of resistance?
Answer:
It refers to all perceptions and conceptualizations associated with the four groups of consciousness, and so forth, as explained at length; this is called perception of resistance.

Furthermore, some say that the various perceptions and conceptualizations associated with the five groups of consciousness, and so forth as extensively explained, are called "perceptions with resistance" (*sapratigha-saṃjñā*).
Furthermore, some say that the various perceptions and conceptualizations associated with ill-will, and so forth as extensively explained, are called "perceptions with resistance."

In this context, the various perceptions and conceptualizations associated with the four groups of consciousness, and so forth as extensively explained, are called "perceptions of resistance" (*sapratigha-saṃjñā*).

When entering this meditative absorption, those perceptions of resistance have been abandoned, fully understood, distanced, specifically distanced, subdued, specifically subdued, extinguished, and destroyed; therefore, it is said that "perceptions of resistance are ceased."
Regarding "not contemplating various perceptions," what are these various perceptions?
Answer:

They are all defiled perceptions of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles belonging to those bound by the enveloping afflictions (*paryavasthāna*); furthermore, they include all unwholesome perceptions and all perceptions induced by improper conduct that can obstruct meditative concentration—all such things as these are called various perceptions.

When entering this meditative absorption, one does not initiate various perceptions, does not follow their initiation, does not initiate them equally, does not contemplate them, has not contemplated them, and will not contemplate them; for this reason, it is said that one does not contemplate various perceptions.
Regarding "entering and dwelling fully in the sphere of infinite space through the emptiness of infinite space": Question:
What is the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) for this liberation of the sphere of infinite space?
By what means does the practitioner of meditation enter the meditative absorption of the liberation of the sphere of infinite space?
Answer:

When a beginner first practices meditation, they should first contemplate the fourth dhyāna as coarse, painful, and obstructive; subsequently, they should contemplate the sphere of infinite space as peaceful, sublime, and detached.

Since he has already contemplated the fourth dhyāna as coarse, painful, and obstructive, and has likewise contemplated the sphere of infinite space as peaceful, sublime, and secluded, his mind becomes distracted and wanders toward various signs; thus, he is unable to focus one-pointedly on a single object with continuous mindfulness while contemplating the sphere of infinite space.

Because that mind is distracted and flows toward various signs, it is unable to focus one-pointedly on a single object and engage in continuous contemplation of the sphere of infinite space; therefore, he has not yet been able to settle the mind and enter the meditative absorption of the liberation of the sphere of infinite space.

In order to gather the scattered and wandering mind, one focuses the mindfulness exclusively on the signs (*nimitta*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). One contemplates these signs with diligent vigor until the mind remains in continuous succession; through such preparatory application (*prayoga*), one enters the meditative absorption of liberation (*vimokṣa-samādhi*) of the sphere of infinite space.

Having diligently and repeatedly practiced this preliminary application (*prayoga*), one further advances in the cultivation of the means for this meditative concentration (*samādhi*); that is, one repeatedly practices, repeatedly cultivates, and repeatedly performs the path induced by that preliminary application.

Once the path induced by the preparatory application has been repeatedly practiced, repeatedly cultivated, and performed many times, the mind then becomes settled, thoroughly settled, and closely settled; it flows in a continuous stream toward a single direction, binds mindfulness to a single object, and contemplates: "This is the sphere of infinite space."

By means of the mind abiding, abiding closely, and abiding near; by continuity, single-pointedness, and binding the mindfulness to a single object, one contemplates this sphere of infinite space. Being without duality and without fluctuation, one is then able to realize and enter the meditative absorption of the liberation of the sphere of infinite space.
The fourth refers to that which is the fourth in number within the sequence of successive, gradual, and continuous meditative absorptions (*samādhi*).
As for "liberation" (*vimokṣa*), it refers to all wholesome feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness present within this absorption; these are all termed liberation.
Regarding "transcending the entire sphere of infinite space": how does one transcend the entire sphere of infinite space?
Answer:

When about to enter the sphere of infinite consciousness, one is able to transcend all perceptions of the sphere of infinite space—transcending them equally and transcending them most thoroughly; therefore, it is called "transcending the entire sphere of infinite space."
Regarding "entering and abiding fully in the sphere of infinite consciousness":
Question—What is the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) for this liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness?
By what means does the practitioner of meditation enter the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness?
Answer:

When a beginner first practices meditation, they should first contemplate the sphere of infinite space as coarse, painful, and obstructive; subsequently, they should contemplate the sphere of infinite consciousness as calm, sublime, and detached.

Having reflected that the sphere of infinite space is suffering, coarse, and an obstruction, he further reflects that the sphere of infinite consciousness is peaceful, sublime, and a departure [from the former]. Consequently, his mind becomes distracted and wanders toward various signs; he is unable to focus one-pointedly on a single object or to maintain continuous reflection upon the sphere of infinite consciousness.

Because that mind is distracted and flows toward various signs, unable to focus one-pointedly on a single object to continuously contemplate the sphere of infinite consciousness, he has not yet been able to stabilize the mind and enter the meditative absorption of the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness.

In order to collect the mind that is distracted and wandering, one focuses one’s mindfulness exclusively on the signs of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). One contemplates these signs with diligence and vigor, even to the point of causing the mind to remain in continuous succession; through such preparatory application (*prayoga*), one enters the meditative absorption of liberation (*vimokṣa-samādhi*) in the sphere of infinite consciousness.

Having diligently and repeatedly practiced this preliminary application (*prayoga*), one further advances to practice the skillful means for this meditative concentration; that is, one repeatedly practices, repeatedly cultivates, and repeatedly performs the path induced by that preliminary application.

Once the path induced by the preparatory stage has been repeatedly practiced, repeatedly cultivated, and performed many times, the mind then becomes settled, thoroughly settled, and closely settled; it flows in a continuous stream toward a single direction, binding mindfulness to a single object, contemplating: "This is the sphere of infinite consciousness."

By means of the mind abiding, abiding closely, and abiding near, with continuity directed toward a single goal and attention bound to a single object, one contemplates this sphere of infinite consciousness; being without duality and without fluctuation, one is then able to realize and enter the meditative absorption of the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
The fifth refers to that which is counted as the fifth in the gradual, sequential, continuous, and successive order among the various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*).
As for "liberation" (*vimokṣa*), it means that all wholesome feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness within this concentration are termed liberation.
Regarding "transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness": how does one transcend the sphere of infinite consciousness?
Answer:

When one is about to enter the sphere of nothingness, one is able to transcend all perceptions of the sphere of infinite consciousness—transcending them equally and transcending them most thoroughly; therefore, it is called "transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness."
Regarding "entering and dwelling fully in the sphere of nothingness where there is nothing": Question:
What is the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) for this liberation of the sphere of nothingness?
By what means does a practitioner of meditation enter the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the liberation of the sphere of nothingness?
Answer:

When a beginner first practices meditation, they should first contemplate the sphere of infinite consciousness as suffering, coarse, and an obstacle; subsequently, they should contemplate the sphere of nothingness as peaceful, sublime, and a liberation.

Having reflected that the sphere of infinite consciousness is a coarse hindrance characterized by suffering, and having further reflected that the sphere of nothingness is peaceful, sublime, and secluded, his mind then becomes distracted and wanders toward various signs; he is unable to focus one-pointedly on a single object or to maintain continuous reflection upon the sphere of nothingness.

Because that mind is distracted and flows toward various signs, unable to focus one-pointedly on a single object to continuously contemplate the sphere of nothingness, he has not yet been able to stabilize the mind and enter the meditative absorption of the liberation of the sphere of nothingness.
In order to collect the mind that is distracted, agitated, and wandering, one focuses the attention exclusively on the sign of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

One contemplates this sign with diligent vigor until the mind remains in continuous succession for a long duration; through such preparatory application (*prayoga*), one enters the meditative absorption of liberation (*vimokṣa-samādhi*) of the sphere of nothingness.

Having diligently and repeatedly practiced this preliminary application, one further advances in the cultivation of the means for this meditative concentration; that is, one repeatedly practices, repeatedly cultivates, and repeatedly performs the path induced by that preliminary application.

Once the path induced by the preparatory application has been repeatedly practiced, repeatedly cultivated, and frequently performed, the mind then becomes settled, well-settled, and closely settled; it proceeds in a continuous stream, focused on a single object, contemplating: "This is the sphere of nothingness."

By means of the mind abiding, abiding closely, and abiding near—continuously directed toward a single course and bound to a single object—one contemplates this sphere of nothingness; being without duality and without fluctuation, one is then able to realize and enter the meditative concentration of the liberation of the sphere of nothingness.
The sixth refers to that which is numbered as the sixth within the sequence of meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), following their gradual, successive, and continuous order.
As for "liberation" (*vimokṣa*), it refers to all wholesome feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness present within this absorption; these are all termed liberation.
Regarding "transcending all bases of nothingness": how does one transcend all bases of nothingness?
Answer:

When one is about to enter the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one is able to transcend all bases of nothingness, transcend them equally, and transcend them most thoroughly; therefore, it is called "transcending all bases of nothingness."
Regarding "entering and abiding fully in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception," the question is:
What is the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) for this liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
By what means does the practitioner of contemplation enter the meditative absorption of the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
Answer:

When a beginner first practices meditation, they should first contemplate the sphere of nothingness as suffering, coarse, and an obstacle; subsequently, they should contemplate the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as peaceful, sublime, and a state of liberation.

Having reflected that the sphere of nothingness is painful, coarse, and obstructive, he further reflects that the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is peaceful, sublime, and secluded; consequently, his mind becomes distracted and wanders among various signs, unable to focus one-pointedly on a single object to maintain continuous reflection upon the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Because that mind is distracted and flows toward various signs, unable to focus one-pointedly on a single object and continuously contemplate the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he has not yet been able to settle the mind and enter the liberation-concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

In order to collect the mind that is distracted and wandering, one focuses the mindfulness and contemplates the sign of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Contemplating this sign with diligent vigor, one causes the mind to remain in continuous succession for a long time; through such preparatory application (*prayoga*), one enters the meditative absorption of liberation (*vimokṣa-samādhi*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Having diligently and repeatedly practiced this preliminary application (*prayoga*), one further advances in the cultivation of the means for this meditative concentration (*samādhi*); that is, one repeatedly practices, repeatedly cultivates, and repeatedly performs the path induced by that preliminary application.

Once the path induced by the preparatory application has been repeatedly practiced, repeatedly cultivated, and performed many times, the mind then becomes settled, well-settled, and closely settled; it proceeds in a continuous stream toward a single direction and binds mindfulness to a single object, contemplating this as the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

By means of the mind abiding, abiding closely, and abiding near; by continuity, single-pointedness, and binding the mindfulness to a single object; and by contemplating the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in this manner—without duality and without fluctuation—one is able to realize and enter the meditative absorption of the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Regarding the "seventh": this refers to its being the seventh in number within the sequence of meditative absorptions (dhyāna), following the gradual, regular, continuous, and successive order.
Regarding "liberation" (vimokṣa): all wholesome feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness present within this absorption are termed liberation.
Regarding "transcending all states of neither-perception-nor-non-perception": how does one transcend all states of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
Answer:

When one is about to enter the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling, one is able to transcend all perceptions of the state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—transcending them equally and transcending them to the ultimate degree; therefore, it is said that one transcends all states of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Regarding "entering the cessation of perception and feeling, realizing it with the body, and dwelling in its fulfillment": Question:
What is the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) for this liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling?
By what means does the practitioner of meditation enter the meditative absorption of the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling?
Answer:

When a beginner first practices meditation, they enter into concentration without wishing to engage in the formation of any conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and without desiring volitional thought; they simply form this thought:
"How may unarisen perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita*) not arise for a time, and how may arisen perception and feeling be temporarily extinguished?"
He enters meditative absorption without aspiring to formative activities (*saṃskāra*), without desiring volitional thought, but simply with this reflection:
"How might I cause unarisen perception and feeling not to arise for a time, and cause arisen perception and feeling to cease for a time?"

Therefore, according to one's aspiration, it is sometimes possible to cause thoughts and feelings that have not yet arisen not to arise for a time, and to cause those thoughts and feelings that have already arisen to temporarily cease; up to this point, it is called entering the meditative absorption of the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-vimokṣa-samādhi*).
The eighth refers to that which is counted as the eighth in the gradual, sequential, continuous, and successive order among the various meditative absorptions (*samādhi*).

As for "liberation" (*vimokṣa*), it refers to all liberations, distinct liberations, distinct supreme liberations, those already liberated, and those yet to be liberated within these meditative absorptions; this is called liberation.

Furthermore, if a phenomenon has subtle ideation as its cause and subtle ideation as its immediately preceding condition, because of the sense that ideation is not conjoined—yet not in the sense that it is not accomplished—this is called liberation.

Regarding the meditative absorption of the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha-vimokṣa-samādhi*): what is the cessation of perception and feeling? What is the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling? And what is the meditative absorption of the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling, such that it is called the "meditative absorption of the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling"?

Answer: Regarding the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*): it refers to the cessation, tranquility, and disappearance of perception and feeling; this is called the cessation of perception and feeling.

Regarding the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodhavimokṣa*): it refers to all liberations, distinct liberations, further distinct liberations, already liberated, and those yet to be liberated, which arise from the cessation of perception and feeling; this is called the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling.

The meditative absorption of the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling refers to the cessation of perception and feeling, as well as the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling; it is that which is realized by the body when it is not concealed, not turned away from, and is present with mastery—this is called the meditative absorption of the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling.
