Question:
What is the preparatory practice for the totality of space concentration?
By what means does a practitioner of meditation enter the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space?
Answer:

When a beginner first practices meditation, they focus upon the empty space above this world—whether it be the space above the ground, above trees, above cliffs, above mountains, or within rivers and valleys.

Taking any one of these signs of emptiness, through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), one binds the mind in contemplation and performs a conceptual observation, establishing a firm conviction that "this is the sign of such-and-such emptiness."

Because he relies on this through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) to bind his mindfulness and engage in conceptual reflection, imaginative observation, and established belief that "this is some kind of emptiness," his mind becomes distracted and flows toward various signs (*nimitta*); it cannot become one-pointed in binding its mindfulness to a single object, contemplating that "this object is empty and nothing else."

Because that mind is distracted and flows toward various signs, unable to focus one-pointedly on a single object by contemplating that this object is certainly empty, it has not yet been able to realize the meditative absorption of the sphere of totality of emptiness (*ākāśakṛtsnāyatana-samādhi*).

In order to collect the mind that is distracted, agitated, and wandering, one binds the mindfulness to contemplate a single characteristic of emptiness, thinking: "This is emptiness; it is not consciousness or other aggregates.

One contemplates this characteristic with diligent vigor until the mind remains in continuous succession for a long duration; through such preparatory application (*prayoga*), one is able to enter the meditative absorption of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).

Having diligently and repeatedly practiced this preliminary application (*prayoga*), one further advances in the cultivation of the means for this meditative concentration (*samādhi*); that is, one repeatedly practices, repeatedly cultivates, and repeatedly performs the path induced by that preliminary application.

Once the path induced by the preparatory application has been repeatedly practiced, repeatedly cultivated, and frequently performed, the mind then becomes settled, thoroughly settled, and closely settled; it proceeds in a continuous stream toward a single direction, binding mindfulness to a single object, contemplating that this very object is definitively characterized by emptiness.

Through the mind abiding, abiding closely, and abiding near, with a continuous flow directed toward a single object and mindfulness bound to a single focal point, one contemplates that this object is definitively characterized by emptiness; being non-dual and non-fluctuating, one is able to enter the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), yet has not yet realized the meditative attainment of the sphere of universal emptiness (*śūnyatā-kṛtsnāyatana-samāpatti*).
Question:
If one is as yet unable to enter the meditative absorption of the totality of space (*ākāśakṛtsnāyatana-samādhi*), what is the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) for this totality of space?
By what means does a practitioner of meditation (*yogin*) attain entry into the meditative absorption of the totality of space?
Answer:

Based on the very same concentration on emptiness entered as previously described, one causes the mind to become compliant, subdued, and directed toward it, gradually becoming pliant and universally pliant.

Once the mind has attained one-pointed concentration, one further visualizes this emptiness as gradually expanding and increasing, such that the east, south, west, and north are entirely filled with emptiness.

As he perceives this emptiness gradually expanding and widening—since the east, south, west, and north are entirely empty—the mind becomes distracted and scattered, racing toward various signs; it is unable to focus single-mindedly on a single object, contemplating that this entire environment is pervasively empty.

Because that mind is distracted and flows toward various signs, it cannot be focused one-pointedly on a single object; since it cannot contemplate that this object is entirely empty, it has not yet been able to realize the meditative absorption of the sphere of totality of emptiness (*ākāśakṛtsnāyatana-samādhi*).

In order to collect the mind that is distracted, agitated, and wandering, one binds the attention to the characteristic of universal emptiness and contemplates: "This is universally empty; it is not universally consciousness, and so forth.

One contemplates this characteristic with diligence and vigor until the mind remains in continuous succession for a long time; through such preparatory application (*prayoga*), one is gradually able to enter the meditative absorption of the sphere of universal emptiness (*ākāśakṛtsnāyatana-samādhi*).

Having diligently and repeatedly practiced this preliminary application (*prayoga*), one further advances in the cultivation of the means for this meditative concentration (*samādhi*), namely, by repeatedly practicing, repeatedly cultivating, and repeatedly performing the path induced by that preliminary application.

Once the path induced by the preparatory application has been repeatedly practiced, repeatedly cultivated, and frequently performed, the mind then becomes settled, well-settled, and closely settled; it proceeds in a continuous stream toward a single direction, with mindfulness bound to a single object, contemplating that this entire object is universally empty.

By means of the mind abiding, abiding closely, and abiding near—continuously directed toward a single course and bound to a single object—one contemplates that this entire object is empty, without duality or fluctuation; from this, one enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*).
"Up and down" refers to the upper and lower directions.
"Spreading sideways" refers to the southeast and so forth.
"Without duality" means being free from intermixture.
"Boundless and limitless" means that its limits are difficult to fathom.
"It is the ninth" means that among the various meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), it is the ninth when counted according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and orderly progression.

Regarding the term "totality" (kṛtsnāyatana): it refers to all wholesome form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness within this concentration of the sphere of infinite space; these are all called totalities.
Question:
What is the preparatory practice for the concentration of the totality of consciousness?
By what means does a practitioner of meditation enter the meditative absorption of the totality of consciousness (*vijñāna-kṛtsnāyatana*)?
Answer:

When a beginner first practices meditation, they take up within this body either the sign of pure visual consciousness, or the sign of pure auditory consciousness, or the sign of pure olfactory consciousness, or the sign of pure gustatory consciousness, or the sign of pure tactile consciousness, or the sign of pure mental consciousness.

Regarding these various consciousnesses, one takes up any single characteristic and, through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), binds the attention to it, contemplating and imaginatively observing it while establishing the conviction that "this is the characteristic of such-and-such a consciousness."

Because he, by means of the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), binds his mindfulness to conceptual reflection and imaginative observation, establishing the firm conviction that "this is a certain consciousness," his mind then becomes distracted and flows toward various signs; it cannot become one-pointed in binding its mindfulness to a single object, contemplating that this object is consciousness and nothing else.

Because his mind is distracted and flows toward various signs, unable to focus one-pointedly on a single object by contemplating that this object is certainly consciousness, he has not yet been able to realize the meditative absorption of the totality of consciousness (*vijñāna-kṛtsnāyatana-samādhi*).

In order to gather the mind that is distracted, agitated, and wandering, one binds mindfulness to a single characteristic of consciousness and reflects, thinking: "This is consciousness; it is not emptiness, nor anything else.

One reflects upon this characteristic with diligence and vigor until the mind remains in continuous succession for a long duration; through such preparatory application (*prayoga*), one is able to enter the meditative absorption of consciousness (*vijñāna-samādhi*).

Having diligently and repeatedly practiced this preliminary application (*prayoga*), one further advances in the cultivation of the means for this meditative concentration (*samādhi*); that is, one repeatedly practices, repeatedly cultivates, and repeatedly performs the path induced by that preliminary application.

Once the path induced by the preparatory application has been repeatedly practiced, repeatedly cultivated, and frequently performed, the mind then becomes settled, well-settled, and closely settled; it proceeds in a continuous stream toward a single direction, binding mindfulness to a single object, contemplating that this object is certainly the characteristic of consciousness.

Through the mind’s abiding, constant abiding, and close abiding, with a continuous flow directed toward a single object and mindfulness bound to that one sphere, he contemplates this object as being definitively the characteristic of consciousness. Being non-dual and unwavering, he is able to enter the meditative absorption of consciousness (*vijñāna-samādhi*), yet he is not yet able to enter the meditative absorption of the totality of consciousness (*vijñāna-kṛtsnāyatana-samādhi*).
Question:

If one is as yet unable to enter the meditative absorption of the totality of consciousness (*vijñāna-kṛtsnāyatana-samādhi*), what is the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) for this totality of consciousness?
By what means does a practitioner of meditation (*yogācāra*) succeed in realizing and entering the meditative absorption of the totality of consciousness?
Answer:

Based on the very same meditative absorption of consciousness entered as previously described, one causes the mind to become compliant, disciplined, and directed toward it, gradually becoming supple and universally supple.

Once the mind has attained one-pointed concentration, one further visualizes this consciousness gradually expanding and increasing until the east, south, west, and north are entirely filled with consciousness. Because one visualizes this consciousness gradually expanding and increasing so that the east, south, west, and north are all pervaded by consciousness, the mind then becomes distracted and scattered, flowing toward various signs; it can no longer remain one-pointedly focused on a single object, contemplating that this entire object is pervaded by consciousness.

That mind is distracted and flows toward various signs; unable to focus one-pointedly on a single object because it conceptualizes that object as being entirely consciousness, it has not yet been able to realize the meditative absorption of the totality of consciousness (*vijñāna-kṛtsnāyatana*).

In order to collect the mind that is distracted, agitated, and wandering, one fixes the attention and contemplates the characteristic of universal consciousness, thinking: "This all-pervasiveness is consciousness; it is not all-pervasive emptiness, etc.

One contemplates this characteristic with diligence and vigor until the mind remains in a continuous flow for a long duration; through such preparatory application, one is gradually able to enter the meditative absorption of the sphere of universal consciousness (*vijñāna-kṛtsnāyatana*).

Having diligently and repeatedly practiced this preliminary application (*prayoga*), one further advances to practice the skillful means (*upāya*) for this meditative concentration; that is, one repeatedly practices, repeatedly cultivates, and repeatedly performs the path induced by that preliminary application.

Having repeatedly practiced, repeatedly cultivated, and repeatedly performed the preparatory application, the mind then becomes settled, well-settled, and closely settled; it flows in a continuous stream toward a single direction, binding mindfulness to a single object, contemplating that this entire object is nothing but consciousness.

By means of the mind abiding, abiding closely, and abiding near—continuously directed toward a single object and bound to a single focal point—one contemplates that this entire object is consciousness, without duality or transition; from this, one enters the meditative absorption of the totality of consciousness (*vijñāna-kṛtsnāyatana-samādhi*).
"Up and down" refers to the upper and lower directions.
"Spreading sideways" refers to the southeast and so forth.
"Without duality" means being free from intermixture.
"Boundless and limitless" means that its limits are difficult to fathom.
"This is the tenth" means that among all the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), it is counted as the tenth according to their gradual, sequential, continuous, and successive order.

Regarding the term "totality" (kṛtsnāyatana): it refers to all wholesome feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness present within the meditative absorption of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness; these are all termed "totalities.
As for the ten qualities of one beyond training (daśa-aśaikṣa-dharmāḥ), what are the ten?
Answer:
First, right view of one beyond training;
second, right intention of one beyond training.
3. Right speech of one beyond training;
4. Right action of one beyond training;
5. Right livelihood of one beyond training;
Sixth, the right effort of one beyond training;
seventh, the right mindfulness of one beyond training;
eighth, the right concentration of one beyond training.
9. Right liberation of one beyond training;
10. Right knowledge of one beyond training.
What is right view of one beyond training?
Answer:

The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), as well as the wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) that is not included within the [knowledge of] exhaustion—this is called right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi*).
What is right thought of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyaksaṃkalpa*)?
Answer:

When the noble disciples contemplate suffering as suffering, origination as origination, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path; when they possess all contemplation, equal contemplation, and proximate contemplation associated with the mental attention of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); when they possess seeking, equal seeking, and proximate seeking; and when they possess investigation, equal investigation, and proximate investigation—which cause the mind to turn toward phenomena with coarse movement—this is called right thought of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyaksaṃkalpa*).
What is the right speech of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)? Answer:

When the noble disciples contemplate suffering as suffering, the origin as the origin, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path, by virtue of the power of discernment associated with the mental attention of one beyond training, they attain—apart from the four types of misconduct in speech that lead to wrong livelihood—the untrained state of abstention, superior abstention, proximate abstention, and ultimate abstention regarding other forms of verbal misconduct. This consists of tranquility, restraint, non-action, and non-creation; it is the relinquishment, protection, non-practice, and non-transgression [of such speech]. It is like a boat, raft, bridge, dam, embankment, wall, or moat; it is the non-manifesting vocal karma (*avijñapti-vāg-karman*) characterized by not overstepping and the nature of not overstepping, and not transgressing and the nature of not transgressing, regarding what has been prescribed as a restraint. This is called the right speech of one beyond training.
What is right action of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyak-karmānta*)? Answer:

It is when the noble disciples contemplate suffering as suffering, the origin as the origin, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path; through the power of discernment associated with the mental attention of one beyond training, they achieve—apart from the three bodily misdeeds that lead to wrong livelihood—a state of unlearned abstention, superior abstention, proximate abstention, and ultimate abstention regarding all other bodily misdeeds. This is a tranquil restraint, non-action, and non-creation; it is the relinquishing, guarding, non-performance, and non-transgression [of misconduct]. Like a boat, raft, bridge, embankment, wall, or moat, it is the non-transgressing nature and non-overstepping nature regarding what has been prescribed; it is the unmanifest bodily karma (*avijñapti-kāya-karman*). This is called right action of one beyond training.
What is right livelihood of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagājīva*)?
Answer:

When the noble disciples contemplate suffering as suffering, the origin as the origin, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path, they possess the power of discernment associated with the mental attention of one beyond training. Consequently, regarding the bodily and vocal misconduct that constitutes wrong livelihood, they attain the non-training state of detachment, superior detachment, proximate detachment, and ultimate detachment. This consists of the tranquil restraint, the state of non-action and non-creation, the relinquishment of protection, the non-practicing and non-transgressing of what is prohibited—like a boat, raft, bridge, embankment, wall, or moat—and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) bodily and vocal karma characterized by the nature of not overstepping and the nature of not transgressing those restraints; this is called right livelihood of one beyond training.
What is right effort of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyak-vyāyāma*)?
Answer:

When the noble disciples contemplate suffering as suffering, the origin as the origin, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path, there is a diligence, vigor, exertion, fortitude, intensity, fervor, and irresistible persistence of mind that is associated with the mental attention of one beyond training; this is called right effort of one beyond training.
What is right mindfulness of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
Answer:

When the noble disciples contemplate suffering as suffering, the origin as the origin, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path, there is the mindfulness, recollection, focused mindfulness, and memory associated with the mental attention of one beyond training; that which is non-forgetful, non-losing, non-neglecting, non-leaking, the non-loss of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and the mind’s quality of clear recollection—this is called right mindfulness of one beyond training.
What is the right concentration of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyak-samādhi*)?
Answer:

When the noble disciples contemplate suffering as suffering, the origin as the origin, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path, there is the state of mind associated with the mental attention of one beyond training—its abiding, its even abiding, its close abiding, and its firm abiding; its non-distraction, non-confusion, collectedness, and meditative equipoise (*samādhi*), which is one-pointedness of mind. This is called the right concentration of one beyond training.
What is the right liberation of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
Answer:

For the noble disciples who contemplate suffering as suffering, the origin as the origin, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path, all mental resolve, past resolve, and future resolve associated with the attention of one beyond training—this is called the right liberation of one beyond training.
What is the right knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-samyagjñāna)?
Answer:
The knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna); these are called the right knowledge of one beyond training.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the assembly of bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable ones, you should know that after the Buddha had attained manifest perfect enlightenment regarding one dharma up to ten dharmas, he proclaimed and revealed them to his disciples."

I, together with the great assembly, have all harmoniously united; having personally stood before the World-Honored One, we have completed the compilation. All bhikṣus should uphold it, expound it to others, and cause it to spread widely.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, do not allow any discord; you must ensure that the pure conduct and the Dharma-Vinaya endure for a long time, benefiting and bringing happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, and out of compassion for the world of gods and humans, enabling them to attain supreme benefit and peace.

Chapter Twelve: Encouragement through Praise. At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that Śāriputra had finished preaching the Dharma to the assembly of bhikṣus, rose from his reclining position with body and mind composed and refreshed. He adjusted his robes, sat down cross-legged, and praised Śāriputra:
“Excellent, excellent!
"You have now skillfully brought about harmony between yourself and this assembly of bhikṣus here in this pavilion to compile the Ekottarika-dharma-gate spoken by the Tathāgata.

From this day forward, you should repeatedly proclaim such a dharma-gate for the great assembly; this dharma can cause devas, humans, and others to realize its meaning, benefit, and peace for a long night."
The World-Honored One again addressed the assembly of bhikṣus, saying:
"You all should receive, uphold, read, and recite this 'Dharma-Gate of the Collection of Diverse Phenomena' spoken by Śāriputra.

Such a Dharma-gate can lead to great goodness, great benefit, the Great Dharma, and the pure, white Brahma-conduct; furthermore, it brings about the realization of supernormal knowledges, bodhi, and nirvāṇa."

“Sons of good family who have left the household life out of pure faith, if they receive, uphold, read, and recite such a Dharma-gate as this, they will before long certainly accomplish that which is to be accomplished.
When the Bhagavān had spoken these words, the assembly of bhikṣus rejoiced and leaped for joy; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and, with faith and acceptance, put his teachings into practice.
The Saṃgītiparyāya-pāda-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School, Volume Twenty.
